# Mean Shift in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

MeanShift detects high-density regions and infers cluster count automatically from data density.

This algorithm is especially useful when:

- You want clustering without specifying the number of clusters.
- Density peaks are more meaningful than centroid partitions.
- Your product needs adaptive grouping behavior over time.

## JavaScript implementation

@kanaries/ml gives JavaScript applications access to Mean Shift for cases where clusters form around dense modes rather than around a fixed, user-specified cluster count. That can be useful in browser-based exploratory tools where users want clustering without deciding `k` up front.

Because the implementation is available in JS, you can experiment with bandwidth-driven clustering directly inside Node.js services or interactive frontend tools.

## Interactive Mean Shift playground

Move the bandwidth control to change how local density peaks merge. The chart is recomputed with `Clusters.MeanShift` in your browser, and the diamonds show the modes found by the fitted model.

> The HTML version includes a live clustering playground powered by @kanaries/ml. You can change the dataset and algorithm parameters, add observations, and inspect fitted clusters, noise labels, centers, or exemplars. The runnable guide and API reference continue below. [Open the HTML page](https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/clusters/meanShift).

## Quick start

### MeanShift: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.cluster import MeanShift

X = [[0, 0], [0.1, 0.2], [3, 3], [3.2, 3.1]]

model = MeanShift(bandwidth=1.0)
labels = model.fit_predict(X)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Clusters } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [0.1, 0.2], [3, 3], [3.2, 3.1]];

const model = new Clusters.MeanShift({ bandwidth: 1.0 });
const labels = model.fitPredict(X);
```

### Quick JavaScript example

```ts
import { Clusters } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [0.1, 0.2], [3, 3], [3.2, 3.1]];

const model = new Clusters.MeanShift({ bandwidth: 1.0, max_iter: 300 });
const labels = model.fitPredict(X);
console.log({ labels, centroids: model.getCentroids() });
```

## Detailed API reference

```ts
new Clusters.MeanShift(props?: {
  bandwidth?: number;                  // default: 1
  max_iter?: number;                   // default: 300
  distanceType?: Distance.IDistanceType; // default: 'euclidean'
})
```

*(Legacy positional calls `new Clusters.MeanShift(bandwidth, max_iter, distanceType)` remain supported for backward compatibility, but prefer the options object.)*

Methods:

- `fitPredict(samplesX: number[][]): number[]`
- `getCentroids(): number[][]`

```ts
const ms = new Clusters.MeanShift({ bandwidth: 2 });
const labels = ms.fitPredict(X);
const centers = ms.getCentroids();
```

### Implementation workflow

1. Scale numeric features and choose bandwidth heuristics.
2. Fit and inspect discovered modes and assigned labels.
3. Tune bandwidth to balance over-fragmentation and over-merging.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Spend time tuning bandwidth because it strongly controls cluster granularity.
- Mean Shift is better suited to exploratory analysis than very large real-time workloads.
- For browser apps, prefer smaller datasets or background workers because iterative shifting can be expensive.

# OPTICS in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

OPTICS captures density-based cluster structure across multiple scales and handles varying-density datasets.

This algorithm is especially useful when:

- DBSCAN-style sensitivity to a single epsilon is too limiting.
- You need ordering information to inspect hierarchical density structure.
- Noise handling is required for reliable segmentation.

## JavaScript implementation

@kanaries/ml makes OPTICS available in JavaScript for density-based clustering workflows where cluster shapes are irregular and noise handling matters. This is useful for web-based data exploration products that need to surface structure without assuming spherical clusters.

Running OPTICS in the JS stack means engineering teams can keep clustering logic close to interactive visualizations, upload flows, or Node.js processing jobs instead of depending on a separate Python layer.

## Interactive OPTICS playground

Tune the reachability extraction radius and minimum neighborhood size. The labels below come from a live `Clusters.OPTICS` fit; click the plot to see whether a new observation joins a density-connected region.

> The HTML version includes a live clustering playground powered by @kanaries/ml. You can change the dataset and algorithm parameters, add observations, and inspect fitted clusters, noise labels, centers, or exemplars. The runnable guide and API reference continue below. [Open the HTML page](https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/clusters/optics).

## Quick start

### OPTICS: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.cluster import OPTICS

X = [[0, 0], [0.1, 0.1], [5, 5], [5.2, 5.1], [10, 1]]

model = OPTICS(min_samples=2, max_eps=0.6)
labels = model.fit_predict(X)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Clusters } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [0.1, 0.1], [5, 5], [5.2, 5.1], [10, 1]];

```

### Quick JavaScript example

```ts
import { Clusters } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [0.1, 0.1], [5, 5], [5.2, 5.1], [10, 1]];

const model = new Clusters.OPTICS({ min_samples: 2, eps: 0.6 });
const labels = model.fitPredict(X);
console.log(labels);
```

## Detailed API reference

```ts
interface OPTICSOptions {
    min_samples?: number;
    max_eps?: number;
    metric?: Distance.IDistanceType;
    p?: number;
    eps?: number;
}
constructor(options: OPTICSOptions = {})
```

`fitPredict(samplesX: number[][]): number[]` returns cluster labels. Noise points are marked as `-1`.

```ts
const optics = new Clusters.OPTICS({ eps: 0.6, min_samples: 2 });
const labels = optics.fitPredict(X);
```

### Implementation workflow

1. Prepare distance-scaled features and configure neighborhood constraints.
2. Fit and analyze reachability or extracted cluster labels.
3. Tune min-samples and extraction thresholds for your target behavior.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- OPTICS is a better fit than K-Means when your clusters have uneven density or non-convex structure.
- Use it for exploratory clustering and noise detection rather than low-latency request-time scoring.
- Benchmark runtime carefully on larger datasets, especially in browser environments.

# Transformed Target Regression in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

Regression targets in real applications—prices, session durations, order totals, exponential growth metrics—are often strictly positive and strongly right-skewed. Fitting ordinary least squares directly on raw skewed values lets a few extreme high targets dominate squared error and can even produce negative predictions.

**TransformedTargetRegressor** wraps any base regressor with an **invertible target transformation**: it transforms `y` (for example with `log1p`) before fitting the inner regressor, and automatically applies the exact inverse (`expm1`) inside `predict()` so outputs return cleanly in original business units—eliminating manual back-transformation bugs across training, cross-validation, and production serving.

## JavaScript implementation

`Compose.TransformedTargetRegressor` runs in pure TypeScript across browsers and Node.js. It clones both the base `regressor` and `transformer` before fitting, supports nested `regressor__param` and `transformer__param` addressing in `setParams()` (making it tunable inside `GridSearchCV`), and serializes cleanly via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md) when using named `FunctionTransformer` transforms (`'log1p'` / `'expm1'`, `'sqrt'` / `'square'`, scalers, etc.).

## Interactive transformed-target regression playground

Compare raw vs log-transformed targets on positive skewed data, or click to add observations directly to the chart. `Compose.TransformedTargetRegressor` handles forward transformation, fitting, and inverse prediction live in your browser.

> The HTML version includes an interactive Transformed-Target Regression playground powered by @kanaries/ml. You can change the dataset, noise, and model controls; add observations; and inspect live predictions plus train and holdout metrics. The runnable guide and API reference continue below. [Open the HTML page](https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/compose).

## Quick start

```ts
import { Compose, Linear, utils } from '@kanaries/ml';

const model = new Compose.TransformedTargetRegressor({
  regressor: new Linear.LinearRegression(),
  transformer: new utils.Preprocessing.FunctionTransformer({
    func: 'log1p',
    inverseFunc: 'expm1',
  }),
});

model.fit([[0], [1], [2]], [1, 3, 7]);
console.log(model.predict([[3]])); // approximately [15]
```

### TransformedTargetRegressor: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.compose import TransformedTargetRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

model = TransformedTargetRegressor(
  regressor=Ridge(alpha=1.0),
  func=np.log1p,
  inverse_func=np.expm1,
)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
preds = model.predict(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Compose, Linear, utils } from '@kanaries/ml';

const model = new Compose.TransformedTargetRegressor({
regressor: new Linear.RidgeRegression({ alpha: 1.0 }),
transformer: new utils.Preprocessing.FunctionTransformer({
  func: 'log1p',
  inverseFunc: 'expm1',
}),
});
model.fit(XTrain, yTrain);
const preds = model.predict(XTest);
```

## Detailed API reference

- **`new Compose.TransformedTargetRegressor({ regressor?, transformer?, func?, inverseFunc? })`** — defaults to `LinearRegression` and identity transform. Supply either `transformer` (recommended for JSON serialization) or a `func` / `inverseFunc` pair (mutually exclusive).
- **`fit(X, y)` / `predict(X)` / `score(X, y)`** — `score` computes R² in the **original untransformed** target space.
- **Related pages**: [ML Pipelines](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md), [Generalized Linear Models (Poisson/Gamma)](/docs/apis/linear/generalizedLinearModels.md), [Model Serialization](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

---
title: "Covariance & Graphical Lasso in JavaScript"
description: "Estimate empirical, shrunk, Ledoit-Wolf, OAS, and sparse GraphicalLasso precision matrices in JavaScript and TypeScript with @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/covariance/covarianceEstimators"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/covariance/covarianceEstimators.md"
---
# Covariance & Graphical Lasso in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

When estimating a `p × p` covariance matrix from `n` observations, the maximum-likelihood empirical covariance becomes noisy—or outright singular—whenever `p` is not tiny compared to `n`. **Shrinkage covariance** and **sparse inverse covariance** solve this conditioning problem in complementary ways:

- **`EmpiricalCovariance`**: standard maximum-likelihood covariance and precision matrix for clean datasets where `n >> p`.
- **`ShrunkCovariance`**: blends the empirical covariance toward a scaled identity matrix with a user-chosen `shrinkage` weight in `[0, 1]`.
- **`LedoitWolf`**: computes the analytically optimal L2 shrinkage weight minimizing expected Frobenius error without cross-validation.
- **`OAS` (Oracle Approximating Shrinkage)**: tightens Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage under Gaussian assumptions, often achieving lower estimation error when `p` is large relative to `n`.
- **`GraphicalLasso`**: adds an L1 penalty (`alpha`) to the **inverse covariance (precision) matrix** via block coordinate descent, driving weak partial correlations to zero to uncover sparse conditional-independence graphs.

## JavaScript implementation

All five estimators live under `import { Covariance } from '@kanaries/ml'` in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js applications. Every estimator exposes `location`, `covariance`, `precision`, and `mahalanobis(X)` distances, and serializes via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start

```ts
import { Covariance } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 1], [1, 0], [2, 1], [3, 2], [2, 3]];
const oas = new Covariance.OAS();
oas.fit(X);
console.log({
  shrinkage: oas.shrinkageValue,
  covariance: oas.covariance,
  mahalanobis: oas.mahalanobis([[1, 1]]),
});
```

### LedoitWolf, OAS & GraphicalLasso: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.covariance import LedoitWolf, OAS, GraphicalLasso

lw = LedoitWolf().fit(X)
oas = OAS().fit(X)
gl = GraphicalLasso(alpha=0.1, max_iter=100).fit(X)
sparse_precision = gl.precision_
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Covariance } from '@kanaries/ml';

const lw = new Covariance.LedoitWolf();
lw.fit(X);

const oas = new Covariance.OAS();
oas.fit(X);

const gl = new Covariance.GraphicalLasso({ alpha: 0.1, maxIter: 100 });
gl.fit(X);
const sparsePrecision = gl.precision;
```

## Detailed API reference

### Estimators & options

| Class                 | Options                                                                                                                     | Key properties                                          |
| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `EmpiricalCovariance` | `{ assumeCentered?: boolean }`                                                                                              | `location`, `covariance`, `precision`                   |
| `ShrunkCovariance`    | `{ shrinkage?: number (0.1), assumeCentered?: boolean }`                                                                    | `location`, `covariance`, `precision`                   |
| `LedoitWolf`          | `{ assumeCentered?: boolean }`                                                                                              | `location`, `covariance`, `precision`, `shrinkageValue` |
| `OAS`                 | `{ assumeCentered?: boolean }`                                                                                              | `location`, `covariance`, `precision`, `shrinkageValue` |
| `GraphicalLasso`      | `{ alpha?: number (0.01), maxIter?: number (100), tol?: number (1e-4), enetTol?: number (1e-4), assumeCentered?: boolean }` | `location`, `covariance`, `precision`, `nIter`          |

### Shared methods

- `fit(X: number[][]): void` — estimates mean (`location`), covariance, and inverse covariance (`precision`).
- `mahalanobis(X: number[][]): number[]` — computes squared Mahalanobis distances using `precision`.
- **Related pages**: [Robust Covariance Overview](/docs/apis/covariance/index.html.md), [MinCovDet (FAST-MCD)](/docs/apis/covariance/minCovDet.md), [Factor Analysis](/docs/apis/decomposition/factorAnalysis.md).

---
title: "EllipticEnvelope Anomaly Detection in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Detect multivariate outliers with robust Gaussian envelopes in JavaScript and TypeScript using Covariance.EllipticEnvelope from @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/covariance/ellipticEnvelope"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/covariance/ellipticEnvelope.md"
---
# EllipticEnvelope Anomaly Detection in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml

## Algorithm overview

**EllipticEnvelope** detects multivariate outliers by fitting a robust Gaussian distribution around the central inlier cloud via [FAST-MCD (`MinCovDet`)](/docs/apis/covariance/minCovDet.md) and flagging observations whose **robust Mahalanobis distance** exceeds a quantile threshold derived from `contamination`.

Unlike univariate z-score or IQR rules—which inspect one column at a time and miss points that look normal on every individual axis yet break feature correlations—`EllipticEnvelope` accounts for feature covariance and draws an elliptical boundary around normal behavior. It works best when clean data forms a roughly unimodal, elliptical Gaussian cloud.

## JavaScript implementation

`Covariance.EllipticEnvelope` wraps `MinCovDet` in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js runtimes. It follows scikit-learn's anomaly convention (`1` for inliers, `-1` for outliers), provides continuous anomaly scores (`scoreSamples`, `decisionFunction`), integrates into [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md), and serializes cleanly via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

*(Convention note: `EllipticEnvelope` returns `1` for normal and `-1` for outlier—matching scikit-learn and `LocalOutlierFactor`—whereas [`Ensemble.IsolationForest`](/docs/apis/ensemble/iforest.md) returns `0` for normal and `1` for anomaly.)*

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Covariance } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [0.1, 0.2], [0.2, 0.1], [-0.1, 0], [8, 8]];
const detector = new Covariance.EllipticEnvelope({
  contamination: 0.2,
  randomState: 42,
});
detector.fit(X);
console.log({
  labels: detector.predict(X),
  scores: detector.decisionFunction(X),
});
```

### EllipticEnvelope: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.covariance import EllipticEnvelope

detector = EllipticEnvelope(contamination=0.1, random_state=42)
detector.fit(X_train)
labels = detector.predict(X_test)      # 1 = inlier, -1 = outlier
scores = detector.decision_function(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Covariance } from '@kanaries/ml';

const detector = new Covariance.EllipticEnvelope({
contamination: 0.1,
randomState: 42,
});
detector.fit(XTrain);
const labels = detector.predict(XTest); // 1 = inlier, -1 = outlier
const scores = detector.decisionFunction(XTest);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Covariance.EllipticEnvelope(props?)`

| Parameter         | Type      | Default               | Description                                                                                               |
| ----------------- | --------- | --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `contamination`   | `number`  | `0.1`                 | Expected outlier proportion in `(0, 0.5]`, setting the `offset` cutoff on negative Mahalanobis distances. |
| `supportFraction` | `number`  | sklearn `h` heuristic | Fraction of points included in the raw MCD subset `(0, 1]`.                                               |
| `assumeCentered`  | `boolean` | `false`               | If `true`, skips location estimation and centers at zero.                                                 |
| `randomState`     | `number`  | `undefined`           | Seed for reproducible FAST-MCD elemental subsampling.                                                     |

### Methods & properties

- `fit(X)` — fits robust location, covariance, and `offset` threshold.
- `scoreSamples(X)` — returns negative squared robust Mahalanobis distances (higher = more normal).
- `decisionFunction(X)` — returns `scoreSamples(X) - offset` (`>= 0` inlier, `< 0` outlier).
- `predict(X)` — returns `1` for inliers and `-1` for outliers.
- Properties: `location`, `covariance`, `offset`.
- **Non-Gaussian or multimodal data?** Compare against [`Ensemble.IsolationForest`](/docs/apis/ensemble/iforest.md) and [`Neighbors.LocalOutlierFactor`](/docs/apis/neighbors/localOutlierFactor.md), or read our [Outlier Detection Methods Guide](/docs/guides/outlier-methods.md).

---
title: "Robust Covariance in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Estimate empirical, shrinkage, sparse Graphical Lasso, and robust FAST-MCD covariance matrices in JavaScript and TypeScript with @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/covariance"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/covariance/index.html.md"
---
# Robust Covariance in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml

## Module overview

A **covariance matrix** captures the pairwise variances and correlations among numeric features. Accurate covariance (and its inverse, the **precision matrix**) powers Mahalanobis distance calculations, multivariate outlier detection, Gaussian scoring, portfolio risk modeling, and conditional-independence graph discovery.

However, the sample covariance matrix breaks down in two common situations:

1. **Outliers contaminate the cloud**: a handful of corrupted rows can inflate variances and rotate eigenvectors away from the true inlier distribution—solved by robust estimators (`MinCovDet`, `EllipticEnvelope`).
2. **High dimensionality relative to sample size (`p` near or exceeding `n`)**: empirical covariance becomes ill-conditioned or singular—solved by shrinkage (`ShrunkCovariance`, `LedoitWolf`, `OAS`) or sparse inverse covariance (`GraphicalLasso`).

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides the complete scikit-learn `covariance` estimator family under `import { Covariance } from '@kanaries/ml'` in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js runtimes:

| Estimator                                                                         | Method                                 | Best for                                                  |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`Covariance.EmpiricalCovariance`](/docs/apis/covariance/covarianceEstimators.md) | Maximum-likelihood covariance          | Clean datasets where `n >> p`                             |
| [`Covariance.ShrunkCovariance`](/docs/apis/covariance/covarianceEstimators.md)    | Fixed shrinkage toward scaled identity | Manual regularization of noisy covariance                 |
| [`Covariance.LedoitWolf`](/docs/apis/covariance/covarianceEstimators.md)          | Analytical MSE-optimal shrinkage       | General-purpose well-conditioned covariance               |
| [`Covariance.OAS`](/docs/apis/covariance/covarianceEstimators.md)                 | Oracle Approximating Shrinkage         | Gaussian-like high-dimensional datasets                   |
| [`Covariance.GraphicalLasso`](/docs/apis/covariance/covarianceEstimators.md)      | L1-penalized sparse precision matrix   | Discovering sparse conditional independence graphs        |
| [`Covariance.MinCovDet`](/docs/apis/covariance/minCovDet.md)                      | FAST-MCD robust location & scatter     | Robust Mahalanobis distances with outlier resistance      |
| [`Covariance.EllipticEnvelope`](/docs/apis/covariance/ellipticEnvelope.md)        | Robust Gaussian anomaly detector       | Flagging multivariate outliers (`1` inlier, `-1` outlier) |

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Covariance } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [0.1, 0.2], [0.2, 0.1], [-0.1, 0], [8, 8]];
const detector = new Covariance.EllipticEnvelope({ contamination: 0.2, randomState: 42 });
detector.fit(X);
console.log(detector.predict(X)); // [1, 1, 1, 1, -1]
```

## Choosing the right covariance estimator

- Need **multivariate outlier detection** on roughly elliptical data? Start with [`EllipticEnvelope`](/docs/apis/covariance/ellipticEnvelope.md) (or compare with [`IsolationForest`](/docs/apis/ensemble/iforest.md) and [`LocalOutlierFactor`](/docs/apis/neighbors/localOutlierFactor.md) in our [outlier methods guide](/docs/guides/outlier-methods.md)).
- Need **robust location, scatter, or Mahalanobis distances** without hard thresholding? Use [`MinCovDet`](/docs/apis/covariance/minCovDet.md).
- Need **well-conditioned covariance or sparse precision** for downstream modeling? Use [`LedoitWolf`, `OAS`, or `GraphicalLasso`](/docs/apis/covariance/covarianceEstimators.md).

<!-- Source: https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/covariance/minCovDet -->

---
title: "MinCovDet (FAST-MCD) in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Estimate outlier-resistant multivariate location, covariance, and Mahalanobis distances in JavaScript and TypeScript with MinCovDet from @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/covariance/minCovDet"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/covariance/minCovDet.md"
---
# MinCovDet (FAST-MCD) in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml

## Algorithm overview

Classical sample mean and covariance have a breakdown point of zero: a single extreme outlier can drag the mean and stretch the covariance matrix arbitrarily far. **Minimum Covariance Determinant (`MinCovDet`)** finds the subset of `h` observations (at least half the dataset) whose empirical covariance matrix has the **smallest determinant**, yielding a high-breakdown robust estimate of multivariate center (`location`) and spread (`covariance`).

`@kanaries/ml` implements the **FAST-MCD** algorithm (Rousseeuw & Van Driessen): random elemental starts, iterative concentration steps (C-steps) that monotonically reduce the determinant, Gaussian consistency scaling, and chi-square distance reweighting (`support`) to recover high statistical efficiency without sacrificing outlier resistance.

## JavaScript implementation

`Covariance.MinCovDet` runs entirely in pure TypeScript across browsers and Node.js—powering both direct robust Mahalanobis scoring and [`Covariance.EllipticEnvelope`](/docs/apis/covariance/ellipticEnvelope.md). Because FAST-MCD performs repeated `p × p` covariance inversions across C-steps, it is best suited for small-to-moderate feature widths (`p ≤ 30`) and tabular browser datasets; for large jobs, run inside a Web Worker. Fitted models serialize via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Covariance } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [0.1, 0.2], [0.2, 0.1], [-0.1, 0], [8, 8]];
const robust = new Covariance.MinCovDet({ supportFraction: 0.8, randomState: 42 });
robust.fit(X);

console.log({
  location: robust.location,
  support: robust.support,
  mahalanobis: robust.mahalanobis(X),
});
```

### MinCovDet (FAST-MCD): Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.covariance import MinCovDet

mcd = MinCovDet(support_fraction=0.8, random_state=42)
mcd.fit(X)
dist_sq = mcd.mahalanobis(X)
inliers = mcd.support_
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Covariance } from '@kanaries/ml';

const mcd = new Covariance.MinCovDet({
supportFraction: 0.8,
randomState: 42,
});
mcd.fit(X);
const distSq = mcd.mahalanobis(X);
const inliers = mcd.support;
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Covariance.MinCovDet(props?)`

| Parameter         | Type      | Default              | Description                                                                                                                     |
| ----------------- | --------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `supportFraction` | `number`  | `(n + p + 1) / (2n)` | Proportion of samples in `(0, 1]` used in the raw MCD subset. Lower values tolerate higher outlier contamination (up to \~50%). |
| `assumeCentered`  | `boolean` | `false`              | If `true`, assumes data is already centered at the origin and estimates scatter only.                                           |
| `randomState`     | `number`  | `undefined`          | Seed for reproducible elemental subsampling.                                                                                    |

### Methods & properties

- `fit(X: number[][]): void` — computes raw FAST-MCD and chi-square reweighted estimates.
- `mahalanobis(X: number[][]): number[]` — returns squared robust Mahalanobis distances `(x - μ)ᵀ Σ⁻¹ (x - μ)`.
- Reweighted properties: `location`, `covariance`, `precision`, `support` (boolean inlier mask).
- Raw pre-reweighting properties: `rawLocation`, `rawCovariance`, `rawSupport`.
- **Related pages**: [EllipticEnvelope](/docs/apis/covariance/ellipticEnvelope.md), [Covariance Estimators](/docs/apis/covariance/covarianceEstimators.md), [Robust Regression](/docs/apis/linear/robustRegressors.md).

---
title: "PLS Regression and CCA in JavaScript"
description: "Model paired multivariate feature and target blocks in JavaScript and TypeScript with CrossDecomposition.PLSRegression and CCA from @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/cross_decomposition"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/cross_decomposition/index.html.md"
---
# PLS Regression and CCA in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

When a dataset has many strongly collinear predictors (`X`)—or even more columns than samples—and multiple correlated targets (`Y`), ordinary least squares becomes ill-conditioned while unsupervised [PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/pca.md) can discard low-variance directions that actually predict `Y`. **Cross Decomposition** finds paired latent projections of both `X` and `Y` simultaneously:

- **`PLSRegression` (Partial Least Squares)**: extracts latent components maximizing **covariance** between `X` scores and `Y` scores via mode-A NIPALS with regression deflation—a staple in chemometrics, spectroscopy, and wide multi-output tabular forecasting.
- **`CCA` (Canonical Correlation Analysis)**: extracts latent projections maximizing **correlation** between `X` and `Y` via mode-B weights with canonical deflation—ideal for multi-view alignment (comparing two paired sensor arrays or behavioral feature blocks).

## JavaScript implementation

`CrossDecomposition.PLSRegression` and `CrossDecomposition.CCA` run in pure TypeScript across browsers and Node.js, support both `transform()` (latent score extraction) and `predict()` (multi-target prediction), compose inside [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md), and serialize via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Interactive PLS regression playground

Adjust the number of latent components (`nComponents`) and dataset noise below. A live multi-output `CrossDecomposition.PLSRegression` fits in your browser and plots holdout accuracy and fitted curve updates immediately.

> The HTML version includes an interactive PLS Regression playground powered by @kanaries/ml. You can change the dataset, noise, and model controls; add observations; and inspect live predictions plus train and holdout metrics. The runnable guide and API reference continue below. [Open the HTML page](https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/cross_decomposition).

## Quick start

```ts
import { CrossDecomposition } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 5]];
const Y = [[1], [2], [4], [7]];
const model = new CrossDecomposition.PLSRegression({ nComponents: 2 });
model.fit(X, Y);
console.log(model.predict([[4, 6]]));
```

### PLSRegression & CCA: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.cross_decomposition import PLSRegression, CCA

pls = PLSRegression(n_components=2).fit(X_train, Y_train)
Y_pred = pls.predict(X_test)

cca = CCA(n_components=2).fit(X_view1, Y_view2)
X_c, Y_c = cca.transform(X_view1, Y_view2)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { CrossDecomposition } from '@kanaries/ml';

const pls = new CrossDecomposition.PLSRegression({ nComponents: 2 });
pls.fit(XTrain, YTrain);
const YPred = pls.predict(XTest);

const cca = new CrossDecomposition.CCA({ nComponents: 2 });
cca.fit(XView1, YView2);
const scores = cca.transform(XView1, YView2);
```

## Detailed API reference

| Option            | Default        | Description                                                                                        |
| ----------------- | -------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nComponents`     | `2`            | Number of latent cross-decomposition components (at most `min(nSamples, nFeaturesX, nFeaturesY)`). |
| `scale`           | `true`         | Standardize `X` and `Y` internally before NIPALS iterations.                                       |
| `maxIter` / `tol` | `500` / `1e-6` | NIPALS iteration cap and convergence tolerance.                                                    |

Both estimators expose `fit(X, Y)`, `transform(X, Y?)`, `predict(X)`, plus fitted `xWeights`, `yWeights`, `xLoadings`, `yLoadings`, `xRotations`, `yRotations`, `coef`, and `nIter`.

- **Related pages**: [PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/pca.md), [Ridge Regression](/docs/apis/linear/ridgeRegression.md), [RegressorChain](/docs/apis/multioutput/regressorChain.md).

<!-- Source: https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/data -->

---
title: "CSRMatrix Sparse Matrices in JS"
description: "Represent high-dimensional sparse text and tabular features efficiently in JavaScript and TypeScript with CSRMatrix from @kanaries/ml for browser and Node.js."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/data"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/data/index.html.md"
---
# CSRMatrix Sparse Matrices in JS

## Algorithm overview

Text vectorizers ([`CountVectorizer`](/docs/apis/feature_extraction/countVectorizer.md), [`TfidfVectorizer`](/docs/apis/feature_extraction/tfidfVectorizer.md), [`HashingVectorizer`](/docs/apis/feature_extraction/hashingAndDictionaries.md)) and one-hot encoded categorical tables frequently contain 95%–99.9% zeros. Storing a 10,000-document × 20,000-term matrix as a dense JavaScript `number[][]` wastes gigabytes of heap memory and triggers heavy garbage collection in browsers and Node.js.

A **Compressed Sparse Row matrix (`CSRMatrix`)** stores only non-zero entries across three compact flat arrays:

- `data`: the non-zero numeric values, grouped row by row.
- `indices`: the strictly increasing column index for each value in `data`.
- `indptr`: length `nRows + 1` row-pointer array where row `r` occupies slice `[indptr[r], indptr[r + 1])`.

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` exports `CSRMatrix` at both the top level (`import { CSRMatrix } from '@kanaries/ml'`) and under `Data` (`import { Data } from '@kanaries/ml'`), along with matrix helper utilities (`isCSRMatrix`, `matrixShape`, `matrixRow`, `forEachNonZeroInRow`).

`CSRMatrix` validates structural invariants at construction (non-negative dimensions, strictly increasing column indices per row, no explicit zeros), returns defensive copies on array getters to prevent accidental corruption, flows directly between sparse-aware steps inside [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md), and is registered with the serialization engine so models storing sparse state work seamlessly with `toJSON()` and [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start example

### CSRMatrix vs scipy.sparse.csr_matrix: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from scipy.sparse import csr_matrix
import numpy as np

dense = np.array([
  [0, 2, 0],
  [3, 0, 1],
  [0, 0, 0],
])
csr = csr_matrix(dense)
print(csr.shape, csr.nnz, csr[1, 2])
back_to_dense = csr.toarray()
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { CSRMatrix, Data } from '@kanaries/ml';

const csr = CSRMatrix.fromDense([
[0, 2, 0],
[3, 0, 1],
[0, 0, 0],
]);

console.log(csr.shape); // [3, 3]
console.log(csr.nnz);   // 3
console.log(csr.get(1, 2)); // 1

// Iterate non-zeros in row 1 without allocating a dense row
csr.forEachNonZeroInRow(1, (col, val) => {
console.log({ col, val });
});

const subset = csr.selectRows([1, 0]);
const dense = Data.isCSRMatrix(subset) ? subset.toDense() : subset;
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new CSRMatrix(data, indices, indptr, shape)`

| Parameter | Type               | Description                                                                                                      |
| --------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `data`    | `number[]`         | Non-zero values (explicit `0` entries throw an error).                                                           |
| `indices` | `number[]`         | Column index for each entry in `data`, strictly increasing within every row and bounded in `[0, nCols)`.         |
| `indptr`  | `number[]`         | Non-decreasing integer offsets of length `nRows + 1` with `indptr[0] === 0` and `indptr[nRows] === data.length`. |
| `shape`   | `[number, number]` | `[nRows, nCols]` non-negative integer dimensions.                                                                |

### Static constructors, properties & methods

| Member                              | Signature                                                       | Description                                                                                              |
| ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `CSRMatrix.fromDense`               | `(matrix: number[][]) => CSRMatrix`                             | Builds a `CSRMatrix` from a rectangular dense 2D array, skipping all zeros.                              |
| `shape` / `nRows` / `nCols` / `nnz` | `[number, number]` / `number`                                   | Dimensions and count of stored non-zero entries.                                                         |
| `data` / `indices` / `indptr`       | `readonly number[]`                                             | Defensive copies of the three CSR backing arrays.                                                        |
| `get`                               | `(row: number, column: number) => number`                       | Binary-searches row `row` in `O(log nnz_row)` time; returns `0` if absent.                               |
| `row`                               | `(row: number) => number[]`                                     | Materializes a single row as a dense `number[]` of length `nCols`.                                       |
| `forEachNonZeroInRow`               | `(row: number, cb: (col: number, val: number) => void) => void` | Zero-allocation iteration over non-zero entries in `row`.                                                |
| `selectRows`                        | `(rows: number[]) => CSRMatrix`                                 | Slices arbitrary row indices into a new `CSRMatrix` (ideal for train/test splits and k-fold CV).         |
| `toDense`                           | `() => number[][]`                                              | Converts the entire sparse matrix to a dense 2D array (use cautiously on high-dimensional vocabularies). |

### Polymorphic `Data` helpers

For code that accepts `NumericMatrix = number[][] | CSRMatrix`:

- `Data.isCSRMatrix(value)` — TypeScript type guard checking `value instanceof CSRMatrix`.
- `Data.matrixShape(X)` — returns `[nRows, nCols]` for either dense or CSR input.
- `Data.matrixRow(X, row)` — returns row `row` as a dense `number[]`.
- `Data.forEachNonZeroInRow(X, row, cb)` — iterates non-zero `(column, value)` pairs uniformly across dense and CSR matrices.
- **Related pages**: [Feature Extraction (TF-IDF & CountVectorizer)](/docs/apis/feature_extraction/index.html.md), [ML Pipelines](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md), [Model Serialization](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

---
title: "Synthetic ML Datasets in JavaScript"
description: "Generate reproducible synthetic datasets (makeBlobs, makeMoons, makeCircles, makeClassification, makeRegression) in JavaScript and TypeScript with @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/datasets"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/datasets/index.html.md"
---
# Synthetic ML Datasets in JavaScript

## Module overview

Testing machine learning pipelines, benchmarking clustering speed in browsers, building interactive visualizations, and writing deterministic unit tests all require controlled data with known ground-truth structure.

The **`Datasets`** module provides pure-JavaScript ports of scikit-learn's synthetic dataset generators—allowing you to create isotropic Gaussian clusters, interleaving moons, concentric circles, multi-class tabular benchmarks with informative/redundant/noise features, and linear or low-rank regression problems with exact seeded reproducibility (`randomState`).

## JavaScript implementation

Import synthetic generators from `import { Datasets } from '@kanaries/ml'`. Every generator uses a deterministic PRNG and Box-Muller Gaussian sampling, producing plain `number[][]` feature matrices and `number[]` label/target vectors directly usable by every `@kanaries/ml` estimator in browser and Node.js environments—with zero external data downloads.

| Generator                     | sklearn equivalent     | Primary use case                                                                      |
| ----------------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Datasets.makeBlobs`          | `make_blobs`           | Isotropic Gaussian clusters for K-Means, GMM, HDBSCAN                                 |
| `Datasets.makeMoons`          | `make_moons`           | Two non-linear interleaving half-circles for DBSCAN, kernel SVM, kNN                  |
| `Datasets.makeCircles`        | `make_circles`         | Concentric circles for radial/kernel classifiers and spectral clustering              |
| `Datasets.makeClassification` | `make_classification`  | Configurable multi-class tabular problems with noise, redundancy, and class imbalance |
| `Datasets.makeRegression`     | `make_regression`      | Controlled linear or low-rank regression with optional ground-truth `coef`            |
| `Datasets.makeLowRankMatrix`  | `make_low_rank_matrix` | Matrices with bell-shaped singular value profiles for PCA/SVD benchmarks              |

## Quick start example

### Synthetic Dataset Generators: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs, make_moons, make_classification, make_regression

X_blobs, y_blobs = make_blobs(n_samples=200, centers=3, cluster_std=0.8, random_state=42)
X_moons, y_moons = make_moons(n_samples=200, noise=0.08, random_state=42)
X_cls, y_cls = make_classification(n_samples=300, n_features=10, n_informative=4, random_state=42)
X_reg, y_reg, coef = make_regression(n_samples=200, n_features=8, noise=5.0, coef=True, random_state=42)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Datasets } from '@kanaries/ml';

const blobs = Datasets.makeBlobs({ nSamples: 200, centers: 3, clusterStd: 0.8, randomState: 42 });
const moons = Datasets.makeMoons({ nSamples: 200, noise: 0.08, randomState: 42 });
const cls = Datasets.makeClassification({ nSamples: 300, nFeatures: 10, nInformative: 4, randomState: 42 });
const reg = Datasets.makeRegression({ nSamples: 200, nFeatures: 8, noise: 5.0, coef: true, randomState: 42 });

// Access { X, y } (plus reg.coef when coef: true)
console.log(blobs.X.length, moons.y.length, reg.coef);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `Datasets.makeBlobs(props?)` → `{ X: number[][], y: number[] }`

| Option                    | Type                   | Default              | Description                                                                                   |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------- | -------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nSamples`                | `number \| number[]`   | `100`                | Total sample count or explicit per-cluster counts.                                            |
| `nFeatures`               | `number`               | `2`                  | Feature width (inferred if explicit `centers` coordinates are passed).                        |
| `centers`                 | `number \| number[][]` | `3`                  | Number of random centers inside `centerBox`, or explicit `[nCenters][nFeatures]` coordinates. |
| `clusterStd`              | `number \| number[]`   | `1`                  | Cluster standard deviation (single number or per-cluster array).                              |
| `centerBox`               | `[number, number]`     | `[-10, 10]`          | Coordinate bounds for randomly placed centers.                                                |
| `shuffle` / `randomState` | `boolean` / `number`   | `true` / `undefined` | Shuffle rows and control reproducibility.                                                     |

### `Datasets.makeMoons(props?)` & `Datasets.makeCircles(props?)` → `{ X, y }`

- `nSamples`: total count or `[nOuter, nInner]` (default `100`).
- `noise`: Gaussian standard deviation added to coordinates.
- `factor` (`makeCircles` only): inner-to-outer radius scale in `[0, 1)` (default `0.8`).
- `shuffle` (default `true`) and `randomState`.

### `Datasets.makeClassification(props?)` → `{ X, y }`

Supports `nSamples` (`100`), `nFeatures` (`20`), `nInformative` (`2`), `nRedundant` (`2`), `nRepeated` (`0`), `nClasses` (`2`), `nClustersPerClass` (`2`), `weights` (class proportions), `flipY` (`0.01` label noise), `classSep` (`1`), `hypercube` (`true`), `shift` (`0` or `null` for random), `scale` (`1` or `null` for random), `shuffle` (`true`), and `randomState`.

### `Datasets.makeRegression(props?)` → `{ X, y, coef? }`

Supports `nSamples` (`100`), `nFeatures` (`100`), `nInformative` (`min(nFeatures, 10)`), `nTargets` (`1`), `bias` (`0`), `effectiveRank` (switches to low-rank singular-value matrix via `makeLowRankMatrix`), `tailStrength` (`0.5`), `noise` (`0`), `shuffle` (`true`), `coef` (`false` — set `true` to return ground-truth coefficients), and `randomState`.

### Related pages

- [Clustering Playgrounds](/playground/kmeans), [Model Selection & Cross-Validation](/docs/apis/utils/modelSelection.md), [Dummy Baselines](/docs/apis/dummy/index.html.md).

---
title: "Factor Analysis in JavaScript and TypeScript"
description: "Fit Gaussian latent factor models with per-feature noise variance and varimax rotation in JavaScript and TypeScript using FactorAnalysis from @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/factorAnalysis"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/factorAnalysis.md"
---
# Factor Analysis in JavaScript and TypeScript

## Algorithm overview

**Factor Analysis** is a probabilistic generative model that explains correlations among observed numeric variables using a smaller set of shared latent factors (`nComponents`) plus **independent per-feature noise variance** (`noiseVariance`).

Whereas [PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/pca.md) assumes isotropic (equal) noise across every column and simply maximizes total variance—including noisy columns—Factor Analysis explicitly models heteroscedastic measurement noise (`Ψ = diag(noiseVariance)`). That makes Factor Analysis invariant to individual feature rescaling and well suited for psychometrics, survey analytics, financial factor modeling, and multi-sensor telemetry where each instrument carries a different noise floor.

## JavaScript implementation

`Decomposition.FactorAnalysis` in `@kanaries/ml` implements scikit-learn's EM/SVD log-likelihood optimization in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js runtimes. It supports optional orthogonal **`'varimax'`** and **`'quartimax'`** factor rotations to produce sparser, easier-to-interpret factor loadings, exposes full model covariance/precision matrices (`getCovariance()`, `getPrecision()`), and serializes cleanly via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start

```ts
import { Decomposition } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[1, 2, 1], [2, 4, 1], [3, 6, 2], [4, 8, 2]];
const model = new Decomposition.FactorAnalysis({ nComponents: 2 });
const scores = model.fitTransform(X);
console.log({ scores, noiseVariance: model.noiseVariance });
```

### FactorAnalysis: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.decomposition import FactorAnalysis

fa = FactorAnalysis(n_components=2, rotation="varimax", max_iter=1000)
scores = fa.fit_transform(X)
loadings = fa.components_
noise = fa.noise_variance_
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Decomposition } from '@kanaries/ml';

const fa = new Decomposition.FactorAnalysis({
nComponents: 2,
rotation: 'varimax',
maxIter: 1000,
});
const scores = fa.fitTransform(X);
const loadings = fa.components;
const noise = fa.noiseVariance;
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Decomposition.FactorAnalysis(props?)`

| Parameter           | Type                               | Default     | Description                                                                                                     |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nComponents`       | `number`                           | `nFeatures` | Number of latent factors to extract.                                                                            |
| `tol`               | `number`                           | `1e-2`      | Stopping threshold on log-likelihood gain between EM iterations.                                                |
| `maxIter`           | `number`                           | `1000`      | Maximum EM iterations.                                                                                          |
| `noiseVarianceInit` | `number[]`                         | all ones    | Optional initial per-feature noise variances (length `nFeatures`).                                              |
| `rotation`          | `'varimax' \| 'quartimax' \| null` | `null`      | Post-fit orthogonal rotation (`'varimax'` simplifies columns/factors; `'quartimax'` simplifies rows/variables). |

### Methods & properties

- `fit(X)` / `transform(X)` / `fitTransform(X)` — fit latent factors and compute posterior expected factor scores.
- `getCovariance()` / `getPrecision()` — returns the model-implied `WᵀW + Ψ` covariance matrix and its inverse.
- Fitted properties: `components` (`[nComponents][nFeatures]`), `mean`, `noiseVariance`, `loglike` (trace of log-likelihoods), and `nIter`.
- **Related pages**: [PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/pca.md), [FastICA](/docs/apis/decomposition/fastICA.md), [Covariance Estimators](/docs/apis/covariance/covarianceEstimators.md).

---

<!-- Source: https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/fastICA -->

---
title: "FastICA in JavaScript and TypeScript"
description: "Separate independent mixed signals and extract non-Gaussian components in JavaScript and TypeScript with Decomposition.FastICA from @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/fastICA"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/fastICA.md"
---
# FastICA in JavaScript and TypeScript

## Algorithm overview

**Independent Component Analysis (FastICA)** separates a multivariate dataset into additive, **statistically independent** latent sources by maximizing non-Gaussianity (approximated via negentropy contrast functions such as `logcosh`, `exp`, or `cube`).

Whereas [PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/pca.md) only produces *uncorrelated* orthogonal directions based on second-order covariance, FastICA leverages higher-order statistics to untangle mixed signals—famous for the "cocktail party problem" (separating overlapping audio recordings), removing eye-blink artifacts from EEG/sensor streams, or uncovering independent drivers in multivariate financial and telemetry series.

## JavaScript implementation

`Decomposition.FastICA` in `@kanaries/ml` provides both `'parallel'` (symmetric) and `'deflation'` fixed-point updates in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js runtimes, with configurable whitening modes (`'unit-variance'`, `'arbitrary-variance'`, or `false`), deterministic `randomState` initialization, forward `transform()`, signal reconstruction via `inverseTransform()`, and JSON serialization (`toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md)).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Decomposition } from '@kanaries/ml';

const observedSignals = [[0, 1], [1, 0], [2, 1], [1, 2], [-1, 0]];
const ica = new Decomposition.FastICA({
  nComponents: 2,
  whiten: 'unit-variance',
  randomState: 0,
});
const sources = ica.fitTransform(observedSignals);
const reconstructed = ica.inverseTransform(sources);
console.log({ sources, reconstructed });
```

### FastICA: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.decomposition import FastICA

ica = FastICA(
  n_components=2,
  algorithm="parallel",
  whiten="unit-variance",
  fun="logcosh",
  random_state=0,
)
sources = ica.fit_transform(X)
reconstructed = ica.inverse_transform(sources)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Decomposition } from '@kanaries/ml';

const ica = new Decomposition.FastICA({
nComponents: 2,
algorithm: 'parallel',
whiten: 'unit-variance',
fun: 'logcosh',
randomState: 0,
});
const sources = ica.fitTransform(X);
const reconstructed = ica.inverseTransform(sources);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Decomposition.FastICA(props?)`

| Parameter         | Type                                               | Default           | Description                                                                                                                      |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nComponents`     | `number`                                           | `nFeatures`       | Number of independent sources to extract (ignored when `whiten: false`, matching scikit-learn).                                  |
| `algorithm`       | `'parallel' \| 'deflation'`                        | `'parallel'`      | `'parallel'` estimates all components simultaneously; `'deflation'` extracts components one by one.                              |
| `whiten`          | `'unit-variance' \| 'arbitrary-variance' \| false` | `'unit-variance'` | Centers and decorrelates data via PCA whitening before unmixing (`false` assumes input is already whitened and skips centering). |
| `fun`             | `'logcosh' \| 'exp' \| 'cube'`                     | `'logcosh'`       | Negentropy contrast nonlinearity (`'logcosh'` is robust general-purpose; `'exp'` works well for super-Gaussian signals).         |
| `funArgs`         | `{ alpha?: number }`                               | `{ alpha: 1.0 }`  | Parameter `alpha` in `[1, 2]` for `'logcosh'`.                                                                                   |
| `maxIter` / `tol` | `number`                                           | `200` / `1e-4`    | Fixed-point convergence budget and tolerance.                                                                                    |
| `randomState`     | `number`                                           | `undefined`       | Seed for initial unmixing matrix.                                                                                                |

### Methods & properties

- `fit(X)` / `transform(X)` / `fitTransform(X)` / `inverseTransform(S)` — unmix signals and reconstruct observations.
- Learned fields: `components` (unmixing matrix), `mixing` (pseudo-inverse mixing matrix), `mean`, and `nIter`.
- **Related pages**: [PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/pca.md), [Factor Analysis](/docs/apis/decomposition/factorAnalysis.md), [NMF](/docs/apis/decomposition/nmf.md).

---
title: "Incremental PCA in JavaScript and TypeScript"
description: "Run streaming out-of-core PCA one batch at a time in JavaScript and TypeScript with IncrementalPCA from @kanaries/ml for memory-aware browser and Node.js apps."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/incrementalPCA"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/incrementalPCA.md"
---
# Incremental PCA in JavaScript and TypeScript

## Algorithm overview

Standard [PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/pca.md) loads the entire centered feature matrix into memory at once to compute its singular value decomposition. When processing large CSV uploads in a browser tab, streaming telemetry chunks in Node.js, or running inside memory-capped serverless functions, holding every row simultaneously can exhaust heap limits.

**Incremental PCA** updates a mean-corrected low-rank SVD **one mini-batch at a time** via `partialFit()`, maintaining constant memory proportional to `batchSize × nFeatures` rather than total dataset size. Once all batches have been seen, it supports the exact same `transform()` and `inverseTransform()` projections as batch PCA.

## JavaScript implementation

`Decomposition.IncrementalPCA` in `@kanaries/ml` implements Ross et al.'s mean-corrected incremental SVD update (matching `sklearn.decomposition.IncrementalPCA`) in pure TypeScript. You can stream arbitrary chunks manually with chained `partialFit(batch)` calls, or pass a full matrix to `fit(X)` and let `batchSize` chunk it automatically. Fitted models serialize via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Decomposition } from '@kanaries/ml';

const batchOne = [[0, 1, 2], [1, 2, 3], [2, 1, 4]];
const batchTwo = [[3, 4, 2], [4, 3, 1], [5, 5, 0]];
const nextBatch = [[2, 3, 2]];

const pca = new Decomposition.IncrementalPCA({ nComponents: 2 });
pca.partialFit(batchOne).partialFit(batchTwo);
const embedding = pca.transform(nextBatch);
console.log({ embedding, seen: pca.nSamplesSeen });
```

### IncrementalPCA: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.decomposition import IncrementalPCA

ipca = IncrementalPCA(n_components=2, batch_size=256)
ipca.partial_fit(batch_one)
ipca.partial_fit(batch_two)
embedding = ipca.transform(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Decomposition } from '@kanaries/ml';

const ipca = new Decomposition.IncrementalPCA({
nComponents: 2,
batchSize: 256,
});
ipca.partialFit(batchOne).partialFit(batchTwo);
const embedding = ipca.transform(XTest);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Decomposition.IncrementalPCA(props?)`

| Parameter     | Type             | Default                              | Description                                                   |
| ------------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nComponents` | `number \| null` | `null` (`min(batchSize, nFeatures)`) | Number of principal components retained across batches.       |
| `batchSize`   | `number`         | `5 * nFeatures`                      | Chunk size used when calling `fit(X)` on an in-memory matrix. |

### Methods & properties

| Member                                                                          | Signature                       | Description                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `partialFit`                                                                    | `(X: number[][]) => this`       | Updates the running mean, sample count, and low-rank SVD with a new batch (chainable).            |
| `fit`                                                                           | `(X: number[][]) => void`       | Resets state and streams `X` in `batchSize` chunks through `partialFit()`.                        |
| `transform` / `inverseTransform`                                                | `(X: number[][]) => number[][]` | Projects samples onto principal axes or reconstructs them in feature space.                       |
| `components` / `mean` / `explainedVariance` / `singularValues` / `nSamplesSeen` | Learned getters                 | Inspects principal directions, running column means, variance spectrum, and total rows processed. |

### Practical constraints

- **Minimum first batch size**: The very first `partialFit()` call must contain at least `nComponents` rows (and `nFeatures >= nComponents`), otherwise there are not enough samples to initialize the requested rank.
- **Related pages**: [PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/pca.md), [PCA Interactive Playground](/playground/pca), [TruncatedSVD](/docs/apis/decomposition/truncatedSVD.md), [SparsePCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/sparsePCA.md).

---
title: "Dimensionality Reduction in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Explore PCA, Kernel PCA, FastICA, NMF, Incremental PCA, Sparse PCA, and Truncated SVD in JavaScript and TypeScript with @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/index.html.md"
---
# Dimensionality Reduction in JavaScript

## Module overview

The Decomposition module reduces feature dimensions while preserving useful signal for visualization, denoising, compression, and downstream modeling. These algorithms are often used before clustering, classification, or charting when raw feature spaces are too large or too noisy.

This module is a strong fit when:

- you need lower-dimensional inputs for charts or interactive analysis
- you want to compress features before training another model
- you need different strategies for dense versus sparse matrices

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides decomposition algorithms directly in JavaScript and TypeScript so frontend and full-stack teams can run feature compression in the same runtime that already owns embeddings, visualizations, or data pipelines. This is especially useful when dimensionality reduction is part of a browser-based analytics experience or a Node.js preprocessing step.

If someone searches for "PCA in JavaScript" or "Truncated SVD in TypeScript", this module is the right entry point.

## Quick navigation

- [PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/pca.md): dense feature compression and variance-preserving projections
- [Sparse PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/sparsePCA.md): more interpretable sparse components
- [Truncated SVD](/docs/apis/decomposition/truncatedSVD.md): latent factors for sparse or vectorized inputs
- [Kernel PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/kernelPCA.md): nonlinear kernel embeddings
- [FastICA](/docs/apis/decomposition/fastICA.md): independent signal separation
- [NMF](/docs/apis/decomposition/nmf.md): non-negative, parts-based latent factors
- [Incremental PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/incrementalPCA.md): batch-wise, memory-aware PCA
- [Factor Analysis](/docs/apis/decomposition/factorAnalysis.md): latent Gaussian factors with per-feature noise
- [Latent Dirichlet Allocation](/docs/apis/decomposition/latentDirichletAllocation.md): topic mixtures from word counts

## Detailed module guide

### How to choose an algorithm

1. Use [PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/pca.md) for dense numeric features when variance preservation matters most.
2. Use [Truncated SVD](/docs/apis/decomposition/truncatedSVD.md) for sparse matrices such as TF-IDF or one-hot vectors.
3. Use [Sparse PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/sparsePCA.md) when component interpretability matters alongside dimensionality reduction.
4. Use [Kernel PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/kernelPCA.md) for nonlinear structure, [FastICA](/docs/apis/decomposition/fastICA.md) for independent sources, [NMF](/docs/apis/decomposition/nmf.md) for non-negative additive factors, or [Incremental PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/incrementalPCA.md) for streamed batches.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Standardize dense continuous features before PCA-style methods when appropriate.
- Use decomposition to simplify data before charting, clustering, or supervised learning.
- In browser apps, dimensionality reduction is often most valuable when it feeds directly into interactive visualizations.

---

<!-- Source: https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/kernelPCA -->

---
title: "Kernel PCA in JavaScript and TypeScript"
description: "Run nonlinear dimensionality reduction with RBF, polynomial, and cosine kernels in JavaScript and TypeScript using KernelPCA from @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/kernelPCA"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/kernelPCA.md"
---
# Kernel PCA in JavaScript and TypeScript

## Algorithm overview

Standard [PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/pca.md) finds orthogonal linear projections—so if data lies on concentric circles, spirals, or curved manifolds, linear PCA collapses distinct classes right on top of each other. **Kernel PCA** applies the kernel trick to project observations implicitly into a higher-dimensional reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) and performs eigen-decomposition on the centered `n × n` Gram (kernel) matrix.

Use Kernel PCA when:

- Linear PCA fails to separate curved or concentric clusters before visualization or linear classification.
- You need **out-of-sample `transform(XTest)`** on unseen points (unlike non-parametric embeddings such as [t-SNE](/docs/apis/manifold/tsne.md)).
- You want optional pre-image reconstruction (`fitInverseTransform: true`) via kernel ridge regression.

## JavaScript implementation

`Decomposition.KernelPCA` in `@kanaries/ml` supports `'linear'`, `'poly'`, `'rbf'`, `'sigmoid'`, and `'cosine'` kernels in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js workflows. It composes directly inside [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md) and serializes via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

**Memory & scaling note**: Because Kernel PCA builds and eigendecomposes an `O(n²)` Gram matrix (`n × n`), keep browser datasets under roughly 1,000–1,500 rows, or approximate RBF kernels at scale with [`Kernel.Nystroem`](/docs/apis/kernel/nystroem.md) or [`Kernel.RBFSampler`](/docs/apis/kernel/rbfSampler.md) followed by linear PCA.

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Decomposition } from '@kanaries/ml';

const model = new Decomposition.KernelPCA({
  nComponents: 2,
  kernel: 'rbf',
  gamma: 2,
});
const embedded = model.fitTransform([[1, 0], [0, 1], [-1, 0], [0, -1]]);
console.log(embedded);
```

### KernelPCA: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.decomposition import KernelPCA

kpca = KernelPCA(
  n_components=2,
  kernel="rbf",
  gamma=2.0,
  fit_inverse_transform=True,
)
embedded = kpca.fit_transform(X_train)
test_embedded = kpca.transform(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Decomposition } from '@kanaries/ml';

const kpca = new Decomposition.KernelPCA({
nComponents: 2,
kernel: 'rbf',
gamma: 2.0,
fitInverseTransform: true,
});
const embedded = kpca.fitTransform(XTrain);
const testEmbedded = kpca.transform(XTest);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Decomposition.KernelPCA(props?)`

| Parameter                       | Type                                                   | Default                           | Description                                                               |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nComponents`                   | `number \| null`                                       | `null` (all positive eigenvalues) | Number of nonlinear components to retain.                                 |
| `kernel`                        | `'linear' \| 'poly' \| 'rbf' \| 'sigmoid' \| 'cosine'` | `'linear'`                        | Kernel function computing pairwise similarity.                            |
| `gamma`                         | `number`                                               | `1 / nFeatures`                   | Kernel coefficient for `'rbf'`, `'poly'`, and `'sigmoid'`.                |
| `degree` / `coef0`              | `number`                                               | `3` / `1`                         | Degree and independent offset for `'poly'` and `'sigmoid'` kernels.       |
| `fitInverseTransform` / `alpha` | `boolean` / `number`                                   | `false` / `1.0`                   | Enables kernel-ridge `inverseTransform()` with L2 regularization `alpha`. |
| `randomState`                   | `number`                                               | `undefined`                       | Seed for deterministic sign/eigensolver tie-breaking.                     |

### Methods & properties

- `fit(X)` / `transform(X)` / `fitTransform(X)` / `inverseTransform(X)` (requires `fitInverseTransform: true`).
- `eigenvalues` and `eigenvectors` expose defensive copies of the centered Gram spectrum.
- **Related pages**: [PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/pca.md), [Kernel Approximation (`Nystroem` / `RBFSampler`)](/docs/apis/kernel/index.html.md), [Isomap](/docs/apis/manifold/isomap.md).

---
title: "Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) in JavaScript"
description: "Run probabilistic topic modeling over document-term count matrices in JavaScript and TypeScript with LatentDirichletAllocation from @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/latentDirichletAllocation"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/latentDirichletAllocation.md"
---
# Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

**Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA)** is a generative probabilistic topic model that discovers hidden semantic themes across a collection of text documents. It assumes every document is a soft probability mixture over `nComponents` latent topics, and every topic is a probability distribution over vocabulary terms.

Unlike [NMF](/docs/apis/decomposition/nmf.md) (which operates cleanly on TF-IDF weights via matrix factorization), LDA is designed specifically for **raw non-negative word-count matrices** produced by [`CountVectorizer`](/docs/apis/feature_extraction/countVectorizer.md). Each row returned by `transform()` is a normalized topic-proportion vector summing to `1`, making it easy to cluster articles, tag support logs, or chart theme distributions directly in a frontend dashboard.

*(Note: For supervised classification/projection Linear Discriminant Analysis, see [`DiscriminantAnalysis.LDA`](/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/lda.md).)*

## JavaScript implementation

`Decomposition.LatentDirichletAllocation` runs batch variational Bayes inference in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js environments. It accepts both dense `number[][]` and sparse [`CSRMatrix`](/docs/apis/data/index.html.md) count matrices, chains directly after `FeatureExtraction.CountVectorizer` inside a [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md), and serializes trained topic models via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start

```ts
import { Decomposition, FeatureExtraction } from '@kanaries/ml';

const documents = ['cats chase mice', 'dogs chase balls', 'cats and dogs', 'mice eat cheese'];
const counts = new FeatureExtraction.CountVectorizer().fitTransform(documents);
const lda = new Decomposition.LatentDirichletAllocation({
  nComponents: 2,
  maxIter: 15,
  randomState: 0,
});
const topics = lda.fitTransform(counts);
console.log({ topics, nTopics: lda.components.length });
```

### LatentDirichletAllocation (Topic Modeling): Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.decomposition import LatentDirichletAllocation

counts = CountVectorizer().fit_transform(documents)
lda = LatentDirichletAllocation(n_components=5, max_iter=10, random_state=0)
doc_topics = lda.fit_transform(counts)
topic_words = lda.components_
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Decomposition, FeatureExtraction } from '@kanaries/ml';

const counts = new FeatureExtraction.CountVectorizer().fitTransform(documents);
const lda = new Decomposition.LatentDirichletAllocation({
nComponents: 5,
maxIter: 10,
randomState: 0,
});
const docTopics = lda.fitTransform(counts);
const topicWords = lda.components;
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Decomposition.LatentDirichletAllocation(props?)`

| Parameter          | Type     | Default           | Description                                                                                                       |
| ------------------ | -------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nComponents`      | `number` | `10`              | Number of latent topics to infer.                                                                                 |
| `docTopicPrior`    | `number` | `1 / nComponents` | Dirichlet prior `alpha` controlling document-topic sparsity (smaller values encourage fewer topics per document). |
| `topicWordPrior`   | `number` | `1 / nComponents` | Dirichlet prior `eta` controlling topic-word sparsity (smaller values produce sharper top-word lists).            |
| `maxIter`          | `number` | `10`              | Number of variational EM passes over the corpus.                                                                  |
| `maxDocUpdateIter` | `number` | `100`             | Inner E-step iterations per document.                                                                             |
| `meanChangeTol`    | `number` | `1e-3`            | Convergence threshold for per-document variational updates.                                                       |
| `randomState`      | `number` | `undefined`       | Seed for reproducible topic initialization.                                                                       |

### Methods & properties

- `fit(X)` / `transform(X)` / `fitTransform(X)` — accept dense or `CSRMatrix` non-negative counts; `transform` returns normalized document-topic distributions.
- `components` — unnormalized topic-word variational parameters (`[nComponents][nVocab]`); sort each row descending to inspect top keywords per topic.
- **Related pages**: [CountVectorizer](/docs/apis/feature_extraction/countVectorizer.md), [NMF](/docs/apis/decomposition/nmf.md), [CSRMatrix](/docs/apis/data/index.html.md).
