---
title: "Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) in JS"
description: "Factor non-negative matrices into additive latent parts in JavaScript and TypeScript with Decomposition.NMF from @kanaries/ml for topics and embeddings."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/nmf"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/nmf.md"
---
# Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) in JS

## Algorithm overview

**Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF)** approximates a non-negative feature matrix `X` (`nSamples × nFeatures`) as the product of two lower-rank non-negative matrices `W × H`, where `W` holds per-sample component weights and `H` (`components`) holds additive basis patterns.

Unlike [PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/pca.md) or [TruncatedSVD](/docs/apis/decomposition/truncatedSVD.md), which allow positive and negative cancellations across components, NMF's strict non-negativity constraint forces representations to be **purely additive**. That makes NMF especially interpretable for:

- **Topic modeling over TF-IDF or bag-of-words counts**: each component in `H` reads like a coherent list of top weighted keywords.
- **Parts-based signal & spectrogram analysis**: decomposing audio spectra, image patches, or user-activity counts into reusable additive building blocks.
- **Recommender & behavior profiles**: expressing each customer as a positive blend of latent archetypes.

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides `Decomposition.NMF` using multiplicative Frobenius-loss updates with optional L1/L2 regularization (`alphaW`, `alphaH`, `l1Ratio`) and scikit-learn's `nndsvd` / `nndsvda` / `nndsvdar` / `random` initializers. Everything runs in pure TypeScript across browsers and Node.js, composes with [`TfidfVectorizer`](/docs/apis/feature_extraction/tfidfVectorizer.md) inside [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md), and serializes cleanly via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Decomposition } from '@kanaries/ml';

const nmf = new Decomposition.NMF({ nComponents: 2, init: 'nndsvda', randomState: 0 });
const W = nmf.fitTransform([[1, 2, 0], [0, 1, 3], [1, 3, 3]]);
const approximation = nmf.inverseTransform(W);
console.log({ W, approximation, err: nmf.reconstructionErr });
```

### Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF): Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.decomposition import NMF

nmf = NMF(n_components=2, init="nndsvda", random_state=0)
W = nmf.fit_transform(X)
H = nmf.components_
X_hat = nmf.inverse_transform(W)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Decomposition } from '@kanaries/ml';

const nmf = new Decomposition.NMF({
nComponents: 2,
init: 'nndsvda',
randomState: 0,
});
const W = nmf.fitTransform(X);
const H = nmf.components;
const XHat = nmf.inverseTransform(W);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Decomposition.NMF(props?)`

| Parameter           | Type                                              | Default     | Description                                                                                                                |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nComponents`       | `number`                                          | `nFeatures` | Number of additive latent factors (`k`).                                                                                   |
| `init`              | `'random' \| 'nndsvd' \| 'nndsvda' \| 'nndsvdar'` | `'nndsvda'` | Initialization strategy. `'nndsvda'` is deterministic and works well for dense matrices; `'nndsvd'` favors sparse factors. |
| `maxIter`           | `number`                                          | `200`       | Maximum multiplicative-update iterations.                                                                                  |
| `tol`               | `number`                                          | `1e-4`      | Stopping tolerance on relative reconstruction-error change.                                                                |
| `alphaW` / `alphaH` | `number`                                          | `0`         | Regularization multipliers for factor matrices `W` and `H`.                                                                |
| `l1Ratio`           | `number`                                          | `0`         | Balance between L2 (`0`) and L1 (`1`) sparsity regularization.                                                             |
| `randomState`       | `number`                                          | `undefined` | Seed for stochastic initializations (`'random'`, `'nndsvdar'`).                                                            |

### Methods & properties

- `fit(X)` / `transform(X)` / `fitTransform(X)` / `inverseTransform(W)` — require finite, rectangular, non-negative matrices (negative values throw an error).
- Learned fields: `components` (`H`), `reconstructionErr` (Frobenius norm of `X - W H`), and `nIter`.
- **Related pages**: [Latent Dirichlet Allocation](/docs/apis/decomposition/latentDirichletAllocation.md), [TfidfVectorizer](/docs/apis/feature_extraction/tfidfVectorizer.md), [TruncatedSVD](/docs/apis/decomposition/truncatedSVD.md).

title: "PCA in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Learn what PCA does, when to use it, and how to run PCA in JavaScript or TypeScript with @kanaries/ml for browser and Node.js applications."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/pca"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/pca.md"
---
# PCA in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

Linear dimensionality reduction using Singular Value Decomposition of the data to project it to a lower dimensional space. The input data is centered but not scaled for each feature before applying the SVD.

PCA compresses correlated numeric features into orthogonal components while preserving maximal variance.

This algorithm is especially useful when:

- Feature dimensions are high and training speed needs improvement.
- You need 2D/3D projections for exploratory visualization.
- Multicollinearity hurts stability in downstream supervised models.

## JavaScript implementation

@kanaries/ml gives frontend and full-stack teams a JavaScript PCA implementation for feature compression, denoising, and 2D or 3D visualization. That is useful when your embeddings or tabular features are already flowing through a JS application and you want dimensionality reduction without switching runtimes.

In practice, PCA is often one of the most useful browser-friendly ML utilities because it helps simplify data before charting, clustering, or downstream modeling.

## Quick start

### PCA: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

X = [[1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 4], [3, 5, 7], [4, 6, 8]]

pca = PCA(n_components=2)
embedding = pca.fit_transform(X)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Decomposition } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 4], [3, 5, 7], [4, 6, 8]];

const pca = new Decomposition.PCA({ nComponents: 2 });
const embedding = pca.fitTransform(X);
```

### Quick JavaScript example

```ts
import { Decomposition } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 4], [3, 5, 7], [4, 6, 8]];

const pca = new Decomposition.PCA({ nComponents: 2 });
const embedding = pca.fitTransform(X);
console.log({ embedding, explainedVariance: pca.getExplainedVariance() });
```

Want to visualize principal axes and variance explained interactively? Try the [PCA Interactive Playground](/playground/pca).

## Detailed API reference

### Algorithm

The covariance matrix of the centered samples is decomposed via symmetric eigendecomposition. The resulting eigenvectors form the principal components sorted by explained variance.

```ts
new Decomposition.PCA(props?: {
  nComponents?: number | null; // default: null (keep all features)
})
```

*(Legacy positional calls `new Decomposition.PCA(2)` remain supported for backward compatibility, but prefer `{ nComponents: 2 }`.)*

### Parameters

- `nComponents` (number | null, default `null`): number of principal components to retain. If `null`, all components are used.

### Methods

- `fit(X: number[][]): void`
- `transform(X: number[][]): number[][]`
- `fitTransform(X: number[][]): number[][]`
- `inverseTransform(X: number[][]): number[][]`
- `getComponents(): number[][]`
- `getMean(): number[]`
- `getExplainedVariance(): number[]`

### Implementation workflow

1. Standardize continuous features before decomposition.
2. Fit PCA and select component count by explained variance.
3. Use transformed features for visualization or downstream training.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Standardize continuous features before PCA so dominant dimensions do not reflect raw scale alone.
- Use PCA as a preprocessing step before visualization, clustering, or other downstream models.
- In browser tools, PCA is a practical way to reduce feature count before rendering or interactive analysis.

title: "Sparse PCA in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Learn what Sparse PCA does, when to use it, and how to run SparsePCA in JavaScript or TypeScript with @kanaries/ml for browser and Node.js applications."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/sparsePCA"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/sparsePCA.md"
---
# Sparse PCA in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

Sparse Principal Components Analysis using truncated power iteration with soft thresholding. The algorithm stops when the updates change by less than `tol` or when `maxIter` is reached.

SparsePCA learns sparse components so each latent dimension uses only a subset of original features.

This algorithm is especially useful when:

- Interpretability of component-feature relationships is important.
- You need dimensionality reduction with built-in sparsity constraints.
- Dense PCA components are too hard to explain to stakeholders.

## JavaScript implementation

@kanaries/ml includes Sparse PCA for JavaScript teams that want more interpretable components than standard PCA. This is useful when you need compressed features but also want each component to depend on a smaller subset of the original dimensions.

That makes it relevant for browser-based analytics and Node.js pipelines where component interpretability matters alongside dimensionality reduction.

## Quick start

### SparsePCA: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.decomposition import SparsePCA

X = [[1, 2, 0], [2, 1, 0], [3, 4, 1], [4, 3, 1]]

model = SparsePCA(n_components=2, alpha=0.1, random_state=0)
embedding = model.fit_transform(X)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Decomposition } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[1, 2, 0], [2, 1, 0], [3, 4, 1], [4, 3, 1]];

const model = new Decomposition.SparsePCA({ nComponents: 2, alpha: 0.1 });
const embedding = model.fitTransform(X);
```

### Quick JavaScript example

```ts
import { Decomposition } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[1, 2, 0], [2, 1, 0], [3, 4, 1], [4, 3, 1]];

const model = new Decomposition.SparsePCA({ nComponents: 2, alpha: 0.1 });
const embedding = model.fitTransform(X);
console.log(embedding);
```

## Detailed API reference

### Algorithm

Each component is extracted by iterative thresholding of the covariance matrix.
The process encourages sparsity by shrinking small coefficients towards zero.

```ts
interface SparsePCAProps {
    nComponents?: number | null;
    alpha?: number;
    maxIter?: number;
    tol?: number;
}
constructor(props: SparsePCAProps = {})
```

### Parameters

- `nComponents` (number | null, default `null`): number of sparse components to compute. `null` keeps all components.
- `alpha` (number, default `1`): sparsity controlling parameter. Higher values lead to more zero coefficients.
- `maxIter` (number, default `100`): maximum number of iterations for each component.
- `tol` (number, default `1e-8`): stopping criterion for convergence of the iterative updates.

### Implementation workflow

1. Scale input features and choose sparsity-related hyperparameters.
2. Fit SparsePCA and inspect component loadings for feature selection signals.
3. Use sparse transformed outputs in linear or tree-based downstream models.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Use Sparse PCA when interpretability of components matters more than pure reconstruction quality.
- Expect to tune `alpha` because sparsity strength directly affects component structure.
- It is a good middle ground between raw high-dimensional features and dense latent embeddings.

markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/decomposition/truncatedSVD.md"

# Truncated SVD in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

Dimensionality reduction using truncated Singular Value Decomposition of the data. Unlike PCA, the input data is not centered before decomposition.

TruncatedSVD reduces dimensionality of large sparse matrices without centering, making it practical for text/vectorized data.

This algorithm is especially useful when:

- Your feature matrix is sparse (for example TF-IDF or one-hot encodings).
- You need latent semantic compression before classification or retrieval.
- PCA centering is too expensive or undesirable for sparse data.

## JavaScript implementation

@kanaries/ml brings Truncated SVD to JavaScript for workflows that work with large sparse matrices, vectorized text, or one-hot encoded features. This is especially useful in Node.js search, recommendation, and document pipelines where you want latent factors without centering the matrix first.

For product teams working with sparse representations in TypeScript, this keeps feature compression and downstream modeling inside the same JS stack.

## Quick start

### TruncatedSVD: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.decomposition import TruncatedSVD

X = [[1, 0, 1], [0, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]]

svd = TruncatedSVD(n_components=2, random_state=0)
embedding = svd.fit_transform(X)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Decomposition } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[1, 0, 1], [0, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]];

const svd = new Decomposition.TruncatedSVD({ nComponents: 2 });
const embedding = svd.fitTransform(X);
```

### Quick JavaScript example

```ts
import { Decomposition } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[1, 0, 1], [0, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]];

const svd = new Decomposition.TruncatedSVD({ nComponents: 2 });
const embedding = svd.fitTransform(X);
console.log({ embedding, ratio: svd.getExplainedVarianceRatio() });
```

## Detailed API reference

### Algorithm

Decomposes the uncentered cross-product matrix and retains the top components corresponding to the largest singular values.

```ts
new Decomposition.TruncatedSVD(props?: {
  nComponents?: number; // default: 2
})
```

*(Legacy positional calls `new Decomposition.TruncatedSVD(2)` remain supported for backward compatibility, but prefer `{ nComponents: 2 }`.)*

### Parameters

- `nComponents` (number, default `2`): number of singular vectors to retain.

### Methods

- `fit(X: number[][]): void`
- `transform(X: number[][]): number[][]`
- `fitTransform(X: number[][]): number[][]`
- `inverseTransform(X: number[][]): number[][]`
- `getComponents(): number[][]`
- `getSingularValues(): number[]`
- `getExplainedVariance(): number[]`
- `getExplainedVarianceRatio(): number[]`

### Implementation workflow

1. Build sparse-compatible numeric input matrix.
2. Fit TruncatedSVD with candidate component counts.
3. Evaluate retrieval/classification quality on reduced features.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Prefer Truncated SVD over PCA when working with sparse or high-cardinality vectorized inputs.
- Use it before retrieval, classification, or visualization when you need lower-dimensional latent features.
- It is particularly practical in Node.js pipelines that already generate sparse text or categorical vectors.

---
title: "Discriminant Analysis in JavaScript"
description: "Run Linear (LDA) and Quadratic (QDA) Discriminant Analysis in JavaScript and TypeScript with @kanaries/ml for classification and supervised projection."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/index.html.md"
---
# Discriminant Analysis in JavaScript

## Module overview

**Discriminant Analysis** models each class as a multivariate Gaussian distribution and applies Bayes' rule to compute closed-form class posteriors—requiring no iterative gradient descent or learning-rate tuning.

- **[Linear Discriminant Analysis (`LDA`)](/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/lda.md)** assumes all classes share a single pooled covariance matrix. This yields linear decision boundaries and also serves as a **supervised dimensionality-reduction transformer** (`transform` / `fitTransform`) that projects data onto up to `min(nClasses - 1, nFeatures)` maximally class-separating axes.
- **[Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (`QDA`)](/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/qda.md)** estimates a separate covariance matrix for every class, producing curved quadratic decision boundaries when classes differ significantly in variance or correlation structure.

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` exports both canonical scikit-learn names and short aliases under `import { DiscriminantAnalysis } from '@kanaries/ml'`:

| Canonical class                                      | Alias                      | Decision boundary                | Supervised `transform()`            |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- | -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `DiscriminantAnalysis.LinearDiscriminantAnalysis`    | `DiscriminantAnalysis.LDA` | Linear (shared covariance)       | Yes (`nComponents ≤ min(K - 1, p)`) |
| `DiscriminantAnalysis.QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis` | `DiscriminantAnalysis.QDA` | Quadratic (per-class covariance) | No (classifier only)                |

Both classes extend `ClassifierBase`, use SVD-based numerical solvers that stay well-behaved in pure TypeScript without external linear-algebra binaries, work seamlessly inside [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md), and serialize via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { DiscriminantAnalysis } from '@kanaries/ml';

const lda = new DiscriminantAnalysis.LDA({ solver: 'svd', nComponents: 2 });
lda.fit(XTrain, yTrain);

const predictions = lda.predict(XTest);
const probabilities = lda.predictProba(XTest);
const projected = lda.transform(XTest); // supervised 2D projection
```

## Choosing between LDA, QDA, and Logistic Regression

- Start with **[LDA](/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/lda.md)** when features are roughly Gaussian per class, you want closed-form fitting with zero learning-rate tuning, or you need supervised dimensionality reduction before plotting or downstream modeling.
- Switch to **[QDA](/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/qda.md)** when classes clearly have different covariance shapes and you have enough samples per class to estimate per-class covariances (use `regParam > 0` to stabilize small classes).
- Use **[Logistic Regression](/docs/apis/linear/logisticRegression.md)** when class distributions are heavily non-Gaussian or sparse and you prefer discriminative regularization.
- **Related pages**: [Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)](/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/lda.md), [Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA)](/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/qda.md), [PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/pca.md), [Logistic Regression](/docs/apis/linear/logisticRegression.md).

---
title: "Linear Discriminant Analysis in JS"
description: "Run Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) classification and supervised projection in JavaScript and TypeScript with @kanaries/ml using SVD or eigen solvers."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/lda"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/lda.md"
---
# Linear Discriminant Analysis in JS

## Algorithm overview

**Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)** is both a closed-form generative classifier and a supervised dimensionality-reduction technique. It models each class with a multivariate Gaussian sharing a common within-class covariance matrix, yielding linear decision boundaries without iterative gradient descent.

As a transformer (`transform` / `fitTransform`), LDA finds linear combinations of features that maximize the ratio of **between-class scatter** to **within-class scatter**—unlike unsupervised [PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/pca.md), which maximizes total variance regardless of class labels. This makes LDA ideal for visualizing class separation in 1D–2D charts or compressing correlated features inside a [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md).

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides `DiscriminantAnalysis.LinearDiscriminantAnalysis` and its alias `DiscriminantAnalysis.LDA`. It implements scikit-learn's `'svd'` solver (default—avoids explicitly forming the covariance matrix, making it robust on high-dimensional or rank-deficient features) and `'eigen'` solver (solves the generalized eigenproblem with optional covariance `shrinkage` in `[0, 1]`).

Everything runs synchronously in pure TypeScript across browsers and Node.js, and trained LDA models serialize cleanly with `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { DiscriminantAnalysis } from '@kanaries/ml';

const XTrain = [
  [-2, -1], [-1.5, -1.2], [-1, -2],
  [1, 1], [1.5, 1.3], [2, 1.1],
  [5, -2], [5.5, -1.8], [6, -2.2],
];
const yTrain = [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2];

const lda = new DiscriminantAnalysis.LinearDiscriminantAnalysis({
  solver: 'svd',
  nComponents: 2,
});

const projected = lda.fitTransform(XTrain, yTrain);
const preds = lda.predict([[-1.4, -1.5], [1.2, 1.2], [5.4, -2.0]]);
console.log({ preds, varianceRatio: lda.getExplainedVarianceRatio(), projectedShape: [projected.length, projected[0].length] });
```

### LinearDiscriminantAnalysis (LDA): Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis

lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(solver="svd", n_components=2)
X_proj = lda.fit_transform(X_train, y_train)
preds = lda.predict(X_test)
proba = lda.predict_proba(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { DiscriminantAnalysis } from '@kanaries/ml';

const lda = new DiscriminantAnalysis.LinearDiscriminantAnalysis({
solver: 'svd',
nComponents: 2,
});

const XProj = lda.fitTransform(XTrain, yTrain);
const preds = lda.predict(XTest);
const proba = lda.predictProba(XTest);
```

### Shrinkage LDA for high-dimensional data

When `nFeatures` approaches `nSamples`, switch to `solver: 'eigen'` with `shrinkage` to regularize the within-class covariance toward a scaled identity matrix:

```ts
import { DiscriminantAnalysis } from '@kanaries/ml';

const shrunkLda = new DiscriminantAnalysis.LDA({
  solver: 'eigen',
  shrinkage: 0.2,
});
shrunkLda.fit([[-2, -1], [-1, -2], [2, 1], [1, 2]], [0, 0, 1, 1]);
console.log(shrunkLda.predict([[-1.5, -1.5], [1.5, 1.5]]));
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new DiscriminantAnalysis.LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(props?)`

*(Also exported as `DiscriminantAnalysis.LDA`.)*

| Parameter     | Type               | Default                        | Description                                                                                                                                    |
| ------------- | ------------------ | ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `solver`      | `'svd' \| 'eigen'` | `'svd'`                        | `'svd'` avoids forming the covariance matrix and handles rank-deficient features cleanly; `'eigen'` solves `Sw⁻¹ Sb` and supports `shrinkage`. |
| `shrinkage`   | `number`           | `undefined`                    | Shrinkage weight in `[0, 1]` for within-class covariance. Supported only when `solver: 'eigen'` (throws with `'svd'`).                         |
| `priors`      | `number[]`         | empirical class frequencies    | Custom class prior probabilities in sorted-class order.                                                                                        |
| `nComponents` | `number`           | `min(nClasses - 1, nFeatures)` | Number of discriminant components returned by `transform()` and `fitTransform()`.                                                              |
| `tol`         | `number`           | `1e-4`                         | Singular-value rank threshold for the `'svd'` solver.                                                                                          |

### Methods

| Method                                      | Signature                                       | Description                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `fit`                                       | `(X: number[][], y: number[]) => void`          | Fits class means, priors, linear decision weights, and discriminant scalings.                                        |
| `predict`                                   | `(testX: number[][]) => number[]`               | Predicts the highest-posterior class label for each sample.                                                          |
| `predictProba`                              | `(testX: number[][]) => number[][]`             | Computes softmax-normalized class posterior probabilities.                                                           |
| `decisionFunction`                          | `(testX: number[][]) => number[] \| number[][]` | Returns signed binary margins (`number[]`) for 2 classes or per-class scores (`number[][]`) for multiclass problems. |
| `transform`                                 | `(X: number[][]) => number[][]`                 | Projects `X` onto the top `nComponents` discriminant axes.                                                           |
| `fitTransform`                              | `(X: number[][], y: number[]) => number[][]`    | Fits LDA on `(X, y)` and returns `transform(X)`.                                                                     |
| `getClasses` / `getMeans` / `getPriors`     | `() => number[]` / `number[][]`                 | Inspects sorted labels, per-class feature means, and class priors.                                                   |
| `getCoef` / `getIntercept`                  | `() => number[][]` / `number[]`                 | Returns linear scoring coefficients and intercepts.                                                                  |
| `getScalings` / `getExplainedVarianceRatio` | `() => number[][]` / `number[]`                 | Returns discriminant projection vectors and fraction of between-class variance explained per axis.                   |

### Compatibility & practical notes

- **Maximum projection dimensions**: LDA can extract at most `min(nClasses - 1, nFeatures)` components—so binary classification produces at most 1 discriminant axis.
- **sklearn note**: scikit-learn's `'lsqr'` solver is omitted intentionally because it produces the same classifier as `'eigen'` without supporting `transform()`.
- **Related pages**: [Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA)](/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/qda.md), [Discriminant Analysis Overview](/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/index.html.md), [PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/pca.md), [ML Pipelines](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md).

---
title: "Quadratic Discriminant Analysis in JS"
description: "Train Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) classifiers with per-class covariances in JavaScript and TypeScript using @kanaries/ml for browser and Node.js."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/qda"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/qda.md"
---
# Quadratic Discriminant Analysis in JS

## Algorithm overview

**Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA)** is a generative Bayes classifier that fits a separate multivariate Gaussian—with its own mean vector and its own covariance matrix—to each class. Because covariances are not shared across classes, the log-posterior boundary between classes is **quadratic**, allowing QDA to separate elliptical, rotated, or nested class distributions that linear classifiers cannot split cleanly.

QDA is most effective when:

- Classes clearly differ in spread, correlation, or orientation.
- Each class has enough training samples to estimate its covariance reliably (or `regParam` is tuned to stabilize small-sample classes).
- You want closed-form training and calibrated Gaussian posterior probabilities (`predictProba`) without tuning a learning rate.

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides `DiscriminantAnalysis.QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis` and its short alias `DiscriminantAnalysis.QDA`. Rather than inverting dense covariance matrices explicitly, `@kanaries/ml` fits each class through a centered per-class SVD and regularizes covariance eigenvalues via `(1 - regParam) * s² + regParam`.

A practical improvement over scikit-learn: on rank-deficient class data with `regParam: 0`, directions whose covariance eigenvalue is `≤ tol` are cleanly dropped from the Mahalanobis distance and log-determinant so predictions stay finite instead of producing `NaN` or `Infinity`.

## Quick start example

```ts
import { DiscriminantAnalysis } from '@kanaries/ml';

const XTrain = [
  [-2, -1], [-1.8, -1.5], [-2.2, -0.8], [-1.5, -1.1],
  [2, 2], [4, 0], [0, 4], [3, 3],
];
const yTrain = [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1];

const qda = new DiscriminantAnalysis.QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis({
  regParam: 0.1,
});

qda.fit(XTrain, yTrain);
console.log({
  preds: qda.predict([[-1.9, -1.0], [2.5, 2.5]]),
  proba: qda.predictProba([[-1.9, -1.0], [2.5, 2.5]]),
});
```

### QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis (QDA): Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis

qda = QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis(reg_param=0.1)
qda.fit(X_train, y_train)
preds = qda.predict(X_test)
proba = qda.predict_proba(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { DiscriminantAnalysis } from '@kanaries/ml';

const qda = new DiscriminantAnalysis.QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis({
regParam: 0.1,
});

qda.fit(XTrain, yTrain);
const preds = qda.predict(XTest);
const proba = qda.predictProba(XTest);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new DiscriminantAnalysis.QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis(props?)`

*(Also exported as `DiscriminantAnalysis.QDA`.)*

| Parameter  | Type       | Default                     | Description                                                                                                                   |
| ---------- | ---------- | --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `priors`   | `number[]` | empirical class frequencies | Prior probabilities in sorted-class order.                                                                                    |
| `regParam` | `number`   | `0`                         | Regularization strength in `[0, 1]`. Blends each class covariance eigenvalue toward `1` via `(1 - regParam) * s² + regParam`. |
| `tol`      | `number`   | `1e-4`                      | Eigenvalue rank threshold for dropping collinear directions during Mahalanobis scoring.                                       |

### Methods

| Method                                  | Signature                                       | Description                                                                                                                                    |
| --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `fit`                                   | `(X: number[][], y: number[]) => void`          | Estimates per-class means, priors, and SVD covariance factors (requires at least 2 classes).                                                   |
| `predict`                               | `(testX: number[][]) => number[]`               | Returns the class label maximizing `log P(x \| k) + log P(k)`.                                                                                 |
| `predictProba`                          | `(testX: number[][]) => number[][]`             | Returns softmax-normalized class posterior probabilities.                                                                                      |
| `decisionFunction`                      | `(testX: number[][]) => number[] \| number[][]` | Returns signed binary log-posterior differences (`number[]`) for 2 classes or per-class log-posteriors (`number[][]`) for multiclass problems. |
| `getClasses` / `getMeans` / `getPriors` | `() => number[]` / `number[][]`                 | Inspects sorted class labels, per-class means, and class priors.                                                                               |
| `getCovariance`                         | `() => number[][][]`                            | Reconstructs the `[nClasses][nFeatures][nFeatures]` per-class covariance matrices.                                                             |

### Tuning tips

- Increase `regParam` (for example `0.05` to `0.5`) when any class has relatively few samples compared to `nFeatures`, shrinking noisy per-class covariance estimates toward isotropic Gaussians.
- Standardize features with [`StandardScaler`](/docs/apis/utils/preprocessing.md) when `regParam > 0`, because isotropic regularization assumes comparable feature scales.
- **Related pages**: [Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)](/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/lda.md), [Discriminant Analysis Overview](/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/index.html.md), [Gaussian Naive Bayes](/docs/apis/bayes/gaussianNB.md), [GaussianMixture](/docs/apis/mixture/gaussian-mixture.md).

---
title: "Dummy Baselines in JavaScript"
description: "Benchmark classifiers and regressors against simple baseline strategies in JavaScript and TypeScript using DummyClassifier and DummyRegressor from @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/dummy"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/dummy/index.html.md"
---
# Dummy Baselines in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

Before celebrating 95% accuracy on an imbalanced fraud dataset—or tuning hyperparameters on a noisy regression problem—you need a **sanity-check baseline**. **Dummy estimators** ignore all input features `X` and generate predictions strictly from simple rules over the training target `y` (such as the majority class, empirical class priors, target mean, median, or a chosen quantile).

Comparing real models against a dummy baseline immediately answers two critical questions:

1. **Is my model learning real signal?** If a tuned classifier barely beats `DummyClassifier({ strategy: 'prior' })`, the problem needs better features or different framing rather than heavier models.
2. **Is my evaluation metric misleading?** On a 98/2 imbalanced dataset, `DummyClassifier` achieves 98% accuracy while scoring `0.0` on positive-class F1—exposing why precision, recall, F1, or ROC-AUC should drive model selection.

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides `Dummy.DummyClassifier` and `Dummy.DummyRegressor` matching `sklearn.dummy`. Both extend `ClassifierBase` / `RegressorBase`, integrate cleanly with cross-validation utilities in [`utils.ModelSelection`](/docs/apis/utils/modelSelection.md) and [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md), and serialize via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

Note one deliberate improvement over scikit-learn: for stochastic strategies (`'stratified'`, `'uniform'`), `DummyClassifier` stores `randomState` and derives a fresh seeded generator on every `predict()` / `predictProba()` call, making repeated predictions deterministic and serialization-safe.

## Quick start example

### DummyClassifier & DummyRegressor: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier, DummyRegressor

clf = DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent")
clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
baseline_acc = clf.score(X_test, y_test)

reg = DummyRegressor(strategy="median")
reg.fit(X_train, y_train_num)
baseline_preds = reg.predict(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Dummy, Metrics } from '@kanaries/ml';

const clf = new Dummy.DummyClassifier({ strategy: 'mostFrequent' });
clf.fit(XTrain, yTrain);
const baselineAcc = Metrics.accuracyScore(yTest, clf.predict(XTest));

const reg = new Dummy.DummyRegressor({ strategy: 'median' });
reg.fit(XTrain, yTrainNum);
const baselineRmse = Math.sqrt(Metrics.meanSquaredError(yTestNum, reg.predict(XTest)));
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Dummy.DummyClassifier(props?)`

| Parameter     | Type                                                                   | Default     | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `strategy`    | `'prior' \| 'mostFrequent' \| 'stratified' \| 'uniform' \| 'constant'` | `'prior'`   | `'prior'` predicts majority class and returns empirical priors from `predictProba`; `'mostFrequent'` returns one-hot mode in `predictProba`; `'stratified'` draws from empirical class frequencies; `'uniform'` samples classes equally; `'constant'` always predicts `constant`. |
| `constant`    | `number`                                                               | `undefined` | Required when `strategy: 'constant'`; must appear in training `y`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `randomState` | `number`                                                               | `undefined` | Seed for `'stratified'` and `'uniform'` strategies.                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Methods**: `fit(X, y, sampleWeight?)`, `predict(X)`, `predictProba(X)`, `score(X, y)`, `getParams()`, `setParams()`, `clone()`, `toJSON()`.

### `new Dummy.DummyRegressor(props?)`

| Parameter  | Type                                             | Default     | Description                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------ | ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `strategy` | `'mean' \| 'median' \| 'quantile' \| 'constant'` | `'mean'`    | `'mean'` predicts the (optionally weighted) target mean; `'median'` predicts the exact median; `'quantile'` predicts linear-interpolated `quantile`; `'constant'` always predicts `constant`. |
| `quantile` | `number`                                         | `undefined` | Required in `[0, 1]` when `strategy: 'quantile'` (`0.5` equals median).                                                                                                                       |
| `constant` | `number`                                         | `undefined` | Required when `strategy: 'constant'`.                                                                                                                                                         |

**Methods**: `fit(X, y, sampleWeight?)`, `predict(X)`, `score(X, y)`, `getParams()`, `setParams()`, `clone()`, `toJSON()`.

- **Compatibility note**: `sampleWeight` in `DummyRegressor` is supported for `strategy: 'mean'` (passing weights with `'median'` or `'quantile'` throws a clear error).
- **Related pages**: [Evaluation Metrics](/docs/apis/metrics/index.html.md), [Model Selection & Cross-Validation](/docs/apis/utils/modelSelection.md), [Confusion Matrix Calculator](/tools/confusion-matrix-calculator).

---
title: "AdaBoost Classifier in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Train boosted ensemble classifiers in JavaScript and TypeScript with AdaBoostClassifier in @kanaries/ml. Includes runnable browser/Node.js code and API docs."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/ensemble/adaboostClassifier"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/ensemble/adaboostClassifier.md"
---
# AdaBoost Classifier in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

AdaBoostClassifier focuses on hard examples across rounds to improve classification performance over weak learners.

This algorithm is especially useful when:

- Baseline classifiers miss difficult boundary regions.
- You need improved recall/precision without switching to heavy models.
- You can invest in hyperparameter tuning for learning rate and rounds.

## JavaScript implementation

@kanaries/ml exposes AdaBoost classification in JavaScript so you can build stronger tabular classifiers without leaving the browser or Node.js ecosystem. It is a good option when a single weak learner is too simple, but you still want a relatively compact model with straightforward prediction logic.

That makes it attractive for product-side decision systems and TypeScript services that need boosting behavior without operating a separate Python inference path.

## Quick start

### AdaBoostClassifier: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.ensemble import AdaBoostClassifier

X = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [1, 0], [0, 1]]
y = [0, 1, 1, 0]

clf = AdaBoostClassifier(n_estimators=25, learning_rate=0.5, random_state=0)
clf.fit(X, y)
pred = clf.predict([[0.9, 0.8], [0.1, 0.2]])
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Ensemble } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [1, 0], [0, 1]];
const y = [0, 1, 1, 0];

const clf = new Ensemble.AdaBoostClassifier({ nEstimators: 25, learningRate: 0.5 });
clf.fit(X, y);
const pred = clf.predict([[0.9, 0.8], [0.1, 0.2]]);
```

### Quick JavaScript example

```ts
import { Ensemble } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [1, 0], [0, 1]];
const y = [0, 1, 1, 0];

const clf = new Ensemble.AdaBoostClassifier({ nEstimators: 25, learningRate: 0.5 });
clf.fit(X, y);
const pred = clf.predict([[0.9, 0.8], [0.1, 0.2]]);
console.log(pred);
```

## Detailed API reference

```ts
interface AdaBoostClassifierProps {
    nEstimators?: number;
    learningRate?: number;
    randomState?: number;
}
constructor(props: AdaBoostClassifierProps = {})
```

### Parameters

| name         | type   | default   | description                   |
| ------------ | ------ | --------- | ----------------------------- |
| nEstimators  | number | 50        | Number of boosting iterations |
| learningRate | number | 1.0       | Weight applied to each stump  |
| randomState  | number | undefined | Seed for reproducibility      |

### Algorithm

AdaBoostClassifier trains decision stumps sequentially and reweights samples so that misclassified points receive more focus in subsequent rounds. It selects the number of classes automatically:

- **Binary (K = 2):** discrete AdaBoost over polarity stumps with the one-sided SAMME weight update. Any two numeric labels are supported (they no longer have to be literal `0`/`1`); classes are sorted numerically and predictions are mapped back to the original labels.
- **Multiclass (K > 2):** SAMME (Zhu et al., 2009), sklearn's `AdaBoostClassifier` algorithm. The weak learner is a weighted-misclassification-optimal multiclass stump (each side predicts its weighted-majority class), a stump is accepted while its weighted error stays below `1 - 1/K`, and `alpha = learning_rate * (log((1 - err) / err) + log(K - 1))`. Misclassified samples are up-weighted by `exp(alpha)`, and `predict` takes the argmax of the alpha-weighted votes.

### Methods

- `fit(trainX: number[][], trainY: number[]): void`
- `predict(testX: number[][]): number[]`
- `predictProba(testX: number[][]): number[][]`
- `getFeatureImportances(): number[]`

`predictProba` returns one column per class, ordered by the sorted class labels (for multiclass this is the normalized alpha-weighted vote share, a documented heuristic rather than a calibrated probability). `getFeatureImportances` covers both the binary and multiclass paths.

### Implementation workflow

1. Start with balanced preprocessing and clear label quality checks.
2. Fit with several estimator counts and compare classification metrics.
3. Tune threshold and class-weight strategy for product-specific tradeoffs.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Use AdaBoost when a simple linear or shallow-tree baseline is close to useful but misses harder examples.
- Monitor overfitting as you increase the number of estimators, especially on smaller datasets.
- It works best on structured tabular features rather than large-scale unstructured inputs.

title: "AdaBoost Regressor in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"

canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/ensemble/adaboostRegressor"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/ensemble/adaboostRegressor.md"
---
# AdaBoost Regressor in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

AdaBoostRegressor combines weak regressors sequentially to improve predictive accuracy on non-linear regression patterns.

This algorithm is especially useful when:

- Single linear models underfit important non-linear behavior.
- You need stronger regression quality with manageable model complexity.
- Your deployment environment requires fast JS inference.

## JavaScript implementation

@kanaries/ml provides AdaBoost regression in JavaScript for teams that want a stronger non-linear regressor than a single tree or plain linear model, while still keeping inference straightforward. This is useful in product analytics, pricing, or forecasting-style features implemented in Node.js or TypeScript services.

Because the estimator is available in JS, boosted regression can live in the same application layer that owns data fetching, feature building, and API responses.

## Interactive AdaBoost regression playground

Change the boosting rounds and data distribution to see how successive weak learners reshape the prediction. The curve is trained live with `Ensemble.AdaBoostRegressor`.

> The HTML version includes an interactive AdaBoost Regression playground powered by @kanaries/ml. You can change the dataset, noise, and model controls; add observations; and inspect live predictions plus train and holdout metrics. The runnable guide and API reference continue below. [Open the HTML page](https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/ensemble/adaboostRegressor).

## Quick start

### AdaBoostRegressor: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.ensemble import AdaBoostRegressor

X = [[0], [1], [2], [3], [4]]
y = [1.0, 1.8, 3.1, 3.9, 5.2]

reg = AdaBoostRegressor(n_estimators=50, learning_rate=0.5, random_state=0)
reg.fit(X, y)
pred = reg.predict([[1.5], [3.5]])
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Ensemble } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0], [1], [2], [3], [4]];
const y = [1.0, 1.8, 3.1, 3.9, 5.2];

const reg = new Ensemble.AdaBoostRegressor({ n_estimators: 50, learning_rate: 0.5 });
reg.fit(X, y);
const pred = reg.predict([[1.5], [3.5]]);
```

### Quick JavaScript example

```ts
import { Ensemble } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0], [1], [2], [3], [4]];
const y = [1.0, 1.8, 3.1, 3.9, 5.2];

const reg = new Ensemble.AdaBoostRegressor({ n_estimators: 50, learning_rate: 0.5 });
reg.fit(X, y);
const pred = reg.predict([[1.5], [3.5]]);
console.log(pred);
```

## Detailed API reference

```ts
constructor(props?: { estimator?: DecisionTreeRegressor; n_estimators?: number; learning_rate?: number; randomState?: number })
```

Both `n_estimators`/`nEstimators`, `learning_rate`/`learningRate`, and `randomState`/`random_state` casings are accepted.

### Parameters

| name          | type                  | default      | description                                                     |
| ------------- | --------------------- | ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| estimator     | DecisionTreeRegressor | depth 3 tree | Base learner used in boosting                                   |
| n_estimators  | number                | 50           | Number of boosting rounds                                       |
| learning_rate | number                | 1.0          | Shrinks the contribution of each regressor in the weight update |
| randomState   | number                | undefined    | Seed for the weighted resampling, for reproducible fits         |

### Algorithm

This is AdaBoost.R2 (Drucker, 1997), matching sklearn's `AdaBoostRegressor` with linear loss. Each round draws a weighted sample of rows, fits a regressor, computes per-sample linear losses, and reweights samples so hard examples get more focus in later rounds; `learning_rate` scales the weight update. Prediction is the **weighted median** of the estimators' predictions (not the weighted mean), which is robust to outlier estimators. A perfectly-fitting estimator is kept and stops boosting, and the ensemble is never left empty (the first estimator is retained even if its weighted error is too high), so the model does not silently collapse to predicting 0.

### Methods

- `fit(trainX: number[][], trainY: number[]): void`
- `predict(testX: number[][]): number[]`

### Implementation workflow

1. Train with a conservative learning rate and enough estimators.
2. Validate MAE/RMSE on holdout data and monitor overfitting.
3. Tune estimator count and learning rate for stability vs accuracy.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Compare AdaBoost regression against a simple tree or linear baseline to confirm the extra complexity is paying off.
- Tune estimator count and learning rate together rather than adjusting them in isolation.
- This model is best suited to tabular regression problems where moderate boosting depth improves fit quality.

# BaggingClassifier in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml

## Algorithm overview

**BaggingClassifier** (Bootstrap Aggregating) trains an ensemble of `nEstimators` classifiers—each fitted on a different random subset of the training rows—and combines their outputs by majority vote. Bagging is specifically designed to reduce **variance** in high-variance, low-bias base learners such as unpruned decision trees, k-nearest neighbors, or small neural models without increasing bias.

Unlike [RandomForestClassifier](/docs/apis/ensemble/randomForestClassifier.md), which specifically pairs decision trees with per-split feature subsampling, `BaggingClassifier` is a general meta-ensemble: you can bag the default `DecisionTreeClassifier` or wrap any custom classifier via `estimatorFactory`.

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides `Ensemble.BaggingClassifier` in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js runtimes. By default it uses `DecisionTreeClassifier` members with `bootstrap: true` (sampling with replacement) and deterministic `randomState` seeding. Passing `bootstrap: false` switches from bagging to **pasting** (sampling subsets without replacement).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Ensemble } from '@kanaries/ml';

const clf = new Ensemble.BaggingClassifier({
  nEstimators: 20,
  maxSamples: 3,
  randomState: 12,
});

clf.fit([[0, 0], [0, 1], [3, 3], [4, 3]], [0, 0, 1, 1]);
const pred = clf.predict([[1, 1], [4, 4]]);
console.log(pred);
```

### BaggingClassifier: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier

clf = BaggingClassifier(
  n_estimators=20,
  max_samples=0.8,
  bootstrap=True,
  random_state=12,
)
clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
preds = clf.predict(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Ensemble } from '@kanaries/ml';

const clf = new Ensemble.BaggingClassifier({
nEstimators: 20,
maxSamples: 3,
bootstrap: true,
randomState: 12,
});
clf.fit(XTrain, yTrain);
const preds = clf.predict(XTest);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Ensemble.BaggingClassifier(props?)`

| Parameter          | Type                                  | Default                  | Description                                                                            |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nEstimators`      | `number`                              | `10`                     | Number of base classifiers in the ensemble.                                            |
| `maxSamples`       | `number`                              | `X.length`               | Samples drawn per estimator (integer count or fraction in `(0, 1]`).                   |
| `bootstrap`        | `boolean`                             | `true`                   | Sample with replacement (`true` = bagging) or without replacement (`false` = pasting). |
| `randomState`      | `number`                              | `undefined`              | Seed for reproducible subsampling and member seeds.                                    |
| `estimatorFactory` | `(seed?: number) => { fit, predict }` | `DecisionTreeClassifier` | Optional factory returning a fresh base classifier per ensemble member.                |

### Methods & usage guidance

- `fit(trainX: number[][], trainY: number[]): void` — draws `nEstimators` sample subsets and fits each member.
- `predict(testX: number[][]): number[]` — predicts by majority vote across all fitted members.
- **When to prefer Random Forest**: If your base estimator is a decision tree and your dataset has many correlated features, [`Ensemble.RandomForestClassifier`](/docs/apis/ensemble/randomForestClassifier.md) usually outperforms plain bagging by also subsampling features at every split.
- **Related pages**: [BaggingRegressor](/docs/apis/ensemble/baggingRegressor.md), [RandomForestClassifier](/docs/apis/ensemble/randomForestClassifier.md), [AdaBoostClassifier](/docs/apis/ensemble/adaboostClassifier.md).

# BaggingRegressor in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml

## Algorithm overview

**BaggingRegressor** (Bootstrap Aggregating for regression) fits multiple cloned regressors on independent random subsets of the training data and averages their continuous predictions. Averaging smooths out the sharp variance of unstable base learners—most commonly unpruned [regression trees](/docs/apis/tree/decisionTreeRegressor.md)—while preserving their flexibility on non-linear curves.

Because `BaggingRegressor` accepts any registered `@kanaries/ml` regressor as its `estimator` prototype, you can also bag ridge regressors, k-nearest-neighbor regressors, or polynomial models to stabilize predictions on noisy datasets.

## JavaScript implementation

`Ensemble.BaggingRegressor` runs in pure TypeScript across browsers and Node.js, clones the base `estimator` cleanly via `BaseEstimator.clone()`, supports deterministic `randomState` seeding, integrates into [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md), and serializes with `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Interactive bagging regression playground

Vary the ensemble size and noise level to see bootstrap averaging smooth out individual tree predictions. The curve is fitted live with `Ensemble.BaggingRegressor` and responds immediately when you click to add training points.

> The HTML version includes an interactive Bagging Regression playground powered by @kanaries/ml. You can change the dataset, noise, and model controls; add observations; and inspect live predictions plus train and holdout metrics. The runnable guide and API reference continue below. [Open the HTML page](https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/ensemble/baggingRegressor).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Ensemble } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0], [1], [2], [3], [4]];
const y = [0, 1, 4, 9, 16];
const model = new Ensemble.BaggingRegressor({
  nEstimators: 25,
  maxSamples: 0.8,
  randomState: 42,
});
model.fit(X, y);
console.log(model.predict([[2.5]]));
```

### BaggingRegressor: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python

  n_estimators=25,
  max_samples=0.8,
  bootstrap=True,
  random_state=42,
)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
preds = model.predict(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts

nEstimators: 25,
maxSamples: 0.8,
bootstrap: true,
randomState: 42,

```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Ensemble.BaggingRegressor(props?)`

| Parameter     | Type            | Default                 | Description                                                             |
| ------------- | --------------- | ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `estimator`   | `RegressorBase` | `DecisionTreeRegressor` | Base regressor prototype cloned once per ensemble member.               |
| `nEstimators` | `number`        | `10`                    | Number of bagged regressors averaged during `predict()`.                |
| `maxSamples`  | `number`        | `1.0`                   | Fraction in `(0, 1]` or integer count of samples drawn per member.      |
| `bootstrap`   | `boolean`       | `true`                  | Sample rows with replacement (`true`) or without replacement (`false`). |
| `randomState` | `number`        | `undefined`             | Seed for reproducible resampling.                                       |

### Methods

- `fit(X: number[][], y: number[]): void` — fits `nEstimators` cloned regressors on resampled rows.
- `predict(X: number[][]): number[]` — returns the element-wise mean prediction across all members.
- **Related pages**: [BaggingClassifier](/docs/apis/ensemble/baggingClassifier.md), [RandomForestRegressor](/docs/apis/ensemble/randomForestRegressor.md), [ExtraTreesRegressor](/docs/apis/ensemble/extraTreesRegressor.md).

# ExtraTreesClassifier in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml

## Algorithm overview

**ExtraTreesClassifier** (Extremely Randomized Trees) builds an ensemble of randomized decision trees similar to [RandomForestClassifier](/docs/apis/ensemble/randomForestClassifier.md), but goes one step further in randomization: instead of searching for the exact optimal split threshold on every candidate feature, each node draws **random split thresholds** for each candidate feature and keeps the best among those random cuts.

This extra randomness brings two practical advantages:

- **Lower variance on noisy features**: randomized thresholds prevent trees from clinging to minor fluctuations in continuous measurements.
- **Faster tree construction**: evaluating a few random thresholds instead of scanning every sorted unique value speeds up training in JavaScript, especially on continuous tabular datasets.

## JavaScript implementation

`Ensemble.ExtraTreesClassifier` trains independent [`ExtraTreeClassifier`](/docs/apis/tree/extraTreeClassifier.md) members in pure TypeScript, averages their leaf class probabilities (`predictProba`), and selects the highest-probability class in `predict`. It exposes normalized `featureImportances` and sorted `classes` after fitting, supports deterministic `randomState` seeds, and serializes via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Ensemble } from '@kanaries/ml';

const model = new Ensemble.ExtraTreesClassifier({
  nEstimators: 100,
  max_features: 'sqrt',
  randomState: 42,
});
model.fit([[0, 0], [0, 1], [3, 3], [4, 3]], [0, 0, 1, 1]);
console.log(model.predict([[0.2, 0.1], [3.5, 3]]), model.featureImportances);
```

### ExtraTreesClassifier: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.ensemble import ExtraTreesClassifier

model = ExtraTreesClassifier(
  n_estimators=100,
  max_features="sqrt",
  random_state=42,
)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
preds = model.predict(X_test)
proba = model.predict_proba(X_test)
importances = model.feature_importances_
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Ensemble } from '@kanaries/ml';

const model = new Ensemble.ExtraTreesClassifier({
nEstimators: 100,
max_features: 'sqrt',
randomState: 42,
});
model.fit(XTrain, yTrain);
const preds = model.predict(XTest);
const proba = model.predictProba(XTest);
const importances = model.featureImportances;
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Ensemble.ExtraTreesClassifier(props?)`

| Parameter      | Type                                  | Default     | Description                                                                                                                            |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------- | ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nEstimators`  | `number`                              | `100`       | Number of randomized trees in the ensemble.                                                                                            |
| `bootstrap`    | `boolean`                             | `false`     | Whether to fit each tree on a bootstrap sample (defaults to `false` like scikit-learn, using the full dataset with randomized splits). |
| `max_features` | `number \| 'sqrt' \| 'log2' \| 'all'` | `'sqrt'`    | Candidate features evaluated per node split.                                                                                           |
| `randomState`  | `number`                              | `undefined` | Seed for deterministic threshold draws and sampling.                                                                                   |
| Tree options   | `ExtraTreeClassifier` props           | —           | Supports depth and split controls such as `max_depth`, `min_samples_split`, and `criterion`.                                           |

### Methods & properties

| Member                           | Signature                              | Description                                                                |
| -------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `fit`                            | `(X: number[][], y: number[]) => void` | Fits the ensemble and computes averaged `featureImportances`.              |
| `predictProba`                   | `(X: number[][]) => number[][]`        | Averages leaf class probability distributions across all trees.            |
| `predict`                        | `(X: number[][]) => number[]`          | Returns the highest-probability class per sample.                          |
| `classes` / `featureImportances` | `number[]`                             | Sorted class labels and impurity-based feature importances summing to `1`. |

### Extra Trees vs Random Forest

- Try `ExtraTreesClassifier` when you have many noisy continuous features, need `predictProba` and `featureImportances`, or want faster training in browser sessions.
- Pair with [`FeatureSelection.SelectFromModel`](/docs/apis/feature_selection/selectors.md) to prune low-importance columns automatically.
- **Related pages**: [ExtraTreesRegressor](/docs/apis/ensemble/extraTreesRegressor.md), [RandomForestClassifier](/docs/apis/ensemble/randomForestClassifier.md), [ExtraTreeClassifier](/docs/apis/tree/extraTreeClassifier.md).

# ExtraTreesRegressor in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml

## Algorithm overview

**ExtraTreesRegressor** builds an ensemble of extremely randomized [regression trees](/docs/apis/tree/extraTreeRegressor.md) and averages their numeric outputs. Instead of scanning every candidate cut point to minimize squared error at each node, each tree draws random split thresholds per candidate feature and keeps the best random split.

This extra split randomization frequently produces smoother prediction curves than [RandomForestRegressor](/docs/apis/ensemble/randomForestRegressor.md) on noisy continuous features while training faster in pure JavaScript—because avoiding full threshold sweeps cuts per-node work dramatically.

## JavaScript implementation

`Ensemble.ExtraTreesRegressor` runs in browsers and Node.js with zero native dependencies, supports deterministic `randomState` seeding, exposes averaged `featureImportances` for feature ranking, composes with [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md), and serializes via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Interactive Extra Trees regression playground

Adjust the number of randomized trees, reroll the sample, or click to add a training point. The prediction curve is fitted live with `Ensemble.ExtraTreesRegressor` in your browser.

> The HTML version includes an interactive Extra Trees Regression playground powered by @kanaries/ml. You can change the dataset, noise, and model controls; add observations; and inspect live predictions plus train and holdout metrics. The runnable guide and API reference continue below. [Open the HTML page](https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/ensemble/extraTreesRegressor).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Ensemble } from '@kanaries/ml';

  nEstimators: 100,
  max_features: 'all',
  randomState: 42,
});
model.fit([[0], [1], [2], [3], [4]], [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]);
console.log(model.predict([[2.5]]), model.featureImportances);
```

### ExtraTreesRegressor: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

## Detailed API reference

### `new Ensemble.ExtraTreesRegressor(props?)`

| Parameter      | Type                                  | Default     | Description                                                                                               |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------- | ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nEstimators`  | `number`                              | `100`       | Number of extremely randomized regression trees in the ensemble.                                          |
| `bootstrap`    | `boolean`                             | `false`     | Whether each tree trains on a bootstrap sample (`false` trains each tree on all rows with random splits). |
| `max_features` | `number \| 'sqrt' \| 'log2' \| 'all'` | `'all'`     | Candidate features evaluated per split.                                                                   |

### Methods & properties

- `fit(X: number[][], y: number[]): void` — trains all trees and aggregates `featureImportances`.
- `predict(X: number[][]): number[]` — averages predictions across all trees.
- `featureImportances: number[]` — normalized impurity-reduction importances after fitting.
- **Related pages**: [RandomForestRegressor](/docs/apis/ensemble/randomForestRegressor.md), [ExtraTreesClassifier](/docs/apis/ensemble/extraTreesClassifier.md), [ExtraTreeRegressor](/docs/apis/tree/extraTreeRegressor.md).

title: "Gradient Boosting Classifier in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Train gradient boosted classification trees in JavaScript and TypeScript with @kanaries/ml. Includes Python comparison, interactive options, and API docs."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/ensemble/gradientBoostingClassifier"

# Gradient Boosting Classifier in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

GradientBoostingClassifier builds an additive model of shallow regression trees for classification, using log loss and a per-leaf Newton step so each round sharpens the decision function.

This algorithm is especially useful when:

- A single tree or linear classifier misses non-linear class boundaries.
- You need calibrated-looking probabilities alongside class predictions.
- You want a strong boosting baseline for binary or multiclass tabular data.

## JavaScript implementation

@kanaries/ml provides gradient boosting classification in JavaScript following sklearn's semantics, and it switches automatically between binary and multiclass fits:

- **Binary (K = 2):** log loss. `F_0` is the log-odds of the positive class, each round fits one regression tree to the negative gradient `y - p`, then replaces every leaf value with the Newton step `sum(residuals) / sum(p * (1 - p))`.
- **Multiclass (K > 2):** multinomial deviance. `F_0k = log(prior_k)`, and each round fits K trees (one per class) to `y_k - softmax_k(F)` using the shared pre-round probabilities, with the per-leaf Newton step `(K-1)/K * sum(residuals) / sum(p * (1 - p))`.

Arbitrary numeric labels are supported (sorted internally), and `subsample`, `maxFeatures`, and a seedable `randomState` are available for stochastic, reproducible fits.

## Quick start

### GradientBoostingClassifier: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier

X = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [1, 0], [0, 1]]
y = [0, 1, 1, 0]

clf = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=100, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3, random_state=0)
clf.fit(X, y)
pred = clf.predict([[0.9, 0.8], [0.1, 0.2]])
proba = clf.predict_proba([[0.9, 0.8]])
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Ensemble } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [1, 0], [0, 1]];
const y = [0, 1, 1, 0];

const clf = new Ensemble.GradientBoostingClassifier({ nEstimators: 100, learningRate: 0.1, maxDepth: 3, randomState: 0 });
clf.fit(X, y);
const pred = clf.predict([[0.9, 0.8], [0.1, 0.2]]);
const proba = clf.predictProba([[0.9, 0.8]]);
```

### Quick JavaScript example

```ts
import { Ensemble } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [1, 0], [0, 1]];
const y = [0, 1, 1, 0];

const clf = new Ensemble.GradientBoostingClassifier({ nEstimators: 100, learningRate: 0.1, maxDepth: 3, randomState: 0 });
clf.fit(X, y);
const pred = clf.predict([[0.9, 0.8], [0.1, 0.2]]);
const proba = clf.predictProba([[0.9, 0.8]]);
console.log(proba);
```

## Detailed API reference

```ts
interface GradientBoostingClassifierProps {
    nEstimators?: number;
    learningRate?: number;
    maxDepth?: number;
    minSamplesSplit?: number;
    subsample?: number;
    maxFeatures?: number | 'sqrt' | 'log2';
    randomState?: number;
}

constructor(props: GradientBoostingClassifierProps = {})
```

Every parameter also accepts its snake_case alias (`n_estimators`, `learning_rate`, `max_depth`, `min_samples_split`, `max_features`, `random_state`).

### Parameters

| name            | type                       | default   | description                                                                                        |
| --------------- | -------------------------- | --------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| nEstimators     | number                     | 100       | Number of boosting rounds (binary: 1 tree/round; multiclass: K trees/round)                        |
| learningRate    | number                     | 0.1       | Shrinks the contribution of each tree                                                              |
| maxDepth        | number                     | 3         | Maximum depth of each regression tree                                                              |
| minSamplesSplit | number                     | 2         | Minimum samples required to split a node                                                           |
| subsample       | number                     | 1.0       | Fraction of rows sampled without replacement per round; `< 1` enables stochastic gradient boosting |
| maxFeatures     | number \| 'sqrt' \| 'log2' | undefined | Number/strategy for features considered at each split                                              |
| randomState     | number                     | undefined | Seed for reproducible fits                                                                         |

### Algorithm

For binary problems the model boosts a single decision function with log loss and applies a Newton update to every leaf. For K > 2 classes it fits one tree per class each round against the shared softmax residuals (multinomial deviance) and applies the `(K-1)/K` Newton step per leaf. `predict` and `predictProba` share the same decision function (for binary, `F >= 0` maps to `P >= 0.5`).

### Methods

- `fit(trainX: number[][], trainY: number[]): void`
- `predict(testX: number[][]): number[]`
- `predictProba(testX: number[][]): number[][]`

`predictProba` returns one column per class, ordered by the sorted class labels (K columns; two columns `[1 - p, p]` in the binary case).

### Implementation workflow

1. Prepare cleaned tabular features and clean class labels (binary or multiclass).
2. Fit with a conservative learning rate and enough rounds, validating log loss/accuracy on holdout data.
3. Tune `learningRate`, `nEstimators`, and `maxDepth`, and add `subsample`/`maxFeatures` regularization if the model overfits.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Because a failed refit validates labels before touching model state, an already-fitted classifier stays intact if a later `fit` call throws.
- Keep trees shallow (`maxDepth` 2-4) for classic gradient boosting behavior.
- Read `predictProba` columns in sorted-label order when mapping probabilities back to your class names.

canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/ensemble/gradientBoostingRegressor"
