# Lasso Regression in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml

## Algorithm overview

**Lasso Regression** (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) adds an **L1 penalty** (`alpha * ||w||₁`) to the least-squares regression objective. Because the L1 norm has sharp corners along coordinate axes, soft-thresholding during coordinate descent drives weak or irrelevant feature weights to **exact zero**—performing automatic embedded feature selection alongside regularization.

Use Lasso Regression when:

- Your dataset contains many candidate numeric features but only a subset truly drives the target.
- You want a compact, human-interpretable linear formula with sparse non-zero coefficients.
- You need embedded feature selection inside [`FeatureSelection.SelectFromModel`](/docs/apis/feature_selection/selectors.md) or a browser-side analytics workflow.

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides `Linear.LassoRegression` and its scikit-learn alias `Linear.Lasso`, solved via deterministic coordinate descent in pure TypeScript for browsers and Node.js. It composes with [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md), supports `getParams()` / `setParams()` for hyperparameter search, and serializes via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Interactive Lasso regression playground

Adjust the L1 penalty (`alpha`), dataset shape, and noise level below. The regression curve refits live with `Linear.LassoRegression` in your browser as you drag sliders or click to add data points.

> The HTML version includes an interactive Lasso Regression playground powered by @kanaries/ml. You can change the dataset, noise, and model controls; add observations; and inspect live predictions plus train and holdout metrics. The runnable guide and API reference continue below. [Open the HTML page](https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/linear/lassoRegression).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Linear } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 1], [1, 1], [2, 0], [3, 0]];
const y = [1, 2, 3, 4];

const model = new Linear.LassoRegression({ alpha: 0.1, maxIter: 1000, tol: 1e-6 });
model.fit(X, y);
const pred = model.predict([[4, 0]]);
console.log(pred);
```

### Lasso Regression (LassoRegression / Lasso): Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso

model = Lasso(alpha=0.1, max_iter=1000, tol=1e-6)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
preds = model.predict(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Linear } from '@kanaries/ml';

const model = new Linear.Lasso({ alpha: 0.1, maxIter: 1000, tol: 1e-6 });
model.fit(XTrain, yTrain);
const preds = model.predict(XTest);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Linear.LassoRegression(props?)` / `new Linear.Lasso(props?)`

| Parameter      | Type      | Default | Description                                                                                                 |
| -------------- | --------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `alpha`        | `number`  | `1`     | L1 penalty strength. Larger values push more coefficients to exact zero.                                    |
| `fitIntercept` | `boolean` | `true`  | Estimate an unpenalized intercept term.                                                                     |
| `maxIter`      | `number`  | `1000`  | Maximum coordinate-descent passes. Increase if convergence is slow on small `alpha` or correlated features. |
| `tol`          | `number`  | `1e-6`  | Convergence tolerance on maximum coefficient update per pass.                                               |

### Methods & practical guidance

- `fit(X: number[][], Y: number[]): void` — runs cyclic coordinate descent with soft-thresholding.
- `predict(X: number[][]): number[]` — computes linear predictions from the sparse weights.
- **Standardize features first**: Always pair Lasso with [`StandardScaler`](/docs/apis/utils/preprocessing.md) inside a [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md); unscaled columns receive unequal effective L1 penalties.
- **Highly correlated predictors**: Pure L1 tends to select one arbitrary feature from a correlated group and zero out the rest. Switch to [`Linear.ElasticNet`](/docs/apis/linear/elasticNet.md) when you want grouped selection with stability.
- **Related pages**: [Ridge Regression](/docs/apis/linear/ridgeRegression.md), [ElasticNet](/docs/apis/linear/elasticNet.md), [Feature Selection](/docs/apis/feature_selection/index.html.md).

# Linear Regression in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

LinearRegression models continuous targets with an interpretable linear relationship between features and outputs.

This algorithm is especially useful when:

- You need a transparent baseline for numeric prediction tasks.
- Feature-target relationships are approximately linear after transformation.
- You want fast training and low-latency inference in JavaScript.

## JavaScript implementation

@kanaries/ml gives JavaScript teams a straightforward linear regression implementation for numeric prediction tasks that need to stay in the application layer. This is useful for browser-side demos, pricing calculators, forecasting helpers, and Node.js APIs that want transparent coefficients instead of opaque black-box behavior.

Because the model is simple and explainable, it fits especially well in product contexts where engineers and stakeholders need to reason about why a prediction changed.

## Interactive linear regression playground

Change the dataset and noise, then click the chart to add your own observation. The fitted line and holdout metrics update immediately using `Linear.LinearRegression` in your browser.

> The HTML version includes an interactive Linear Regression playground powered by @kanaries/ml. You can change the dataset, noise, and model controls; add observations; and inspect live predictions plus train and holdout metrics. The runnable guide and API reference continue below. [Open the HTML page](https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/linear/linearRegression).

## Quick start

### LinearRegression: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X = [[0], [1], [2], [3]]
y = [1, 3, 5, 7]

reg = LinearRegression()
reg.fit(X, y)
pred = reg.predict([[4], [5]])
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Linear } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0], [1], [2], [3]];
const y = [1, 3, 5, 7];

const reg = new Linear.LinearRegression();
reg.fit(X, y);
const pred = reg.predict([[4], [5]]);
```

### Quick JavaScript example

```ts
import { Linear } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0], [1], [2], [3]];
const y = [1, 3, 5, 7];

const reg = new Linear.LinearRegression();
reg.fit(X, y);
const pred = reg.predict([[4], [5]]);
console.log(pred);
```

## Detailed API reference

```ts
constructor()
```

This class implements ordinary least squares linear regression. It estimates
coefficients for a linear model by minimizing the squared error between
predicted and actual values.

### Methods

- `fit(X: number[][], Y: number[]): void`
- `predict(X: number[][]): number[]`

#### fit

- `X` - Feature matrix of shape `[nSamples, nFeatures]`.
- `Y` - Target values of length `nSamples`.

#### predict

- `X` - Feature matrix for which to compute predictions.

### Implementation workflow

1. Prepare numeric features and split into train/validation sets.
2. Fit the model and inspect residual patterns for systematic errors.
3. Iterate on feature engineering when residuals show non-linear structure.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Use linear regression as a baseline before moving to more complex non-linear models.
- Inspect residuals to decide whether feature engineering or a different model family is needed.
- This estimator is a strong fit for small to medium tabular problems where interpretability matters.

title: "Logistic Regression in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"

# Logistic Regression in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

Logistic regression is a classic supervised learning algorithm for binary and multiclass classification. It models class probabilities with a sigmoid for two classes and multinomial softmax for three or more classes, which makes it useful when you need both a final prediction and interpretable linear scores.

This algorithm works especially well when:

- you need a strong and explainable baseline for binary or multiclass classification
- you want probability-like outputs for ranking, thresholding, or alerts
- your decision boundary is approximately linear after feature engineering or scaling

Compared with heavier models, logistic regression is fast to train, easy to inspect, and usually a sensible first model before trying trees, SVMs, or ensembles.

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides a JavaScript and TypeScript implementation of logistic regression so you can run classification workflows without leaving the JS ecosystem. That means you can train or serve models in browser applications, Node.js services, and frontend-heavy products that want a scikit-learn-like API without switching to Python at runtime.

This is particularly useful for product decisions, ranking thresholds, and multiclass prediction tasks where teams want coefficients and prediction logic to stay understandable to both engineers and stakeholders.

## Quick start

### LogisticRegression: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [1, 0], [0, 1]]
y = [0, 1, 1, 0]

clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=500, random_state=0)
clf.fit(X, y)
pred = clf.predict([[0.9, 0.8], [0.2, 0.1]])
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Linear } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [1, 0], [0, 1]];
const y = [0, 1, 1, 0];

const clf = new Linear.LogisticRegression({ learningRate: 0.1, maxIter: 800 });
clf.fit(X, y);
const pred = clf.predict([[0.9, 0.8], [0.2, 0.1]]);
```

### Quick JavaScript example

```ts
import { Linear } from '@kanaries/ml';

const trainX = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [1, 0], [0, 1]];
const trainY = [0, 1, 1, 0];

const model = new Linear.LogisticRegression({
    learningRate: 0.1,
    maxIter: 800,
});

model.fit(trainX, trainY);

const predictions = model.predict([[0.9, 0.8], [0.2, 0.1]]);
console.log(predictions);
```

> The HTML version includes an interactive logistic regression visualization. The complete runnable example and API details are included in this Markdown page. [Open the HTML page](https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/linear/logisticRegression).

## Detailed API reference

```ts
interface LogisticRegressionProps {
    learningRate?: number;
    maxIter?: number;
    C?: number | null;
}
constructor(props: LogisticRegressionProps = {})
```

`learningRate` controls the optimizer step size, `maxIter` controls how many optimization rounds the model runs, and `C` is the inverse L2 regularization strength. The default `C: null` preserves the unregularized behavior from earlier releases.

### Parameters

- `learningRate`: gradient descent step size
- `maxIter`: maximum number of training iterations
- `C`: inverse L2 regularization strength; smaller positive values regularize more strongly, while `null` disables L2 regularization

### Methods

- `fit(trainX: number[][], trainY: number[]): void`
- `predict(testX: number[][]): number[]`
- `predictProba(testX: number[][]): number[][]`
- `decisionFunction(testX: number[][]): number[] | number[][]`

#### fit

- `trainX`: training features with shape `[nSamples, nFeatures]`
- `trainY`: numeric class labels for each training sample; at least two distinct classes are required

#### predict

- `testX`: feature matrix to classify

`predictProba` returns columns in sorted class-label order. `decisionFunction` returns one signed score for a binary fit and one logit column per class for a multiclass fit. The `coef` getter similarly returns one coefficient vector for binary classification or a matrix with one row per class.

### Usage notes

- Standardize numeric features before training for more stable optimization.
- Use this model when you want interpretable coefficients and threshold-based decision logic.
- For browser applications, move large training jobs into a Web Worker to keep the UI responsive.

canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/linear/polynomialRegression"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/linear/polynomialRegression.md"
---
# Polynomial Regression in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml

## Algorithm overview

**Polynomial Regression** extends linear regression to smooth non-linear curves by transforming each numeric input feature `x` into powers `[x, x², ..., xᵈ]` up to `degree` and fitting an ordinary least-squares model over the expanded basis. Although the resulting prediction curve is non-linear in `x`, the estimation problem remains strictly linear in the polynomial coefficients—meaning it solves rapidly in closed form with zero gradient-descent tuning.

Polynomial regression works best when:

- A scatter plot shows clear curvature (parabolic growth, diminishing returns, saturation) that a straight line underfits.
- You have a low-dimensional numeric problem where degree `2`–`4` captures the domain trend cleanly.
- You want lightweight, interpretable trendlines embedded directly inside browser charts or CSV calculators.

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides `Linear.PolynomialRegression` as a self-contained estimator in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js apps. Rather than manually constructing a separate polynomial basis transformer before fitting, `PolynomialRegression` encapsulates power expansion, fitting, and prediction inside one serializable estimator (`toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md)).

## Interactive polynomial regression playground

Adjust the polynomial degree, underlying data shape, and noise level below. The curve refits live with `Linear.PolynomialRegression`; click anywhere on the chart to see how an added point—or an overly high degree—bends the fit.

> The HTML version includes an interactive Polynomial Regression playground powered by @kanaries/ml. You can change the dataset, noise, and model controls; add observations; and inspect live predictions plus train and holdout metrics. The runnable guide and API reference continue below. [Open the HTML page](https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/linear/polynomialRegression).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Linear } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0], [1], [2], [3]];
const y = [1, 2, 5, 10];

const model = new Linear.PolynomialRegression({ degree: 2 });
model.fit(X, y);
const pred = model.predict([[4]]);
console.log(pred);
```

### Polynomial Regression: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

model = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree=2), LinearRegression())
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
preds = model.predict(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Linear } from '@kanaries/ml';

const model = new Linear.PolynomialRegression({ degree: 2 });
model.fit(XTrain, yTrain);
const preds = model.predict(XTest);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Linear.PolynomialRegression(props?)`

| Parameter | Type     | Default | Description                                                                                         |
| --------- | -------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `degree`  | `number` | `2`     | Integer `≥ 1` specifying the highest power per feature (`1` reduces to standard linear regression). |

### Methods

- `fit(X: number[][], Y: number[]): void` — expands each column to powers `1..degree` and fits ordinary least squares with an intercept.
- `predict(X: number[][]): number[]` — applies the same power expansion and returns predicted values.

### Avoiding polynomial overfitting

- **Keep degree low (`2` or `3`) unless cross-validation proves higher degree helps**: High degrees oscillate wildly between points (Runge's phenomenon) and diverge rapidly outside the training range. Read our practical guide on [how to choose polynomial degree](/docs/guides/choose-polynomial-degree.md) or test interactively in the [Polynomial Regression Calculator](/tools/polynomial-regression-calculator).
- **Scale inputs before high-degree fits**: Large `x` values (like years `2020..2026`) raised to the 4th power cause numerical ill-conditioning; center or standardize `X` with [`StandardScaler`](/docs/apis/utils/preprocessing.md) first.
- **Related pages**: [Choosing Polynomial Degree Guide](/docs/guides/choose-polynomial-degree.md), [Polynomial Regression Calculator](/tools/polynomial-regression-calculator), [Ridge Regression](/docs/apis/linear/ridgeRegression.md).

---
title: "RidgeClassifier in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Train fast L2-regularized linear classifiers in JavaScript and TypeScript with Linear.RidgeClassifier from @kanaries/ml for browser and Node.js apps."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/linear/ridgeClassifier"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/linear/ridgeClassifier.md"
---
# RidgeClassifier in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml

## Algorithm overview

**RidgeClassifier** repurposes L2-regularized [Ridge Regression](/docs/apis/linear/ridgeRegression.md) for binary and multiclass classification. It encodes target labels into numerical class indicators, solves one closed-form L2-penalized least-squares system per class (one-vs-rest), and predicts the class achieving the highest linear score.

Compared to iterative classifiers such as [Logistic Regression](/docs/apis/linear/logisticRegression.md) or [LinearSVC](/docs/apis/svm/LinearSVC.md), `RidgeClassifier` requires no learning-rate schedule or epoch budget and fits rapidly in closed form—making it a fast, low-variance baseline on numeric tabular datasets and standardized feature matrices.

Use `RidgeClassifier` when:

- You want deterministic, closed-form linear classification without tuning optimizer convergence.
- Features are correlated and benefit from L2 coefficient shrinkage (`alpha`).
- You only need hard class labels (or combine with [`Calibration.CalibratedClassifierCV`](/docs/apis/calibration/index.html.md) when calibrated probabilities are required).

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides `Linear.RidgeClassifier` in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js runtimes. It sorts unique numeric class labels ascending, fits one internal `RidgeRegression` per class, integrates cleanly into [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md) and [`utils.ModelSelection`](/docs/apis/utils/modelSelection.md), and serializes via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Linear } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [0, 1], [2, 2], [3, 2]];
const y = [0, 0, 1, 1];

const clf = new Linear.RidgeClassifier({ alpha: 1 });
clf.fit(X, y);
const pred = clf.predict([[1, 1], [3, 3]]);
console.log(pred);
```

### RidgeClassifier: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeClassifier

clf = RidgeClassifier(alpha=1.0, fit_intercept=True)
clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
preds = clf.predict(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Linear } from '@kanaries/ml';

const clf = new Linear.RidgeClassifier({ alpha: 1.0, fitIntercept: true });
clf.fit(XTrain, yTrain);
const preds = clf.predict(XTest);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Linear.RidgeClassifier(props?)`

| Parameter      | Type      | Default | Description                                                             |
| -------------- | --------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `alpha`        | `number`  | `1`     | Non-negative L2 regularization strength controlling variance reduction. |
| `fitIntercept` | `boolean` | `true`  | Include an unpenalized intercept term per class model.                  |

### Methods

- `fit(trainX: number[][], trainY: number[]): void` — sorts unique class labels and fits one `RidgeRegression` estimator per class.
- `predict(testX: number[][]): number[]` — evaluates every class score and returns the label with the highest score.

### Practical guidance

- Standardize input columns with [`StandardScaler`](/docs/apis/utils/preprocessing.md) inside a [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md) before sweeping `alpha` across logarithmic values (`0.01`, `0.1`, `1`, `10`, `100`).
- Need calibrated class probabilities out of the box? Compare against [`Linear.LogisticRegression`](/docs/apis/linear/logisticRegression.md) or [`DiscriminantAnalysis.LDA`](/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/lda.md).
- **Related pages**: [Logistic Regression](/docs/apis/linear/logisticRegression.md), [Ridge Regression](/docs/apis/linear/ridgeRegression.md), [LinearSVC](/docs/apis/svm/LinearSVC.md), [Confusion Matrix Calculator](/tools/confusion-matrix-calculator).

---
title: "Ridge Regression in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Fit L2-regularized linear regression in JavaScript and TypeScript with Linear.RidgeRegression (Ridge) from @kanaries/ml. Includes live demo and API reference."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/linear/ridgeRegression"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/linear/ridgeRegression.md"
---
# Ridge Regression in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml

## Algorithm overview

**Ridge Regression** adds an **L2 regularization penalty** (`alpha * ||w||²`) to the ordinary least squares objective. Whenever predictors are strongly correlated (multicollinearity), feature count approaches sample count, or unregularized coefficients explode in magnitude, L2 shrinkage pulls weights smoothly toward zero without forcing them to exactly zero—trading a tiny amount of bias for a substantial drop in prediction variance.

Use Ridge Regression when:

- Numeric features are collinear (for example, overlapping telemetry metrics or polynomial expansions).
- Ordinary least squares (`LinearRegression`) overfits training noise or exhibits wild coefficient swings across cross-validation folds.
- You expect most features to carry small, spread-out contributions rather than a handful of sparse nonzero predictors.

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides `Linear.RidgeRegression` along with its scikit-learn alias `Linear.Ridge`. Both run synchronously in pure TypeScript across browsers and Node.js, compose directly inside [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md) with [`StandardScaler`](/docs/apis/utils/preprocessing.md), and serialize cleanly via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Interactive Ridge regression playground

Tune the L2 penalty (`alpha`) and noise level below. `Linear.RidgeRegression` refits live in your browser after every change, including observations you click to add to the chart.

> The HTML version includes an interactive Ridge Regression playground powered by @kanaries/ml. You can change the dataset, noise, and model controls; add observations; and inspect live predictions plus train and holdout metrics. The runnable guide and API reference continue below. [Open the HTML page](https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/linear/ridgeRegression).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Linear } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0], [1], [2], [3]];
const y = [1, 3, 5, 7];

const model = new Linear.RidgeRegression({ alpha: 0.5, fitIntercept: true });
model.fit(X, y);
const pred = model.predict([[4]]);
console.log(pred);
```

### Ridge Regression (RidgeRegression / Ridge): Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

model = Ridge(alpha=0.5, fit_intercept=True)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
preds = model.predict(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Linear } from '@kanaries/ml';

const model = new Linear.Ridge({ alpha: 0.5, fitIntercept: true });
model.fit(XTrain, yTrain);
const preds = model.predict(XTest);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Linear.RidgeRegression(props?)` / `new Linear.Ridge(props?)`

| Parameter      | Type      | Default | Description                                                                                               |
| -------------- | --------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `alpha`        | `number`  | `1`     | Non-negative finite L2 penalty strength. Larger values shrink coefficients more aggressively toward zero. |
| `fitIntercept` | `boolean` | `true`  | Estimate an unpenalized intercept term (`false` assumes centered data).                                   |

### Methods

- `fit(X: number[][], Y: number[]): void` — solves the closed-form L2-regularized normal equations.
- `predict(X: number[][]): number[]` — predicts continuous targets; throws if unfitted or if feature count mismatches.

### Tuning & comparison tips

- **Scale features before regularizing**: Because L2 penalizes squared coefficient magnitude equally across features, wrap `StandardScaler` and `Ridge` inside a [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md) so large-scale columns are not unfairly favored.
- **Ridge vs Lasso vs ElasticNet**: Prefer Ridge when all features matter slightly; switch to [`Linear.LassoRegression`](/docs/apis/linear/lassoRegression.md) for sparse feature selection or [`Linear.ElasticNet`](/docs/apis/linear/elasticNet.md) when correlated groups need sparsity.
- **Related pages**: [Linear Regression](/docs/apis/linear/linearRegression.md), [Lasso Regression](/docs/apis/linear/lassoRegression.md), [ElasticNet](/docs/apis/linear/elasticNet.md), [Bayesian Ridge](/docs/apis/linear/bayesianRegressors.md).

---
title: "Robust Regression in JavaScript and TypeScript"
description: "Fit Huber, RANSAC, Theil-Sen, and Quantile regression in JavaScript and TypeScript with @kanaries/ml to handle outliers and predict quantile bands."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/linear/robustRegressors"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/linear/robustRegressors.md"
---
# Robust Regression in JavaScript and TypeScript

## Algorithm overview

Ordinary least squares minimizes squared residuals, so even one corrupted sensor reading, typo, or extreme transaction can tilt the entire fitted slope dramatically. **Robust regression** estimators limit or eliminate the influence of outliers—or target conditional quantiles instead of conditional means:

| Estimator           | How it resists outliers                                                    | Best when                                                                       |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `HuberRegressor`    | Switches from quadratic loss to linear loss beyond `epsilon * scale`       | Moderate `y`-outliers and you want fast smooth optimization                     |
| `RANSACRegressor`   | Repeatedly fits minimal subsets and keeps the largest consensus inlier set | Severe gross outliers (`20%–40%` bad rows) in `y`                               |
| `TheilSenRegressor` | Computes the spatial median across many subsample slopes                   | Small-to-medium datasets with outliers in both `X` and `y`                      |
| `QuantileRegressor` | Minimizes asymmetric pinball loss (L1 at `quantile: 0.5`) via ADMM         | Median regression or prediction intervals (for example 10th & 90th percentiles) |

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides `Linear.HuberRegressor`, `Linear.RANSACRegressor`, `Linear.TheilSenRegressor`, and `Linear.QuantileRegressor` in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js apps. All four expose scikit-learn-style `fit`/`predict` APIs, integrate inside [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md), and serialize cleanly via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Interactive robust regression playground

Switch between Huber, RANSAC, Theil–Sen, and Quantile regression, select the outlier dataset, or click to add extreme points. Each curve refits live using `@kanaries/ml`.

> The HTML version includes an interactive Robust Regression playground powered by @kanaries/ml. You can change the dataset, noise, and model controls; add observations; and inspect live predictions plus train and holdout metrics. The runnable guide and API reference continue below. [Open the HTML page](https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/linear/robustRegressors).

## Quick start

```ts
import { Linear } from '@kanaries/ml';

const model = new Linear.RANSACRegressor({ randomState: 42 });
model.fit([[0], [1], [2], [3]], [0, 1, 20, 3]);
console.log(model.predict([[4]]), model.inlierMask);
```

### Robust Regressors (Huber, RANSAC, TheilSen, Quantile): Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import HuberRegressor, RANSACRegressor, TheilSenRegressor, QuantileRegressor

huber = HuberRegressor(epsilon=1.35).fit(X, y)
ransac = RANSACRegressor(random_state=42).fit(X, y)
theil = TheilSenRegressor(random_state=42).fit(X, y)
q90 = QuantileRegressor(quantile=0.9, alpha=0.01).fit(X, y)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Linear } from '@kanaries/ml';

const huber = new Linear.HuberRegressor({ epsilon: 1.35 });
huber.fit(X, y);

const ransac = new Linear.RANSACRegressor({ randomState: 42 });
ransac.fit(X, y);

const theil = new Linear.TheilSenRegressor({ randomState: 42 });
theil.fit(X, y);

const q90 = new Linear.QuantileRegressor({ quantile: 0.9, alpha: 0.01 });
q90.fit(X, y);
```

## Detailed API reference

- **`Linear.HuberRegressor({ epsilon = 1.35, alpha = 0.0001, maxIter = 100, tol = 1e-5, fitIntercept = true })`** — smaller `epsilon` (minimum `1.0`) increases robustness; exposes `coef`, `intercept`, `scale`, and boolean `outliers`.
- **`Linear.RANSACRegressor({ estimator, minSamples, residualThreshold, maxTrials = 100, stopProbability = 0.99, randomState })`** — defaults to `LinearRegression`; exposes `estimatorFitted`, boolean `inlierMask`, and `nTrials`.
- **`Linear.TheilSenRegressor({ nSubsamples, maxSubpopulation = 10000, maxIter = 300, tol = 1e-3, randomState })`** — exposes `coef`, `intercept`, and `nIter`.
- **`Linear.QuantileRegressor({ quantile = 0.5, alpha = 1, fitIntercept = true, maxIter = 5000, tol = 1e-7 })`** — fits any conditional quantile in `(0, 1)` via ADMM; fit `quantile: 0.1` and `quantile: 0.9` to build an 80% prediction interval.
- **Related pages**: [Handling Outliers in Regression Guide](/docs/guides/outliers-regression.md), [Outlier Detection Calculator](/tools/outlier-calculator), [Ridge Regression](/docs/apis/linear/ridgeRegression.md).

# Manifold Learning in JavaScript

## Module overview

The Manifold module projects high-dimensional data into lower-dimensional embeddings while trying to preserve important geometric or neighborhood structure. These methods are primarily useful for visualization, exploratory analysis, and pre-processing workflows rather than for low-latency production inference.

This module is a strong fit when:

- you need 2D or 3D visualizations of high-dimensional data
- local neighborhood structure matters more than raw feature axes
- your embeddings will feed directly into browser charts or interactive analysis tools

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides manifold learning algorithms in JavaScript and TypeScript so teams can generate embeddings in the same runtime that renders charts, powers exploratory analysis, or prepares features in Node.js. This is especially practical for frontend-heavy tools where embedding output is consumed immediately by the UI.

If someone searches for "t-SNE in JavaScript" or "Spectral Embedding in TypeScript", this module is the right entry point.

## Quick navigation

- [t-SNE](/docs/apis/manifold/tsne.md): local-neighborhood visualization for high-dimensional data
- [MDS](/docs/apis/manifold/MDS.md): embeddings that preserve pairwise distance structure
- [Locally Linear Embedding](/docs/apis/manifold/lle.md): non-linear manifold learning based on local reconstructions
- [Spectral Embedding](/docs/apis/manifold/spectralEmbedding.md): graph-based low-dimensional embeddings
- [Isomap](/docs/apis/manifold/isomap.md): geodesic-distance embeddings with out-of-sample transforms

## Detailed module guide

### How to choose an algorithm

1. Use [t-SNE](/docs/apis/manifold/tsne.md) for exploratory cluster visualization.
2. Use [MDS](/docs/apis/manifold/MDS.md) when the main input or objective is a distance matrix.
3. Use [Locally Linear Embedding](/docs/apis/manifold/lle.md) or [Spectral Embedding](/docs/apis/manifold/spectralEmbedding.md) when local geometry or graph structure is central to the task.
4. Use [Isomap](/docs/apis/manifold/isomap.md) when global distances along a curved manifold matter and you need to transform new samples.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Treat these methods as exploration and preprocessing tools first, not as default request-time transforms.
- Run heavier embeddings outside the main browser thread when user interaction matters.
- Choose based on the structure you want to preserve: local neighborhoods, graph connectivity, or pairwise distances.

---
title: "Isomap in JavaScript and TypeScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Preserve nonlinear geodesic manifold distances in JavaScript and TypeScript with Manifold.Isomap from @kanaries/ml, including out-of-sample transform()."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/manifold/isomap"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/manifold/isomap.md"
---
# Isomap in JavaScript and TypeScript with @kanaries/ml

## Algorithm overview

**Isomap (Isometric Feature Mapping)** is a nonlinear dimensionality-reduction algorithm that preserves global **geodesic distances** measured *along* a curved manifold rather than straight-line Euclidean chords cutting through empty space. It runs in three stages:

1. Construct a `k`-nearest-neighbor graph connecting locally adjacent samples.
2. Compute all-pairs shortest-path (geodesic) distances across the neighborhood graph.
3. Apply classical Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) to embed the geodesic distance matrix into `nComponents` dimensions.

Compared to [t-SNE](/docs/apis/manifold/tsne.md), Isomap preserves global manifold geometry and supports **out-of-sample `transform(XNew)`** on unseen points via Nyström kernel projection—making it usable both for 2D visualization and as a nonlinear feature extractor inside a [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md).

## JavaScript implementation

`Manifold.Isomap` in `@kanaries/ml` runs in pure TypeScript across browsers and Node.js. If the `k`-NN graph breaks into disconnected components, Isomap automatically warns and bridges each component pair at its closest Euclidean samples (matching scikit-learn's recovery path).

**Browser scaling guidance**: Because Isomap builds an `O(n²)` geodesic distance matrix and runs an `O(n³)` shortest-path + eigendecomposition phase, keep interactive browser datasets to a few hundred samples (or offload fitting to a Web Worker). Fitted embeddings serialize via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Manifold } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [1, 0], [2, 1], [3, 1], [4, 2]];
const model = new Manifold.Isomap({ nNeighbors: 2, nComponents: 2 });
const embedding = model.fitTransform(X);
const newPoints = model.transform([[2.5, 1]]);
console.log({ embedding, newPoints });
```

### Isomap: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.manifold import Isomap

iso = Isomap(n_neighbors=5, n_components=2)
embedding = iso.fit_transform(X_train)
projected = iso.transform(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Manifold } from '@kanaries/ml';

const iso = new Manifold.Isomap({ nNeighbors: 5, nComponents: 2 });
const embedding = iso.fitTransform(XTrain);
const projected = iso.transform(XTest);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Manifold.Isomap(props?)`

| Parameter     | Type     | Default | Description                                                                                                                                          |
| ------------- | -------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nNeighbors`  | `number` | `5`     | Number of nearest neighbors per node in the neighborhood graph. Too small fractures the graph; too large creates "short-circuit" edges across folds. |
| `nComponents` | `number` | `2`     | Target embedding dimensionality.                                                                                                                     |

### Methods & properties

- `fit(X)` / `fitTransform(X)` / `transform(X)` — fit geodesic manifold embedding and project training or unseen samples.
- Read-only `embedding` (`[nSamples][nComponents]`) and `distMatrix` (`[nSamples][nSamples]` geodesic distances).
- **Related pages**: [Locally Linear Embedding (LLE)](/docs/apis/manifold/lle.md), [t-SNE](/docs/apis/manifold/tsne.md), [MDS](/docs/apis/manifold/MDS.md), [Kernel PCA](/docs/apis/decomposition/kernelPCA.md).

---
title: "Locally Linear Embedding in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Preserve local neighborhood geometry with Locally Linear Embedding (LLE) in JavaScript and TypeScript using @kanaries/ml for browser and Node.js apps."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/manifold/lle"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/manifold/lle.md"
---
# Locally Linear Embedding in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

Locally Linear Embedding (LLE) reconstructs each sample from its nearest
neighbors and finds a low‑dimensional representation that preserves these
local relationships.

LocallyLinearEmbedding captures manifold structure by preserving local linear neighborhoods in a low-dimensional embedding.

This algorithm is especially useful when:

- Data lies on a non-linear manifold with meaningful local geometry.
- You want neighborhood-preserving visualization or preprocessing.
- Linear projection methods (like PCA) lose important local structure.

## JavaScript implementation

@kanaries/ml provides Locally Linear Embedding in JavaScript for teams working on non-linear visualization or manifold-aware preprocessing inside browser and Node.js applications. This is useful when you want local neighborhood structure to survive dimensionality reduction better than it would with a linear method like PCA.

Running LLE in the JS stack is particularly helpful for interactive data tools where embeddings feed directly into frontend plots or exploratory workflows.

## Quick start

### LocallyLinearEmbedding: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.manifold import LocallyLinearEmbedding

X = [[0, 0], [1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1], [0.5, 0.5]]

lle = LocallyLinearEmbedding(n_neighbors=3, n_components=2)
embedding = lle.fit_transform(X)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Manifold } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1], [0.5, 0.5]];

const lle = new Manifold.LocallyLinearEmbedding({ nNeighbors: 3, nComponents: 2, randomState: 42 });
const embedding = lle.fitTransform(X);
```

### Quick JavaScript example

```ts
import { Manifold } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1], [0.5, 0.5]];

const lle = new Manifold.LocallyLinearEmbedding({
  nNeighbors: 3,
  nComponents: 2,
  reg: 0.001,
  randomState: 42,
});
const embedding = lle.fitTransform(X);
console.log(embedding);
```

*(Also exported under the short alias `Manifold.LLE`.)*

## Detailed API reference

```ts
new Manifold.LocallyLinearEmbedding(props?: {
  nNeighbors?: number;  // default: 5
  nComponents?: number; // default: 2
  reg?: number;         // default: 0.001
  randomState?: number; // optional deterministic seed
})
```

*(Legacy positional calls remain supported for backward compatibility, but prefer the options object.)*

### Parameters

- `nNeighbors` (number, default `5`): how many neighbors to use for the local
  reconstructions.
- `nComponents` (number, default `2`): dimension of the returned embedding.
- `reg` (number, default `0.001`): regularization value added to the covariance
  matrix to ensure numerical stability.

### Methods

- `fit(X: number[][]): void`
- `transform(X: number[][]): number[][]`
- `fitTransform(X: number[][]): number[][]`

### Implementation workflow

1. Select neighborhood size based on expected local manifold smoothness.
2. Fit and inspect embedding quality visually and with neighborhood metrics.
3. Tune neighbors/components to balance stability and detail.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Use LLE when preserving local neighborhood geometry matters more than preserving global distances.
- Tune neighbor count carefully because it strongly affects the stability of the embedding.
- In product code, treat it primarily as an exploratory or preprocessing tool rather than a low-latency online transform.

---
title: "Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Project pairwise distances into low-dimensional coordinates with Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) in JavaScript and TypeScript using @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/manifold/MDS"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/manifold/MDS.md"
---
# Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

Multidimensional scaling using classical MDS algorithm.

Classical MDS converts a distance matrix into a centered similarity matrix and
computes its dominant eigenvectors to recover coordinates that preserve the
original pairwise dissimilarities.

MDS embeds points into lower dimensions while preserving pairwise distances as much as possible.

This algorithm is especially useful when:

- Distance geometry is more important than original feature axes.
- You need interpretable 2D/3D maps for exploratory analysis.
- You are comparing similarity relationships across entities.

## JavaScript implementation

@kanaries/ml makes classical multidimensional scaling available in JavaScript for cases where you care more about preserving pairwise distances than about modeling the original feature axes directly. That is useful in browser-based visualization tools, similarity explorers, and Node.js analytics pipelines that already work from distance matrices.

Because MDS often feeds directly into charts and exploratory interfaces, keeping it inside the JS layer is especially practical for frontend-heavy products.

## Quick start

### MDS: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.manifold import MDS

X = [[0, 0, 1], [0, 1, 1], [1, 0, 0], [1, 1, 0]]

mds = MDS(n_components=2, random_state=0)
embedding = mds.fit_transform(X)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Manifold } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0, 1], [0, 1, 1], [1, 0, 0], [1, 1, 0]];

const mds = new Manifold.MDS({ nComponents: 2 });
const embedding = mds.fitTransform(X);
```

### Quick JavaScript example

```ts
import { Manifold } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0, 1], [0, 1, 1], [1, 0, 0], [1, 1, 0]];

const mds = new Manifold.MDS({ nComponents: 2 });
const embedding = mds.fitTransform(X);
console.log(embedding);
```

## Detailed API reference

```ts
interface MDSOptions {
    nComponents?: number;
    dissimilarity?: 'euclidean' | 'precomputed';
}
constructor(options: MDSOptions = {})
```

### Options

- `nComponents` (number, default `2`): dimension of the embedded space.
- `dissimilarity` (`'euclidean'` | `'precomputed'`, default `'euclidean'`): if
  `'precomputed'`, the input to `fitTransform` should be a distance matrix.

`fitTransform(data: number[][]): number[][]` computes the embedding and returns it.

`getEmbedding(): number[][]` returns the computed embedding.

### Implementation workflow

1. Choose or compute a distance matrix aligned with your domain.
2. Fit MDS with target component count for visualization.
3. Validate stress/error and inspect neighborhood preservation quality.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Use MDS when your core input is a distance or dissimilarity structure rather than a traditional feature matrix.
- It is especially valuable for interactive visualization and exploratory analysis rather than high-throughput production inference.
- Watch dataset size because pairwise distance handling can become expensive quickly.

title: "Spectral Embedding in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"

---
# Spectral Embedding in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

Spectral embedding for non-linear dimensionality reduction using the Laplacian Eigenmaps algorithm.

The algorithm builds a nearest‑neighbor graph from the data, computes the
normalized graph Laplacian and uses its leading eigenvectors (except for the
trivial one) as the embedding coordinates.

SpectralEmbedding uses graph Laplacian eigenvectors to reveal manifold and community structure in data.

This algorithm is especially useful when:

- Graph or affinity relationships are central to your dataset.
- You need embeddings suitable for downstream clustering.
- Non-linear structure is not captured by purely linear projections.

## JavaScript implementation

@kanaries/ml brings Spectral Embedding to JavaScript for graph-like or neighborhood-based dimensionality reduction tasks. This is useful when your data relationships are better captured by local connectivity than by global linear variance, and when embeddings need to feed directly into web visualizations or JS-native downstream logic.

Because many spectral workflows are exploratory, having the implementation in the same browser or Node.js runtime simplifies iteration and integration with charts.

## Quick start

### SpectralEmbedding: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.manifold import SpectralEmbedding

X = [[0, 0], [0.2, 0.1], [1, 1], [1.1, 1.0], [3, 3]]

embedding = SpectralEmbedding(n_components=2, n_neighbors=2, random_state=0)
embedding = embedding.fit_transform(X)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Manifold } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [0.2, 0.1], [1, 1], [1.1, 1.0], [3, 3]];

const model = new Manifold.SpectralEmbedding({ nComponents: 2, nNeighbors: 2 });
const embedding = model.fitTransform(X);
```

### Quick JavaScript example

```ts
import { Manifold } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [0.2, 0.1], [1, 1], [1.1, 1.0], [3, 3]];

const model = new Manifold.SpectralEmbedding({ nComponents: 2, nNeighbors: 2 });
const embedding = model.fitTransform(X);
console.log(embedding);
```

## Detailed API reference

```ts
interface SpectralEmbeddingProps {
    nComponents?: number;
    nNeighbors?: number;
}
constructor(props: SpectralEmbeddingProps = {})
```

### Parameters

- `nComponents` (number, default `2`): number of embedding dimensions.
- `nNeighbors` (number, default `10`): how many neighbors are connected in the
  affinity graph.

### Methods

- `fit(X: number[][]): void`
- `fitTransform(X: number[][]): number[][]`
- `getEmbedding(): number[][]`

### Implementation workflow

1. Construct an affinity graph with an appropriate similarity metric.
2. Fit SpectralEmbedding and evaluate resulting cluster separability.
3. Tune neighborhood/affinity parameters for stable embeddings.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Spectral Embedding is a good fit when local graph structure matters more than linear explainability.
- Normalize and validate neighborhood settings because they strongly influence the resulting embedding.
- Use it mainly for visualization or preprocessing, then benchmark downstream utility with a supervised model.

title: "t-SNE in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Learn what t-SNE does, when to use it, and how to run TSNE in JavaScript or TypeScript with @kanaries/ml for browser and Node.js applications."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/manifold/tsne"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/manifold/tsne.md"
---
# t-SNE in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

T-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding for visualizing high dimensional data.

TSNE models pairwise similarities both in the original space and in the
embedding. It iteratively updates the embedding using gradient descent to
minimize the Kullback–Leibler divergence between these two distributions.

TSNE creates low-dimensional visualizations that preserve local neighborhoods in high-dimensional data.

This algorithm is especially useful when:

- You need exploratory plots to inspect cluster tendencies or anomalies.
- Local similarity is more important than global distance preservation.
- You can afford iterative optimization for offline analysis workflows.

## JavaScript implementation

@kanaries/ml makes t-SNE available in JavaScript for high-dimensional visualization tasks that need to stay close to interactive frontend tools or Node.js analytics apps. This is valuable when embeddings are primarily used for charting, cluster inspection, or anomaly exploration inside a web product.

Because t-SNE is usually an exploratory visualization method rather than a serving-time model, keeping it inside the JS experience can make experimentation much faster for product teams.

## Quick start

### TSNE: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE

X = [[0, 0, 1], [0, 1, 1], [1, 0, 0], [1, 1, 0]]

tsne = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=2, learning_rate=50, random_state=0)
embedding = tsne.fit_transform(X)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Manifold } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0, 1], [0, 1, 1], [1, 0, 0], [1, 1, 0]];

const tsne = new Manifold.TSNE({ nComponents: 2, perplexity: 2, learningRate: 50, nIter: 300 });
const embedding = tsne.fitTransform(X);
```

### Quick JavaScript example

```ts
import { Manifold } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0, 1], [0, 1, 1], [1, 0, 0], [1, 1, 0]];

const tsne = new Manifold.TSNE({ nComponents: 2, perplexity: 2, learningRate: 50, nIter: 300 });
const embedding = tsne.fitTransform(X);
console.log(embedding);
```

## Detailed API reference

```ts
constructor(options: TSNEOptions = {})
```

### Options

- `nComponents` (number, default `2`): embedding dimensions
- `perplexity` (number, default `30`)
- `learningRate` (number, default `200`)
- `nIter` (number, default `250`)

### Methods

- `fit(X: number[][]): void`
- `fitTransform(X: number[][]): number[][]`
- `getEmbedding(): number[][]`

### Implementation workflow

1. Normalize inputs and optionally reduce dimensions with PCA first.
2. Fit TSNE with tuned perplexity and iteration settings.
3. Interpret clusters carefully and validate findings with quantitative checks.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Use t-SNE for visualization and exploration, not as a primary production feature transform by default.
- Reduce dimensions first when helpful, especially on larger feature spaces.
- In browser apps, run t-SNE outside the main thread because iterative optimization is compute-heavy.

---
title: "Metrics in JavaScript and TypeScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Compute classification, regression, clustering, ROC/PR curve, and pairwise distance metrics in JavaScript and TypeScript with @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/metrics"

# Metrics in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

Metrics turn model outputs into numbers you can compare, monitor, and use for product decisions. The Metrics module covers common classification scores, regression errors, clustering agreement, binary ranking curves, and distance functions.

Use these helpers when you need to:

- compare JavaScript models with consistent scoring code
- report classification quality with accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and confusion matrices
- evaluate regression predictions with MSE and R2
- inspect binary score thresholds with ROC and precision-recall curves
- measure clustering agreement with adjusted Rand index
- reuse distance functions across algorithms and application code

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` exposes metrics as plain JavaScript functions under `Metrics`, so browser tools and Node.js services can evaluate model quality without a Python runtime. The API is intentionally small and works with arrays of numbers, which makes it easy to use next to model predictions, UI charts, and test fixtures.

The function convention is `actual` first and `expected` second for predicted labels or values versus ground truth labels or values.

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Metrics } from '@kanaries/ml';

const predicted = [0, 1, 1, 0, 1];
const truth = [0, 1, 0, 0, 1];

const accuracy = Metrics.accuracyScore(predicted, truth);
const f1 = Metrics.f1Score(predicted, truth, { positiveLabel: 1 });
const matrix = Metrics.confusionMatrix(predicted, truth, [0, 1]);
```

```ts
import { Metrics } from '@kanaries/ml';

const yPred = [2.5, 0.0, 2.1, 7.8];
const yTrue = [3.0, -0.5, 2.0, 7.0];

const mse = Metrics.meanSquaredError(yPred, yTrue);
const r2 = Metrics.r2Score(yPred, yTrue);
```

## Detailed API reference

### Classification metrics

```ts
accuracyScore(actual: number[], expected: number[], normalize = true): number
precisionScore(actual: number[], expected: number[], options?: ClassificationMetricOptions): number
recallScore(actual: number[], expected: number[], options?: ClassificationMetricOptions): number
f1Score(actual: number[], expected: number[], options?: ClassificationMetricOptions): number
precisionRecallFscoreSupport(actual: number[], expected: number[], options?: ClassificationMetricOptions): PrecisionRecallFscoreSupportResult
confusionMatrix(actual: number[], expected: number[], labels?: number[]): number[][]
```

`ClassificationMetricOptions` supports:

- `average?: 'binary' | 'macro'`, default `'binary'`
- `positiveLabel?: number`, default `1`

`precisionRecallFscoreSupport` returns `{ precision, recall, fScore, support }`. For binary scoring, `support` contains the positive label support. For macro scoring, support follows the sorted label order.

`confusionMatrix` returns rows by expected label and columns by actual label. Pass `labels` to control row and column order.

### Regression metrics

```ts
meanSquaredError(actual: number[], expected: number[]): number
r2Score(actual: number[], expected: number[]): number
```

Both functions require non-empty arrays with matching lengths.

### Curves and ranking metrics

```ts
rocCurve(expected: number[], scores: number[], positiveLabel = 1): {
  fpr: number[];
  tpr: number[];
  thresholds: number[];
}

rocAucScore(expected: number[], scores: number[], positiveLabel = 1): number

precisionRecallCurve(expected: number[], scores: number[], positiveLabel = 1): {
  precision: number[];
  recall: number[];
  thresholds: number[];
}
```

Curve functions expect true binary labels in `expected` and model scores in `scores`. The configured `positiveLabel` must be present.

### Clustering agreement

```ts
adjustedRandScore(labelsTrue: number[], labelsPred: number[]): number
```

Adjusted Rand score compares two cluster label assignments while accounting for chance agreement.

### Distance utilities

```ts
Metrics.Distance.manhattan(pos1: number[], pos2: number[]): number
Metrics.Distance.euclidean(pos1: number[], pos2: number[]): number
Metrics.Distance.minkowski(pos1: number[], pos2: number[], p = 2): number
Metrics.Distance.useDistance(distanceType: Distance.IDistanceType): Distance.IDistance
```

Supported distance types are `'manhattan'`, `'euclidean'`, `'minkowski'`, `'1-norm'`, `'2-norm'`, and `'p-norm'`.

```ts
const distance = Metrics.Distance.useDistance('minkowski');
const value = distance([0, 0], [3, 4], 2);
```

## JavaScript deployment notes

- Keep a single metric convention across validation, tests, and UI reporting.
- For binary classifiers, store the positive label next to the model configuration.
- Use curve outputs directly with chart libraries when tuning thresholds in browser-based analysis tools.

---
title: "BayesianGaussianMixture in JavaScript"
description: "Fit Variational Bayesian Gaussian Mixture Models with Dirichlet Process priors in JavaScript and TypeScript using @kanaries/ml for automatic cluster pruning."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/mixture/bayesian-gaussian-mixture"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/mixture/bayesian-gaussian-mixture.md"
---
# BayesianGaussianMixture in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

A **Bayesian Gaussian Mixture Model** replaces maximum-likelihood EM estimation with **variational Bayesian inference** over mixture weights, component means, and precisions. By placing a stick-breaking **Dirichlet Process** prior (or finite Dirichlet distribution prior) on the mixing weights and a Gaussian-Wishart prior on each component's parameters, the model penalizes unnecessary complexity automatically.

In practice, this means you can set `nComponents` to an upper bound (for example, `8`) and let variational inference concentrate weight onto the active clusters while shrinking redundant components toward zero weight—avoiding brittle manual grid searches over cluster counts when the true number of groups is uncertain.

## JavaScript implementation

`Mixture.BayesianGaussianMixture` in `@kanaries/ml` implements Bishop's PRML variational inference updates (matching `sklearn.mixture.BayesianGaussianMixture`) in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js runtimes. It supports both `'dirichletProcess'` (default) and `'dirichletDistribution'` weight priors with `'full'` and `'diag'` covariance parametrizations, deterministic `randomState` seeding, and JSON persistence via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Mixture, Datasets } from '@kanaries/ml';

const { X } = Datasets.makeBlobs({ nSamples: 60, centers: 2, clusterStd: 0.6, randomState: 42 });

const bgmm = new Mixture.BayesianGaussianMixture({
  nComponents: 5,
  covarianceType: 'full',
  weightConcentrationPriorType: 'dirichletProcess',
  weightConcentrationPrior: 0.1,
  randomState: 42,
});

bgmm.fit(X);
const weights = bgmm.getWeights() ?? [];
const activeComponents = weights.filter((w) => w > 0.05).length;
console.log({ activeComponents, labels: bgmm.predict(X.slice(0, 5)) });
```

### BayesianGaussianMixture: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.mixture import BayesianGaussianMixture

bgmm = BayesianGaussianMixture(
  n_components=8,
  covariance_type="full",
  weight_concentration_prior_type="dirichlet_process",
  weight_concentration_prior=0.1,
  random_state=42,
)
bgmm.fit(X)
labels = bgmm.predict(X)
weights = bgmm.weights_
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Mixture } from '@kanaries/ml';

const bgmm = new Mixture.BayesianGaussianMixture({
nComponents: 8,
covarianceType: 'full',
weightConcentrationPriorType: 'dirichletProcess',
weightConcentrationPrior: 0.1,
randomState: 42,
});

bgmm.fit(X);
const labels = bgmm.predict(X);
const weights = bgmm.getWeights();
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Mixture.BayesianGaussianMixture(props?)`

| Parameter                      | Type                                            | Default               | Description                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- | --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nComponents`                  | `number`                                        | `1`                   | Upper bound on the number of mixture components.                                                                                                                                   |
| `covarianceType`               | `'full' \| 'diag'`                              | `'full'`              | Covariance parametrization. (`'tied'` and `'spherical'` are not implemented and throw a clear error.)                                                                              |
| `weightConcentrationPriorType` | `'dirichletProcess' \| 'dirichletDistribution'` | `'dirichletProcess'`  | Prior family on component weights. `'dirichletProcess'` uses stick-breaking to favor fewer active components; `'dirichletDistribution'` places a symmetric finite Dirichlet prior. |
| `weightConcentrationPrior`     | `number`                                        | `1 / nComponents`     | Concentration parameter controlling sparsity of active components. Smaller values push unused component weights closer to zero.                                                    |
| `meanPrecisionPrior`           | `number`                                        | `1`                   | Precision prior on component means. Smaller values allow component means to move further from `meanPrior`.                                                                         |
| `meanPrior`                    | `number[]`                                      | empirical mean of `X` | Prior center for component means.                                                                                                                                                  |
| `degreesOfFreedomPrior`        | `number`                                        | `nFeatures`           | Wishart degrees-of-freedom prior; must exceed `nFeatures - 1`.                                                                                                                     |
| `covariancePrior`              | `number[][] \| number[]`                        | empirical covariance  | `d×d` matrix for `'full'` or length-`d` variance vector for `'diag'`.                                                                                                              |
| `tol`                          | `number`                                        | `1e-3`                | Convergence threshold on the variational lower-bound change.                                                                                                                       |
| `regCovar`                     | `number`                                        | `1e-6`                | Non-negative diagonal regularization.                                                                                                                                              |
| `maxIter`                      | `number`                                        | `100`                 | Maximum variational EM iterations per restart.                                                                                                                                     |
| `nInit`                        | `number`                                        | `1`                   | Number of restarts; retains the run with the highest variational lower bound.                                                                                                      |
| `initParams`                   | `'kmeans' \| 'random'`                          | `'kmeans'`            | Responsibility initialization method.                                                                                                                                              |
| `randomState`                  | `number`                                        | `undefined`           | Seed for reproducible runs.                                                                                                                                                        |

### Methods & properties

| Member                                       | Signature                                | Description                                                                |
| -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `fit`                                        | `(X: number[][]) => this`                | Runs variational inference and returns `this`.                             |
| `predict`                                    | `(X: number[][]) => number[]`            | Assigns each sample to its highest-responsibility component.               |
| `predictProba`                               | `(X: number[][]) => number[][]`          | Returns variational posterior responsibilities `[nSamples][nComponents]`.  |
| `fitPredict`                                 | `(X: number[][]) => number[]`            | Fits on `X` and returns component labels.                                  |
| `scoreSamples` / `score`                     | `(X: number[][]) => number[]` / `number` | Computes per-sample / average predictive log probability density.          |
| `getWeights` / `getMeans` / `getCovariances` | `() => ... \| null`                      | Inspects posterior expected weights, means, and covariances.               |
| `getLowerBound` / `getLowerBoundHistory`     | `() => number` / `number[]`              | Returns the variational evidence lower bound (ELBO) and convergence trace. |
| `converged` / `nIter`                        | `boolean` / `number`                     | Convergence flag and iteration count for the winning run.                  |

### Tuning tips

- Lower `weightConcentrationPrior` (for example `0.01` to `0.1`) to prune redundant clusters more aggressively; raise it (for example `1.0` to `10.0`) when expecting many balanced subpopulations.
- Inspect `getWeights()` after fitting to see how many components carry meaningful mass (for instance `weight > 0.02`).
- **Related pages**: [GaussianMixture](/docs/apis/mixture/gaussian-mixture.md), [Mixture Models Overview](/docs/apis/mixture/index.html.md), [HDBSCAN](/docs/apis/clusters/hdbscan.md).

<!-- Source: https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/mixture/gaussian-mixture -->

---
title: "GaussianMixture (GMM) in JavaScript"
description: "Run Expectation-Maximization Gaussian Mixture Models in JavaScript and TypeScript with @kanaries/ml. Supports full, diag, tied, and spherical covariances."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/mixture/gaussian-mixture"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/mixture/gaussian-mixture.md"
---
# GaussianMixture (GMM) in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

**GaussianMixture (GMM)** models continuous observations as draws from `nComponents` multivariate Gaussian distributions, each parameterized by a mixing weight, a mean vector, and a covariance matrix. Parameters are estimated with **Expectation-Maximization (EM)**:

1. **E-step**: compute log-domain responsibilities (posterior probability that each sample belongs to each component) using numerically stable `logsumexp`.
2. **M-step**: update component weights, means, and covariances from weighted sufficient statistics, adding `regCovar` to covariance diagonals to prevent singular matrices.
3. **Convergence**: stop when the improvement in average per-sample log-likelihood drops below `tol` or `maxIter` is reached, keeping the highest lower-bound run across `nInit` restarts.

GMMs shine when clusters vary in spread or orientation, when observations sit in overlap zones where soft probabilities matter, or when low log-density (`scoreSamples`) is used to flag anomalies.

## JavaScript implementation

`Mixture.GaussianMixture` in `@kanaries/ml` mirrors `sklearn.mixture.GaussianMixture` with camelCase options and zero native dependencies. Because all E-step log-densities and Cholesky decompositions execute in pure TypeScript, you can fit GMMs directly in browser data-exploration apps, Web Workers, or Node.js analytics services—and export fitted models via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Mixture, Datasets } from '@kanaries/ml';

const { X } = Datasets.makeBlobs({ nSamples: 60, centers: 3, clusterStd: 0.6, randomState: 42 });

const gmm = new Mixture.GaussianMixture({
  nComponents: 3,
  covarianceType: 'full',
  nInit: 3,
  randomState: 42,
});

gmm.fit(X);
console.log({
  labels: gmm.predict(X.slice(0, 5)),
  proba: gmm.predictProba(X.slice(0, 2)),
  bic: gmm.bic(X),
});
```

### GaussianMixture: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture

gmm = GaussianMixture(
  n_components=3,
  covariance_type="full",
  n_init=5,
  random_state=42,
)
gmm.fit(X)
labels = gmm.predict(X)
probs = gmm.predict_proba(X)
log_density = gmm.score_samples(X)
bic_score = gmm.bic(X)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Mixture } from '@kanaries/ml';

const gmm = new Mixture.GaussianMixture({
nComponents: 3,
covarianceType: 'full',
nInit: 5,
randomState: 42,
});

gmm.fit(X);
const labels = gmm.predict(X);
const probs = gmm.predictProba(X);
const logDensity = gmm.scoreSamples(X);
const bicScore = gmm.bic(X);
```

### Selecting `nComponents` with BIC

Lower BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) balances goodness of fit against parameter count:

```ts
import { Mixture, Datasets } from '@kanaries/ml';

const { X } = Datasets.makeBlobs({ nSamples: 90, centers: 3, clusterStd: 0.7, randomState: 7 });
const candidates = [2, 3, 4].map((k) => {
  const model = new Mixture.GaussianMixture({ nComponents: k, nInit: 2, randomState: 7 });
  model.fit(X);
  return { k, bic: model.bic(X), aic: model.aic(X) };
});

candidates.sort((a, b) => a.bic - b.bic);
console.log('Best k by BIC:', candidates[0]);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Mixture.GaussianMixture(props?)`

| Parameter        | Type                                        | Default     | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nComponents`    | `number`                                    | `1`         | Positive integer number of mixture components.                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `covarianceType` | `'full' \| 'tied' \| 'diag' \| 'spherical'` | `'full'`    | Covariance structure: `'full'` (each component has its own `d×d` covariance), `'tied'` (shared `d×d`), `'diag'` (axis-aligned per-component variances), or `'spherical'` (single scalar variance per component). |
| `tol`            | `number`                                    | `1e-3`      | Convergence threshold on the change in average per-sample log-likelihood.                                                                                                                                        |
| `regCovar`       | `number`                                    | `1e-6`      | Non-negative diagonal regularization keeping covariance matrices positive definite.                                                                                                                              |
| `maxIter`        | `number`                                    | `100`       | Maximum EM iterations per initialization.                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `nInit`          | `number`                                    | `1`         | Number of EM restarts; the run with the highest lower bound is retained.                                                                                                                                         |
| `initParams`     | `'kmeans' \| 'random'`                      | `'kmeans'`  | Initial responsibility assignment strategy.                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `randomState`    | `number`                                    | `undefined` | Seed for deterministic initialization.                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `weightsInit`    | `number[]`                                  | `undefined` | Optional initial component weights (length `nComponents`).                                                                                                                                                       |
| `meansInit`      | `number[][]`                                | `undefined` | Optional initial means (`[nComponents][nFeatures]`).                                                                                                                                                             |
| `precisionsInit` | `Covariances`                               | `undefined` | Optional initial precision matrices matching `covarianceType` shape.                                                                                                                                             |

### Methods & properties

| Member                                       | Signature                       | Description                                                                         |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `fit`                                        | `(X: number[][]) => this`       | Fits the mixture parameters with EM and returns `this`.                             |
| `predict`                                    | `(X: number[][]) => number[]`   | Returns the most likely component index (`0..nComponents-1`) per row.               |
| `predictProba`                               | `(X: number[][]) => number[][]` | Returns posterior component responsibilities `[nSamples][nComponents]`.             |
| `fitPredict`                                 | `(X: number[][]) => number[]`   | Fits on `X` and returns component labels.                                           |
| `scoreSamples`                               | `(X: number[][]) => number[]`   | Computes per-sample log probability density `log p(x)`.                             |
| `score`                                      | `(X: number[][]) => number`     | Returns the average per-sample log-likelihood across `X`.                           |
| `aic` / `bic`                                | `(X: number[][]) => number`     | Computes Akaike / Bayesian Information Criterion for model selection.               |
| `getWeights` / `getMeans` / `getCovariances` | `() => ... \| null`             | Inspects learned mixing weights, means, and covariance structures.                  |
| `getLowerBound` / `getLowerBoundHistory`     | `() => number` / `number[]`     | Returns the final average log-likelihood and per-iteration trace.                   |
| `converged` / `nIter`                        | `boolean` / `number`            | Public properties indicating EM convergence and iteration count of the winning run. |

### Practical guidance

- **Feature scaling**: Standardize skewed or high-magnitude features with [`StandardScaler`](/docs/apis/utils/preprocessing.md) before fitting `'full'` or `'spherical'` mixtures so one feature does not dominate covariance conditioning.
- **High-dimensional datasets**: Prefer `covarianceType: 'diag'` when `nFeatures` is large relative to `nSamples` to avoid overfitting full `d×d` covariance matrices and to keep browser fit times fast.
- **Related pages**: [Mixture Models Overview](/docs/apis/mixture/index.html.md), [BayesianGaussianMixture](/docs/apis/mixture/bayesian-gaussian-mixture.md), [K-Means Clustering](/docs/apis/clusters/kmeans.md), [Model Serialization](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).
