<!-- Source: https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/mixture -->

---
title: "Gaussian Mixture Models in JavaScript"
description: "Fit Gaussian Mixture and Variational Bayesian Mixture models in JavaScript and TypeScript with @kanaries/ml for soft clustering and density estimation."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/mixture"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/mixture/index.html.md"
---
# Gaussian Mixture Models in JavaScript

## Module overview

**Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs)** represent a dataset as a weighted combination of multivariate Gaussian distributions. Unlike hard-assignment partitioners such as [K-Means](/docs/apis/clusters/kmeans.md), mixture models assign every observation a **soft membership probability** (`predictProba`) across components and estimate the full data log-density (`scoreSamples`), making them well suited for elliptical clusters, overlapping subpopulations, and density-based anomaly scoring.

Use `Mixture` models when:

- Clusters have different sizes, variances, or diagonal/tilted orientations where spherical K-Means boundaries fail.
- You need calibrated cluster responsibilities (`predictProba`) rather than a single hard label.
- You want principled model selection via **AIC** and **BIC** (`GaussianMixture`) or automatic pruning of excess components via a Dirichlet-process prior (`BayesianGaussianMixture`).

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides two scikit-learn-compatible mixture estimators under `import { Mixture } from '@kanaries/ml'`, written in pure TypeScript for browsers and Node.js:

| Estimator                                                                            | Fitting algorithm                                                           | Covariance types                            | Best for                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`Mixture.GaussianMixture`](/docs/apis/mixture/gaussian-mixture.md)                  | Expectation-Maximization (EM) in the log domain                             | `'full'`, `'tied'`, `'diag'`, `'spherical'` | Soft clustering, density estimation, AIC/BIC selection of `nComponents`          |
| [`Mixture.BayesianGaussianMixture`](/docs/apis/mixture/bayesian-gaussian-mixture.md) | Variational Bayesian inference (Dirichlet Process / Dirichlet Distribution) | `'full'`, `'diag'`                          | Automatic pruning of redundant components when the true cluster count is unknown |

Both classes extend `ClusterBase`, support reproducible `randomState` seeds, multiple restarts (`nInit`), and full JSON serialization with `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Mixture, Datasets } from '@kanaries/ml';

const { X } = Datasets.makeBlobs({ nSamples: 150, centers: 3, clusterStd: 0.7, randomState: 42 });

const gmm = new Mixture.GaussianMixture({
  nComponents: 3,
  covarianceType: 'full',
  nInit: 3,
  randomState: 42,
});

gmm.fit(X);
const labels = gmm.predict(X);
const probs = gmm.predictProba(X);
const bic = gmm.bic(X);
```

## Choosing between GMM, Bayesian GMM, and K-Means

- Choose **[K-Means](/docs/apis/clusters/kmeans.md)** or **[E-Means](/docs/apis/clusters/eMeans.md)** when you want fast, spherical hard clustering on large vector sets.
- Choose **[GaussianMixture](/docs/apis/mixture/gaussian-mixture.md)** when clusters are elliptical or overlapping, you need log-densities (`scoreSamples`), or you plan to pick `nComponents` with `aic()` / `bic()`.
- Choose **[BayesianGaussianMixture](/docs/apis/mixture/bayesian-gaussian-mixture.md)** when you prefer to set an upper bound on `nComponents` and let variational priors shrink unused component weights toward zero automatically.
- **Related pages**: [GaussianMixture](/docs/apis/mixture/gaussian-mixture.md), [BayesianGaussianMixture](/docs/apis/mixture/bayesian-gaussian-mixture.md), [Clustering Algorithms](/docs/apis/clusters/index.html.md), [Kernel Density Estimation](/docs/apis/kernel/index.html.md).

---

<!-- Source: https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/multiclass -->

---
title: "Multiclass Wrappers (OvR & OvO) in JS"
description: "Turn any binary classifier into a multiclass model in JavaScript and TypeScript with OneVsRestClassifier and OneVsOneClassifier from @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/multiclass"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/multiclass/index.html.md"
---
# Multiclass Wrappers (OvR & OvO) in JS

## Algorithm overview

Many linear and margin-based classifiers are formulated naturally for binary classification (`0` vs `1`), or benefit from explicit decomposition when class boundaries differ sharply across pairs. **Multiclass meta-estimators** wrap any binary classifier and decompose a `K`-class problem into binary subproblems:

- **One-vs-Rest (`OneVsRestClassifier`)**: fits `K` binary classifiers—one per class against all remaining classes combined. At prediction time, picks the class with the highest continuous score (`predictProba` positive column, `decisionFunction`, or raw vote). Scales linearly (`K` models) and supports normalized `predictProba()`.
- **One-vs-One (`OneVsOneClassifier`)**: fits `K * (K - 1) / 2` binary classifiers—one for every unordered pair of classes `(i, j)` using only samples belonging to those two classes. Prediction counts pairwise votes and uses squashed confidence sums (`ovrDecisionFunction`) strictly as tie-breakers. Often trains faster than OvR for super-linear estimators like kernel SVMs when `K` is modest.

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides `Multiclass.OneVsRestClassifier`, `Multiclass.OneVsOneClassifier`, and the tie-breaking helper `Multiclass.ovrDecisionFunction` in pure TypeScript for browsers and Node.js.

Both wrappers extend `ClassifierBase`, clone the prototype estimator per subproblem without mutating it, support nested `estimator__param` addressing in `setParams()` (making them tunable inside `GridSearchCV` and [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md)), and serialize cleanly via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start example

### OneVsRestClassifier & OneVsOneClassifier: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.multiclass import OneVsRestClassifier, OneVsOneClassifier
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC

ovr = OneVsRestClassifier(LinearSVC(C=1.0))
ovr.fit(X_train, y_train)
ovr_preds = ovr.predict(X_test)

ovo = OneVsOneClassifier(LinearSVC(C=1.0))
ovo.fit(X_train, y_train)
ovo_preds = ovo.predict(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Multiclass, SVM } from '@kanaries/ml';

const ovr = new Multiclass.OneVsRestClassifier({
estimator: new SVM.LinearSVC({ C: 1.0 }),
});
ovr.fit(XTrain, yTrain);
const ovrPreds = ovr.predict(XTest);

const ovo = new Multiclass.OneVsOneClassifier({
estimator: new SVM.LinearSVC({ C: 1.0 }),
});
ovo.fit(XTrain, yTrain);
const ovoPreds = ovo.predict(XTest);

// Tune wrapped estimator hyperparameters via estimator__param
ovr.setParams({ estimator__C: 5.0 });
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Multiclass.OneVsRestClassifier(props)`

| Parameter   | Type            | Default    | Description                                                                                                               |
| ----------- | --------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `estimator` | `BaseEstimator` | *required* | Prototype classifier implementing `fit()` and `predict()`. One unfitted clone is fitted per unique class in sorted order. |

| Member                   | Signature                                                       | Description                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `fit`                    | `(X: number[][], y: number[], sampleWeight?: number[]) => void` | Fits `K` binary clones (`y === cls ? 1 : 0`). Requires at least 2 classes.                                                                                                                          |
| `predict`                | `(X: number[][]) => number[]`                                   | Returns the class with the highest member score (`predictProba` > `decisionFunction` > `predict`).                                                                                                  |
| `predictProba`           | `(X: number[][]) => number[][]`                                 | Normalizes each member's positive-class probability so rows sum to `1` (falls back to uniform `1/K` instead of `NaN` if a row sums to `0`). Requires wrapped members to implement `predictProba()`. |
| `decisionFunction`       | `(X: number[][]) => number[][]`                                 | Returns `[nSamples][nClasses]` matrix of member scores.                                                                                                                                             |
| `classes` / `estimators` | `number[]` / `ClassifierLike[]`                                 | Read-only getters returning sorted labels and fitted member clones.                                                                                                                                 |

### `new Multiclass.OneVsOneClassifier(props)`

| Parameter   | Type            | Default    | Description                                                                           |
| ----------- | --------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `estimator` | `BaseEstimator` | *required* | Prototype classifier cloned and fitted on every class pair `(cI, cJ)` with `cI < cJ`. |

| Member                   | Signature                                                       | Description                                                                                                                                                            |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `fit`                    | `(X: number[][], y: number[], sampleWeight?: number[]) => void` | Fits `K * (K - 1) / 2` pairwise clones on subsets belonging to each pair.                                                                                              |
| `predict`                | `(X: number[][]) => number[]`                                   | Counts pairwise votes with confidence tie-breaking (`ovrDecisionFunction`) that maps confidence sums into `(-1/3, 1/3)` so confidences never overturn a vote majority. |
| `decisionFunction`       | `(X: number[][]) => number[] \| number[][]`                     | Returns pairwise decision scores (`number[]` for 2 classes, `[nSamples][nClasses]` aggregated vote+confidence matrix for `K > 2`).                                     |
| `classes` / `estimators` | `number[]` / `ClassifierLike[]`                                 | Sorted class labels and fitted pairwise members in `(i, j)` order.                                                                                                     |

### OvR vs OvO decision guide

- Prefer **`OneVsRestClassifier`** when `K` is large (say `K > 10`), when you need `predictProba()`, or when training linear models that scale linearly in `nSamples`.
- Prefer **`OneVsOneClassifier`** for kernel SVMs (`SVC`) on datasets with many samples and a small-to-moderate number of classes, because each pairwise fit uses only a fraction of the rows.
- **Related pages**: [SVM Classifiers](/docs/apis/svm/index.html.md), [Probability Calibration](/docs/apis/calibration/index.html.md), [Multi-Output Chains](/docs/apis/multioutput/index.html.md), [ML Pipelines](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md).

---
title: "ClassifierChain in JavaScript and TypeScript"
description: "Model label dependencies in multi-label classification in JavaScript and TypeScript with MultiOutput.ClassifierChain from @kanaries/ml for browser and Node.js."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/multioutput/classifierChain"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/multioutput/classifierChain.md"
---
# ClassifierChain in JavaScript and TypeScript

## Algorithm overview

**ClassifierChain** solves multi-label binary classification (`Y` of shape `[nSamples][nLabels]`) while capturing correlations among output labels. Instead of fitting `L` completely isolated binary classifiers, it arranges the `L` labels in a sequence (`order`):

1. Classifier `0` predicts the first label from the original feature matrix `X`.
2. Classifier `1` receives `[X, label_0]` as input to predict the second label.
3. Classifier `k` receives `[X, label_0, ..., label_{k-1}]`, allowing co-occurrence and mutual-exclusion patterns across labels to directly inform later predictions.

During inference (`predict` / `predictProba`), each link feeds its predicted output forward down the chain. Setting `cv` (for example `cv: 3`) uses out-of-fold predictions rather than ground-truth labels during training, aligning training-time and test-time distributions.

## JavaScript implementation

`MultiOutput.ClassifierChain` accepts any registered single-output `@kanaries/ml` classifier (such as `Bayes.GaussianNB`, `Linear.LogisticRegression`, or `Tree.DecisionTreeClassifier`), runs synchronously in browsers and Node.js, supports explicit or `'random'` seeded ordering, and serializes via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Bayes, MultiOutput } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0], [1], [2]];
const testX = [[1.5]];
const chain = new MultiOutput.ClassifierChain({
  estimator: new Bayes.GaussianNB(),
  order: [0, 1],
});
chain.fit(X, [[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]]);
const labels = chain.predict(testX);
console.log(labels);
```

### ClassifierChain: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.multioutput import ClassifierChain
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB

chain = ClassifierChain(estimator=GaussianNB(), order=[0, 1], random_state=42)
chain.fit(X_train, Y_train)
preds = chain.predict(X_test)
proba = chain.predict_proba(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Bayes, MultiOutput } from '@kanaries/ml';

const chain = new MultiOutput.ClassifierChain({
estimator: new Bayes.GaussianNB(),
order: [0, 1],
randomState: 42,
});
chain.fit(XTrain, YTrain);
const preds = chain.predict(XTest);
const proba = chain.predictProba(XTest);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new MultiOutput.ClassifierChain(props)`

| Parameter     | Type                   | Default            | Description                                                                                                            |
| ------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `estimator`   | `ClassifierBase`       | *required*         | Prototype binary classifier cloned once per label in the chain.                                                        |
| `order`       | `number[] \| 'random'` | `[0, 1, ..., L-1]` | Explicit permutation of label indices or `'random'` for a shuffled chain order.                                        |
| `cv`          | `number \| null`       | `null`             | When set (`≥ 2`), generates out-of-fold predictions for upstream chain columns during `fit()` to reduce exposure bias. |
| `randomState` | `number`               | `undefined`        | Seed for `'random'` order and CV splits.                                                                               |

### Methods & properties

- `fit(X, Y)` / `predict(X)` / `predictProba(X)` (requires base estimator to implement `predictProba`) / `score(X, Y)` (exact-match subset accuracy).
- `chainOrder` and `estimators` return defensive copies of the resolved order and fitted members.
- **Related pages**: [RegressorChain](/docs/apis/multioutput/regressorChain.md), [Multi-Output Overview](/docs/apis/multioutput/index.html.md), [Multiclass Wrappers](/docs/apis/multiclass/index.html.md).

---
title: "Multi-Output Machine Learning in JavaScript"
description: "Predict multiple correlated binary labels or numeric targets in JavaScript and TypeScript using ClassifierChain and RegressorChain from @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/multioutput"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/multioutput/index.html.md"
---
# Multi-Output Machine Learning in JavaScript

## Module overview

Standard classifiers and regressors predict a single scalar target `y[i]` per observation. Many practical problems instead require predicting **multiple correlated outputs simultaneously**—such as multi-label tagging (assigning several topic tags to one article) or joint forecasting (predicting both `revenue` and `order_count` from the same customer features).

Fitting completely independent models per target ignores relationships *between* the targets themselves. **Chain meta-estimators** preserve those correlations by ordering targets into a sequence and feeding earlier target predictions forward as extra input features for subsequent models in the chain.

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides two scikit-learn-compatible chain wrappers under `import { MultiOutput } from '@kanaries/ml'` in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js runtimes:

| Estimator                                                                  | Target matrix `Y`                         | Base estimator            | Use case                                                                |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`MultiOutput.ClassifierChain`](/docs/apis/multioutput/classifierChain.md) | Binary `0/1` matrix `[nSamples][nLabels]` | Any registered classifier | Multi-label classification where labels co-occur or exclude one another |
| [`MultiOutput.RegressorChain`](/docs/apis/multioutput/regressorChain.md)   | Continuous matrix `[nSamples][nTargets]`  | Any registered regressor  | Multi-target regression where outputs share strong correlations         |

Both wrappers clone the prototype estimator safely, support explicit or seeded random target ordering (`order`), optionally use out-of-fold cross-validation (`cv`) to prevent target leakage while building augmented training columns, and serialize cleanly via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Bayes, MultiOutput } from '@kanaries/ml';

const chain = new MultiOutput.ClassifierChain({
  estimator: new Bayes.GaussianNB(),
  order: [0, 1],
});
chain.fit([[0], [1], [2]], [[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]]);
console.log(chain.predict([[1.5]]));
```

## Ordering and cross-validation guidance

- **Choosing `order`**: Place easier-to-predict or causally upstream targets first in the chain so downstream links receive cleaner features. When no natural causal order exists, set `order: 'random'` with a fixed `randomState` or compare multiple orders via cross-validation.
- **Enabling `cv`**: Setting `cv: 3` or `cv: 5` trains downstream links on out-of-fold upstream predictions instead of ground-truth targets, reducing train/inference mismatch.

## Related pages

- [ClassifierChain API Reference](/docs/apis/multioutput/classifierChain.md)
- [RegressorChain API Reference](/docs/apis/multioutput/regressorChain.md)
- [Multiclass Wrappers (`OneVsRest` / `OneVsOne`)](/docs/apis/multiclass/index.html.md)

---
title: "RegressorChain in JavaScript and TypeScript"
description: "Predict multiple correlated continuous targets in JavaScript and TypeScript with MultiOutput.RegressorChain from @kanaries/ml. Includes live playground."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/multioutput/regressorChain"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/multioutput/regressorChain.md"
---
# RegressorChain in JavaScript and TypeScript

## Algorithm overview

**RegressorChain** predicts multiple continuous targets (`Y` of shape `[nSamples][nTargets]`) simultaneously while modeling dependencies across outputs. Targets are arranged in a sequence (`order`): the first regressor predicts target `order[0]` from `X`, the second regressor predicts `order[1]` from `[X, target_0]`, and each subsequent regressor augments `X` with all preceding targets in the chain.

This design is especially valuable when outputs obey physical, financial, or temporal coupling—for example predicting both item demand and fulfillment cost, or multi-step horizon values where earlier predictions strongly inform later ones.

## JavaScript implementation

`MultiOutput.RegressorChain` wraps any registered single-output `@kanaries/ml` regressor in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js runtimes. Prefer regularized base learners like [`Linear.RidgeRegression`](/docs/apis/linear/ridgeRegression.md) when correlated target columns could introduce collinearity into augmented matrices. Setting `cv` uses out-of-fold predictions during training so downstream models adapt to realistic upstream prediction error. Fitted chains serialize via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Interactive regressor chain playground

Tune the Ridge base estimator and modify the dataset below. A two-output `MultiOutput.RegressorChain` is fitted live in your browser; the chart renders its first target while both outputs interact across the chain.

> The HTML version includes an interactive Regressor Chain playground powered by @kanaries/ml. You can change the dataset, noise, and model controls; add observations; and inspect live predictions plus train and holdout metrics. The runnable guide and API reference continue below. [Open the HTML page](https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/multioutput/regressorChain).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Linear, MultiOutput } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0], [1], [2], [3]];
const targets = [[0, 1], [1, 3], [2, 5], [3, 7]];
const testX = [[4]];
const chain = new MultiOutput.RegressorChain({
  estimator: new Linear.RidgeRegression({ alpha: 1 }),
  order: [1, 0],
});
chain.fit(X, targets);
const predictions = chain.predict(testX);
console.log(predictions);
```

### RegressorChain: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.multioutput import RegressorChain
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

chain = RegressorChain(estimator=Ridge(alpha=1.0), order=[1, 0], random_state=42)
chain.fit(X_train, Y_train)
preds = chain.predict(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Linear, MultiOutput } from '@kanaries/ml';

const chain = new MultiOutput.RegressorChain({
estimator: new Linear.RidgeRegression({ alpha: 1.0 }),
order: [1, 0],
randomState: 42,
});
chain.fit(XTrain, YTrain);
const preds = chain.predict(XTest);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new MultiOutput.RegressorChain(props)`

| Parameter     | Type                   | Default            | Description                                                               |
| ------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `estimator`   | `RegressorBase`        | *required*         | Prototype single-output regressor cloned for each target in the chain.    |
| `order`       | `number[] \| 'random'` | `[0, 1, ..., T-1]` | Order in which targets are predicted and appended as features.            |
| `cv`          | `number \| null`       | `null`             | Integer fold count (`≥ 2`) for out-of-fold upstream training predictions. |
| `randomState` | `number`               | `undefined`        | Seed for `'random'` chain order.                                          |

### Methods & properties

- `fit(X, Y)` / `predict(X)` / `score(X, Y)` (mean R² across all outputs).
- `chainOrder` and `estimators` expose defensive copies of the resolved order and fitted regressors.
- **Related pages**: [ClassifierChain](/docs/apis/multioutput/classifierChain.md), [Ridge Regression](/docs/apis/linear/ridgeRegression.md), [Multi-Output Overview](/docs/apis/multioutput/index.html.md).

---
title: "Ball Tree in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Learn what Ball Tree does, when to use it, and how to run BallTree in JavaScript or TypeScript with @kanaries/ml for browser and Node.js applications."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/ballTree"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/ballTree.md"
---
# Ball Tree in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

BallTree accelerates nearest-neighbor queries using hierarchical metric-space partitioning.

This algorithm is especially useful when:

- You run repeated k-nearest-neighbor lookups on static or slowly changing datasets.
- Brute-force distance scans are too slow at your scale.
- Your metric choice is compatible with tree-based neighbor search.

## JavaScript implementation

@kanaries/ml provides Ball Tree in JavaScript for repeated nearest-neighbor queries in retrieval, recommendation, and local-model workflows. This is useful when a JS application needs faster spatial lookup than brute force, especially if the same dataset will be queried many times.

Because the tree lives in the same runtime as your scoring or UI logic, you can build neighbor-based features and interactive search experiences without shipping requests to a Python service.

## Quick start

### BallTree: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.neighbors import BallTree

X = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [2, 2], [3, 3]]
tree = BallTree(X, leaf_size=2)

distances, indices = tree.query([[1.2, 1.1]], k=2)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Neighbors } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [2, 2], [3, 3]];
const tree = new Neighbors.BallTree(X, 2);

const { distances, indices } = tree.query([[1.2, 1.1]], 2);
```

### Quick JavaScript example

```ts
import { Neighbors } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [2, 2], [3, 3]];
const tree = new Neighbors.BallTree(X, 2);

const { distances, indices } = tree.query([[1.2, 1.1]], 2);
console.log(distances);
```

## Detailed API reference

```ts
constructor(
    X: number[][] = [],
    leafSize: number = 40,
    metric: Distance.IDistanceType = 'euclidean',
    p: number = 2
)
```

### Parameters

- `X` *(number\[]\[])*: training data used to build the tree. Can be provided at
  construction time or via `fit`.
- `leafSize` *(number)*: maximum number of points stored in a leaf. Default is
  `40`.
- `metric` *(Distance.IDistanceType)*: distance function for search. Defaults to
  `'euclidean'`.
- `p` *(number)*: norm order for Minkowski distance when applicable. Default is
  `2`.

### Algorithm

Ball tree organizes points in hyperspheres. Each node stores a centroid and
radius covering its children. During queries the tree is traversed to prune
branches that are farther than the currently found neighbors, leading to faster
neighbor search than a brute-force approach.

`query(X: number[][], k: number = 1)` returns distances and indices of nearest neighbors.

`queryRadius(X: number[][], r: number, returnDistance = false)` finds neighbors within given radius.

### Implementation workflow

1. Build the tree from normalized feature vectors.
2. Query nearest points for recommendation, retrieval, or local modeling.
3. Benchmark query latency and rebuild policy as data evolves.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Build the tree once and reuse it when the reference dataset changes slowly.
- Prefer Ball Tree for repeated query workloads rather than one-off nearest-neighbor calls.
- Benchmark query speed against brute force and KD Tree because the best structure depends on the data and metric.

title: "Nearest-Neighbor Algorithms in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Explore k-nearest neighbors, radius neighbors, centroid classifiers, Ball Tree, and KD Tree in JavaScript and TypeScript with @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/index.html.md"
---
# Nearest-Neighbor Algorithms in JavaScript

## Module overview

The Neighbors module supports instance-based learning and efficient nearest-neighbor search. It is useful for similarity tasks, recommendation flows, retrieval systems, and classifiers that reason directly from nearby examples instead of learning a compact parametric model.

This module is a strong fit when:

- prediction or ranking depends on nearby examples
- you need repeated nearest-neighbor queries over a relatively stable dataset
- you want to compare a simple KNN baseline with explicit search structures

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides nearest-neighbor algorithms in JavaScript and TypeScript so teams can keep indexing, lookup, and local prediction inside the same browser or Node.js runtime as the rest of the product logic. This is especially useful for recommendation tools, search experiences, and interactive similarity workflows that need low-friction integration with application code.

If someone searches for "k-nearest neighbors in JavaScript", "KD Tree in JavaScript", or "Ball Tree in TypeScript", this module is the right entry point.

## Quick navigation

- [k-Nearest Neighbors](/docs/apis/neighbors/knn.md): direct classification from nearby labeled examples
- [KNeighborsRegressor](/docs/apis/neighbors/kneighborsRegressor.md): numeric prediction from the nearest labeled examples
- [RadiusNeighborsClassifier](/docs/apis/neighbors/radiusNeighborsClassifier.md): classification from all examples inside a distance radius
- [RadiusNeighborsRegressor](/docs/apis/neighbors/radiusNeighborsRegressor.md): numeric prediction from all examples inside a distance radius
- [NearestCentroid](/docs/apis/neighbors/nearestCentroid.md): fast classification by closest class centroid
- [Ball Tree](/docs/apis/neighbors/ballTree.md): faster repeated nearest-neighbor search in metric spaces
- [KD Tree](/docs/apis/neighbors/kdTree.md): efficient spatial indexing for repeated lookup on suitable data
- [Local Outlier Factor](/docs/apis/neighbors/localOutlierFactor.md): density-based local anomaly detection and novelty scoring
- [NearestNeighbors](/docs/apis/neighbors/nearestNeighbors.md): unlabeled k-neighbor and radius lookup through brute force, KD Tree, or Ball Tree

## Detailed module guide

### How to choose an algorithm

1. Use [k-Nearest Neighbors](/docs/apis/neighbors/knn.md) when you want a direct non-parametric baseline.
2. Use [KNeighborsRegressor](/docs/apis/neighbors/kneighborsRegressor.md) or [RadiusNeighborsRegressor](/docs/apis/neighbors/radiusNeighborsRegressor.md) for continuous targets.
3. Use [RadiusNeighborsClassifier](/docs/apis/neighbors/radiusNeighborsClassifier.md) when a fixed physical or semantic radius matters more than fixed `k`.
4. Use [NearestCentroid](/docs/apis/neighbors/nearestCentroid.md) for a very fast linear-time classifier baseline.
5. Use [Ball Tree](/docs/apis/neighbors/ballTree.md) or [KD Tree](/docs/apis/neighbors/kdTree.md) when repeated query speed matters.
6. Use [Local Outlier Factor](/docs/apis/neighbors/localOutlierFactor.md) when anomalies are defined by unusually low local density.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Scale numeric features before distance-based prediction or lookup.
- Build tree-based indexes once and reuse them when the reference dataset changes slowly.
- Keep nearest-neighbor search close to the application layer when retrieval results immediately drive UI or product logic.

---
title: "KD Tree in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Learn what KD Tree does, when to use it, and how to run KDTree in JavaScript or TypeScript with @kanaries/ml for browser and Node.js applications."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/kdTree"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/kdTree.md"
---
# KD Tree in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

KDTree speeds up nearest-neighbor searches for low-to-medium dimensional numeric feature spaces.

This algorithm is especially useful when:

- You need many repeated neighbor lookups with Euclidean-like distances.
- Dataset dimensionality is not too high for kd-tree pruning to remain effective.
- You want faster KNN-style operations in JS services or browser apps.

## JavaScript implementation

@kanaries/ml exposes KD Tree in JavaScript for spatial indexing and repeated nearest-neighbor lookup in products that already operate in TypeScript. This is useful for search, recommendation, and geometry-heavy applications that want query acceleration without moving indexing logic out of the JS stack.

KD Tree is particularly practical when the data is reasonably low-dimensional and query latency matters more than one-time build cost.

## Quick start

### KDTree: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.neighbors import KDTree

X = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [2, 2], [3, 3]]
tree = KDTree(X, leaf_size=2)

distances, indices = tree.query([[1.2, 1.1]], k=2)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Neighbors } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [2, 2], [3, 3]];
const tree = new Neighbors.KDTree(X, 2);

const { distances, indices } = tree.query([[1.2, 1.1]], 2);
```

### Quick JavaScript example

```ts
import { Neighbors } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [2, 2], [3, 3]];
const tree = new Neighbors.KDTree(X, 2);

const { distances, indices } = tree.query([[1.2, 1.1]], 2);
console.log(distances);
```

## Detailed API reference

```ts
constructor(
    X: number[][] = [],
    leafSize: number = 40,
    metric: Distance.IDistanceType = 'euclidean',
    p: number = 2
)
```

### Parameters

- `X` *(number\[]\[])*: data used to build the tree. You can also call `fit` later.
- `leafSize` *(number)*: maximum samples per leaf. Default is `40`.
- `metric` *(Distance.IDistanceType)*: distance metric used for queries. Default
  `'euclidean'`.
- `p` *(number)*: order of the norm when using Minkowski distance. Default `2`.

### Algorithm

KD-tree recursively splits points by dimension. Each internal node stores a
split dimension and value and points to left and right subtrees. During search
the tree is pruned using bounding boxes to efficiently locate nearest
neighbors.

`query(X: number[][], k: number = 1)` returns distances and indices of nearest neighbors.

`queryRadius(X: number[][], r: number, returnDistance = false)` finds neighbors within given radius.

### Implementation workflow

1. Index feature vectors with KDTree construction.
2. Run neighbor queries and capture distances/indices.
3. Tune leaf/query parameters to balance speed and accuracy.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- KD Tree works best for repeated queries over relatively stable, lower-dimensional datasets.
- Compare it with Ball Tree when the metric or geometry of your data changes the pruning behavior.
- Keep the index close to the application that consumes it so lookup and follow-up logic stay in one runtime.

description: "Predict continuous targets from nearby examples in JavaScript and TypeScript with KNeighborsRegressor from @kanaries/ml. Includes live demo and API docs."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/kneighborsRegressor"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/kneighborsRegressor.md"

# KNeighborsRegressor in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml

## Algorithm overview

**KNeighborsRegressor (k-NN Regression)** is a non-parametric, instance-based regressor that predicts a query sample's continuous target by averaging the `y` values of its `nNeighbors` closest training observations. Rather than fitting a global algebraic equation, it adapts locally to arbitrary curves, step changes, and multi-modal surfaces.

Choosing between uniform and distance weighting controls local smoothness:

- **`weights: 'uniform'`**: every neighbor contributes equally (`1 / k`), smoothing out local measurement noise.
- **`weights: 'distance'`**: closer neighbors receive higher inverse-distance weight (`1 / d`), reducing bias near sharp transitions and reproducing exact training points.

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides `Neighbors.KNeighborsRegressor` in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js runtimes. Prefer the options-object constructor (`{ nNeighbors, weights, metric, p }`) over the deprecated positional form. It supports all distance metrics in `Metrics.Distance`, plugs into [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md), and serializes cleanly via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Interactive K-neighbors regression playground

Tune `k`, adjust sample density, and click to add new training observations. Every prediction comes from a live distance-weighted `Neighbors.KNeighborsRegressor` running in your browser.

> The HTML version includes an interactive K-Neighbors Regression playground powered by @kanaries/ml. You can change the dataset, noise, and model controls; add observations; and inspect live predictions plus train and holdout metrics. The runnable guide and API reference continue below. [Open the HTML page](https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/kneighborsRegressor).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Neighbors } from '@kanaries/ml';

const reg = new Neighbors.KNeighborsRegressor({ nNeighbors: 2, weights: 'distance' });
reg.fit([[0], [1], [3]], [0, 1, 3]);
const pred = reg.predict([[2]]);
console.log(pred);
```

### KNeighborsRegressor: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor

reg = KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=5, weights="distance", metric="euclidean")
reg.fit(X_train, y_train)
preds = reg.predict(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Neighbors } from '@kanaries/ml';

const reg = new Neighbors.KNeighborsRegressor({
nNeighbors: 5,
weights: 'distance',
metric: 'euclidean',
});
reg.fit(XTrain, yTrain);
const preds = reg.predict(XTest);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Neighbors.KNeighborsRegressor(props?)`

| Parameter    | Type                      | Default       | Description                                                                                                       |
| ------------ | ------------------------- | ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nNeighbors` | `number`                  | `5`           | Number of nearest neighbors averaged per prediction. Smaller values fit finer detail; larger values smooth noise. |
| `weights`    | `'uniform' \| 'distance'` | `'uniform'`   | Neighbor weighting scheme.                                                                                        |
| `metric`     | `Distance.IDistanceType`  | `'euclidean'` | Distance metric (`'euclidean'`, `'manhattan'`, `'minkowski'`, `'cosine'`, etc.).                                  |
| `p`          | `number`                  | `2`           | Order parameter when `metric: 'minkowski'` (`1` = Manhattan, `2` = Euclidean).                                    |

### Methods & practical guidance

- `fit(trainX: number[][], trainY: number[]): void` — stores the reference training set.
- `predict(testX: number[][]): number[]` — computes weighted neighbor averages for each query row.
- **Feature scaling is mandatory**: Wrap `StandardScaler` and `KNeighborsRegressor` inside a [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md) so large-magnitude columns do not dominate distance calculations.
- **Related pages**: [K-Nearest Neighbors Classifier](/docs/apis/neighbors/knn.md), [RadiusNeighborsRegressor](/docs/apis/neighbors/radiusNeighborsRegressor.md), [KNN Playground](/playground/knn).

title: "k-Nearest Neighbors in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Classify data with k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) in JavaScript and TypeScript using @kanaries/ml. Includes distance metrics, sklearn comparison, and API docs."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/knn"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/knn.md"
---
# k-Nearest Neighbors in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

KNearestNeighbors predicts from nearby examples and works as a strong non-parametric baseline for classification and regression.

This algorithm is especially useful when:

- Decision boundaries are irregular and hard to model parametrically.
- You need straightforward behavior that is easy to reason about.
- Training time should be minimal and inference latency is acceptable.

## JavaScript implementation

@kanaries/ml makes k-nearest neighbors available in JavaScript for recommendation logic, local classification, and quick non-parametric baselines. This is a strong fit when the model should stay close to application code and when teams want behavior that is easy to inspect because predictions come directly from nearby examples.

In web products, KNN is often useful for prototypes and medium-sized datasets where it is more important to stay flexible than to train a compact parametric model.

## Quick start

### KNearestNeighbors: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

X = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [1, 0], [0, 1]]
y = [0, 1, 1, 0]

clf = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3, weights='distance')
clf.fit(X, y)
pred = clf.predict([[0.9, 0.8], [0.2, 0.1]])
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Neighbors } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [1, 0], [0, 1]];
const y = [0, 1, 1, 0];

const clf = new Neighbors.KNeighborsClassifier({
kNeighbors: 3,
weightType: 'distance',
});
clf.fit(X, y);
const pred = clf.predict([[0.9, 0.8], [0.2, 0.1]]);
```

### Quick JavaScript example

```ts
import { Neighbors } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [1, 0], [0, 1]];
const y = [0, 1, 1, 0];

const clf = new Neighbors.KNeighborsClassifier({
  kNeighbors: 3,
  weightType: 'distance',
  distanceType: 'euclidean',
});
clf.fit(X, y);
const pred = clf.predict([[0.9, 0.8], [0.2, 0.1]]);
console.log(pred);
```

`Neighbors.KNeighborsClassifier` and `Neighbors.KNearestNeighbors` reference the exact same class; `KNearstNeighbors` remains as a deprecated compatibility alias. Explore decision boundaries interactively in the [KNN Playground](/playground/knn).

## Detailed API reference

```ts
new Neighbors.KNeighborsClassifier(props?: {
  kNeighbors?: number;                   // default: 5
  weightType?: 'uniform' | 'distance';   // default: 'uniform'
  distanceType?: Distance.IDistanceType; // default: 'euclidean'
  pNorm?: number;                        // default: 2 (Minkowski)
})
```

*(Legacy positional calls `new Neighbors.KNearestNeighbors(3, 'distance')` remain supported for backward compatibility, but prefer the options object.)*

### Parameters

- `kNeighbors` *(number)*: number of neighbors used for prediction. Default is `5`.
- `weightType` *(`'uniform' | 'distance'`)*: weighting strategy for voting. `'uniform'`
  counts every neighbor equally while `'distance'` weighs closer samples more.
- `distanceType` *(Distance.IDistanceType)*: distance metric. Defaults to
  `'euclidean'` but other metrics from `Distance` can be used.
- `pNorm` *(number)*: order of the norm when using Minkowski distance. Default is
  `2`.

### Algorithm

KNN is a lazy classifier. During prediction it computes the distance between the
query sample and all training points. The closest `kNeighbors` points vote for
the label. Voting can be uniform or weighted by inverse distance depending on
`weightType`.

### Implementation workflow

1. Scale numeric features and choose a distance metric.
2. Fit on labeled examples and test multiple `k` values.
3. Validate accuracy/latency tradeoffs before deployment.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Scale numeric features before distance-based prediction so no single dimension dominates.
- Use KNN when you want a simple, inspectable baseline and can afford query-time distance calculations.
- Consider pairing it with Ball Tree or KD Tree if nearest-neighbor lookup becomes a bottleneck.

title: "Local Outlier Factor in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Detect density-based local anomalies and novelties in JavaScript and TypeScript with Neighbors.LocalOutlierFactor from @kanaries/ml for browser and Node.js."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/localOutlierFactor"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/localOutlierFactor.md"
---
# Local Outlier Factor in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml

## Algorithm overview

**Local Outlier Factor (LOF)** is an unsupervised anomaly-detection algorithm that compares each sample's **local reachability density** against the densities of its `nNeighbors` nearest neighbors. Points residing in a region substantially sparser than their immediate neighborhood receive a high LOF ratio (strongly negative `negativeOutlierFactor`) and are flagged as outliers (`-1`).

LOF solves a classic failure mode of global anomaly detectors: when a dataset contains **multiple clusters of different densities** (for example, one tightly packed urban cluster and one broad rural cluster), global distance thresholds either miss anomalies hovering near the dense cluster or falsely flag normal points inside the sparse cluster. Because LOF normalizes every point relative to its *local* neighborhood, it catches both cleanly.

## JavaScript implementation

`Neighbors.LocalOutlierFactor` runs in pure TypeScript across browsers and Node.js and mirrors scikit-learn's two explicit operating modes:

- **Outlier detection (`novelty: false`, default)**: call `fitPredict(X)` to flag anomalies inside the training batch itself (`1` = inlier, `-1` = outlier).
- **Novelty detection (`novelty: true`)**: call `fit(XClean)` on normal data, then call `predict(XNew)`, `decisionFunction(XNew)`, or `scoreSamples(XNew)` on unseen production rows—and serialize the fitted detector with `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Neighbors } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[0, 0], [0.1, 0.2], [0.2, 0.1], [1, 1], [8, 8]];
const labels = new Neighbors.LocalOutlierFactor({
  nNeighbors: 2,
  contamination: 0.2,
}).fitPredict(X);

const novelty = new Neighbors.LocalOutlierFactor({ nNeighbors: 2, novelty: true });
novelty.fit(X);
console.log({ labels, noveltyPreds: novelty.predict([[0.15, 0.1], [20, 20]]) });
```

### LocalOutlierFactor (LOF): Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor

# Batch outlier detection
lof = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20, contamination=0.05)
labels = lof.fit_predict(X)  # 1 = inlier, -1 = outlier

# Novelty detection on unseen data
nov = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20, novelty=True).fit(X_train)
new_labels = nov.predict(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Neighbors } from '@kanaries/ml';

// Batch outlier detection
const lof = new Neighbors.LocalOutlierFactor({ nNeighbors: 20, contamination: 0.05 });
const labels = lof.fitPredict(X); // 1 = inlier, -1 = outlier

// Novelty detection on unseen data
const nov = new Neighbors.LocalOutlierFactor({ nNeighbors: 20, novelty: true });
nov.fit(XTrain);
const newLabels = nov.predict(XTest);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Neighbors.LocalOutlierFactor(props?)`

| Parameter       | Type               | Default  | Description                                                                                                                  |
| --------------- | ------------------ | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nNeighbors`    | `number`           | `20`     | Neighborhood size used to estimate local density (must be smaller than `X.length`).                                          |
| `contamination` | `number \| 'auto'` | `'auto'` | Expected outlier fraction in `(0, 0.5]`, or `'auto'` (uses offset `-1.5` matching scikit-learn).                             |
| `novelty`       | `boolean`          | `false`  | `false` enables `fitPredict(X)` only; `true` enables `fit(X)` + `predict` / `decisionFunction` / `scoreSamples` on new rows. |

### Methods & properties

- `fitPredict(X)` (`novelty: false`) — returns `1` (inlier) and `-1` (outlier); read `negativeOutlierFactor` (values near `-1` are normal; values much smaller than `-1` are outliers).
- `fit(X)` / `scoreSamples(X)` / `decisionFunction(X)` / `predict(X)` (`novelty: true`) — scores unseen observations against `offset`.
- **Related pages**: [Isolation Forest](/docs/apis/ensemble/iforest.md), [EllipticEnvelope](/docs/apis/covariance/ellipticEnvelope.md), [Outlier Methods Comparison Guide](/docs/guides/outlier-methods.md).

title: "NearestCentroid in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"

markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/nearestCentroid.md"
---
# NearestCentroid in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml

## Algorithm overview

**NearestCentroid** (also known as the **Rocchio classifier** in information retrieval) summarizes each training class by a single prototype vector—the **centroid** (mean) of its samples—and assigns every test observation to the class whose centroid lies closest under the chosen distance metric.

Because prediction only computes distances against `K` class centroids instead of all `N` training samples, `NearestCentroid` offers `O(K * d)` inference time and tiny memory footprints—orders of magnitude faster than full [k-Nearest Neighbors](/docs/apis/neighbors/knn.md) when `N` is large and classes form well-separated convex groups.

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides `Neighbors.NearestCentroid` in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js applications. It supports all distance metrics in `Metrics.Distance` (including `'euclidean'`, `'manhattan'`, `'cosine'`, and Minkowski `p`), composes inside [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md), and serializes into compact JSON payloads via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Neighbors } from '@kanaries/ml';

const clf = new Neighbors.NearestCentroid({ metric: 'euclidean' });
clf.fit([[0, 0], [0, 1], [4, 4], [5, 4]], [0, 0, 1, 1]);
const pred = clf.predict([[1, 1], [4, 5]]);
console.log(pred);
```

### NearestCentroid: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestCentroid

clf = NearestCentroid(metric="euclidean")
clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
preds = clf.predict(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Neighbors } from '@kanaries/ml';

const clf = new Neighbors.NearestCentroid({ metric: 'euclidean' });
clf.fit(XTrain, yTrain);
const preds = clf.predict(XTest);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Neighbors.NearestCentroid(props?)`

| Parameter | Type                     | Default       | Description                                                                                                                      |
| --------- | ------------------------ | ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `metric`  | `Distance.IDistanceType` | `'euclidean'` | Distance function measuring proximity to each class centroid (`'cosine'` works well for normalized TF-IDF or embedding vectors). |
| `p`       | `number`                 | `2`           | Minkowski power parameter when `metric: 'minkowski'`.                                                                            |

### Methods & limitations

- `fit(trainX: number[][], trainY: number[]): void` — computes one centroid vector per unique numeric class label.
- `predict(testX: number[][]): number[]` — returns the label of the nearest centroid (ties resolve to the numerically smaller class label).
- **When to upgrade**: Because `NearestCentroid` assumes spherical, equal-variance classes, it struggles when classes differ in variance or have non-convex shapes. Compare against [`DiscriminantAnalysis.LDA`](/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/lda.md), [`DiscriminantAnalysis.QDA`](/docs/apis/discriminant-analysis/qda.md), or [`Neighbors.KNearestNeighbors`](/docs/apis/neighbors/knn.md).

---
title: "NearestNeighbors Search in JavaScript"
description: "Run unsupervised k-nearest and radius neighbor queries with brute-force, KDTree, or BallTree in JavaScript and TypeScript using @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/nearestNeighbors"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/nearestNeighbors.md"
---
# NearestNeighbors Search in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

**Unsupervised Nearest Neighbors (`NearestNeighbors`)** indexes a reference dataset without target labels and answers two foundational spatial queries:

- **`kneighbors(X, nNeighbors)`**: returns the `k` closest points and their sorted distances for every query vector (or each training point's nearest *other* neighbors when `X` is omitted).
- **`radiusNeighbors(X, radius)`**: returns every reference sample lying within a fixed distance cutoff `radius`.

It powers similarity search, client-side embedding lookup, near-duplicate detection, DBSCAN `eps` knee-plot estimation, and graph construction for manifold learning.

## JavaScript implementation

`Neighbors.NearestNeighbors` in `@kanaries/ml` provides scikit-learn's `fit`, `kneighbors`, and `radiusNeighbors` API in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js environments. You can pick `'brute'`, `'kdTree'`, `'ballTree'`, or `'auto'` indexing; when serialized with `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md), only the reference matrix and parameters are stored and spatial trees rebuild safely on load.

## Quick start

```ts
import { Neighbors } from '@kanaries/ml';

const search = new Neighbors.NearestNeighbors({
  nNeighbors: 2,
  algorithm: 'kdTree',
});
search.fit([[0], [2], [5]]);

console.log(search.kneighbors([[1]]));
// { distances: [[1, 1]], indices: [[0, 1]] }
```

### NearestNeighbors: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=3, algorithm="kd_tree", metric="euclidean")
nn.fit(X_ref)
distances, indices = nn.kneighbors(X_query)
r_dist, r_idx = nn.radius_neighbors(X_query, radius=1.5)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Neighbors } from '@kanaries/ml';

const nn = new Neighbors.NearestNeighbors({
nNeighbors: 3,
algorithm: 'kdTree',
metric: 'euclidean',
});
nn.fit(XRef);
const { distances, indices } = nn.kneighbors(XQuery);
const withinRadius = nn.radiusNeighbors(XQuery, 1.5);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Neighbors.NearestNeighbors(props?)`

| Parameter      | Type                                          | Default             | Description                                                                                                                                                  |
| -------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `nNeighbors`   | `number`                                      | `5`                 | Default number of neighbors returned by `kneighbors()`.                                                                                                      |
| `radius`       | `number`                                      | `1.0`               | Default distance threshold used by `radiusNeighbors()`.                                                                                                      |
| `algorithm`    | `'auto' \| 'brute' \| 'kdTree' \| 'ballTree'` | `'auto'`            | Spatial search backend (`kdTree` shines in low dimensions `d ≤ 15`; `ballTree` handles general metrics; `brute` is fastest in high dimensions or small `n`). |
| `leafSize`     | `number`                                      | `30`                | Leaf bucket size for `kdTree` and `ballTree`.                                                                                                                |
| `metric` / `p` | `Distance.IDistanceType` / `number`           | `'euclidean'` / `2` | Distance metric and Minkowski order.                                                                                                                         |

### Methods

- `fit(X: number[][]): void` — stores the reference dataset and prepares the chosen spatial structure.
- `kneighbors(X?, nNeighbors?, returnDistance?)` — returns `{ distances, indices }` (or `indices` alone when `returnDistance: false`). Omitting `X` queries each training sample against all *other* training points.
- `radiusNeighbors(X?, radius?, returnDistance?)` — returns neighbors within `radius` for each query point.
- **Related pages**: [KDTree](/docs/apis/neighbors/kdTree.md), [BallTree](/docs/apis/neighbors/ballTree.md), [LocalOutlierFactor](/docs/apis/neighbors/localOutlierFactor.md).

---
title: "RadiusNeighborsClassifier in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml"
description: "Classify observations using all neighbors within a fixed radius in JavaScript and TypeScript with Neighbors.RadiusNeighborsClassifier from @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/radiusNeighborsClassifier"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/radiusNeighborsClassifier.md"
---
# RadiusNeighborsClassifier in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml

## Algorithm overview

**RadiusNeighborsClassifier** is a non-parametric classifier that predicts a query point's class by voting across **every training observation within a fixed distance `radius`**, rather than always pulling a fixed count `k` of neighbors.

This distinction matters in unevenly sampled feature spaces:

- In **dense regions**, radius search automatically averages over more nearby evidence for lower variance.
- In **sparse or out-of-distribution regions**, standard k-NN forces votes from distant, unrelated points—whereas `RadiusNeighborsClassifier` recognizes that no neighbors lie within `radius` and explicitly returns your configured `outlierLabel` (or throws an error so your app can flag an unknown input).

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides `Neighbors.RadiusNeighborsClassifier` in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js apps with `'uniform'` or `'distance'` voting, configurable `Metrics.Distance` metrics, explicit `outlierLabel` handling, [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md) support, and JSON persistence via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Neighbors } from '@kanaries/ml';

const clf = new Neighbors.RadiusNeighborsClassifier({
  radius: 1.5,
  weights: 'uniform',
  outlierLabel: -1,
});

clf.fit([[0], [1], [4]], [0, 0, 1]);
const pred = clf.predict([[0.5], [10]]);
console.log(pred); // [0, -1]
```

### RadiusNeighborsClassifier: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.neighbors import RadiusNeighborsClassifier

clf = RadiusNeighborsClassifier(radius=1.5, weights="distance", outlier_label=-1)
clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
preds = clf.predict(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Neighbors } from '@kanaries/ml';

const clf = new Neighbors.RadiusNeighborsClassifier({
radius: 1.5,
weights: 'distance',
outlierLabel: -1,
});
clf.fit(XTrain, yTrain);
const preds = clf.predict(XTest);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Neighbors.RadiusNeighborsClassifier(props?)`

| Parameter      | Type                                | Default             | Description                                                                                                                  |
| -------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `radius`       | `number`                            | `1.0`               | Maximum distance defining the local voting neighborhood.                                                                     |
| `weights`      | `'uniform' \| 'distance'`           | `'uniform'`         | Equal vote per neighbor or inverse-distance weighting.                                                                       |
| `metric` / `p` | `Distance.IDistanceType` / `number` | `'euclidean'` / `2` | Distance metric and Minkowski order.                                                                                         |
| `outlierLabel` | `number \| null`                    | `null`              | Fallback class returned when zero neighbors fall within `radius`. If `null`, `predict()` throws an error on isolated points. |

### Methods & tuning tips

- `fit(trainX, trainY)` / `predict(testX)` — always standardize numeric features with [`StandardScaler`](/docs/apis/utils/preprocessing.md) first so `radius` has consistent scale across dimensions.
- **Related pages**: [RadiusNeighborsRegressor](/docs/apis/neighbors/radiusNeighborsRegressor.md), [K-Nearest Neighbors](/docs/apis/neighbors/knn.md), [NearestNeighbors](/docs/apis/neighbors/nearestNeighbors.md).

description: "Predict numeric targets from neighbors inside a fixed radius in JavaScript and TypeScript with Neighbors.RadiusNeighborsRegressor from @kanaries/ml."
canonical_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/radiusNeighborsRegressor"
markdown_url: "https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/radiusNeighborsRegressor.md"
---
# RadiusNeighborsRegressor in JavaScript with @kanaries/ml

## Algorithm overview

**RadiusNeighborsRegressor** predicts a query sample's continuous target by averaging (uniformly or by inverse distance) all training observations within a fixed `radius` of the query. Unlike [`KNeighborsRegressor`](/docs/apis/neighbors/kneighborsRegressor.md), which always averages `k` points no matter how far away they sit, radius regression refuses to average over distant unrelated observations—returning `Number.NaN` wherever a query falls in an empty gap of the feature space.

This makes `RadiusNeighborsRegressor` ideal for spatial interpolation, physical sensor lookup tables, and uneven tabular regions where you want local smoothing inside dense clusters and explicit `NaN` uncertainty markers outside known coverage.

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides `Neighbors.RadiusNeighborsRegressor` in pure TypeScript for browser and Node.js applications, supporting `'uniform'` and `'distance'` weighting, all `Metrics.Distance` metrics, [`Pipeline`](/docs/apis/pipeline/index.html.md) composition, and JSON serialization via `toJSON()` / [`loadModel()`](/docs/apis/serialization/index.html.md).

## Interactive radius-neighbors regression playground

Change the neighborhood radius to see which points contribute at each x coordinate. The curve is fitted live with `Neighbors.RadiusNeighborsRegressor`; gaps indicate regions where no training observation falls within `radius`.

> The HTML version includes an interactive Radius-Neighbors Regression playground powered by @kanaries/ml. You can change the dataset, noise, and model controls; add observations; and inspect live predictions plus train and holdout metrics. The runnable guide and API reference continue below. [Open the HTML page](https://ml.kanaries.net/docs/apis/neighbors/radiusNeighborsRegressor).

## Quick start example

```ts
import { Neighbors } from '@kanaries/ml';

const reg = new Neighbors.RadiusNeighborsRegressor({ radius: 1.25, weights: 'distance' });
reg.fit([[0], [1], [4]], [0, 1, 4]);
const pred = reg.predict([[0.5], [10]]);
console.log(pred); // [0.5, NaN]
```

### RadiusNeighborsRegressor: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.neighbors import RadiusNeighborsRegressor

reg = RadiusNeighborsRegressor(radius=1.25, weights="distance")
reg.fit(X_train, y_train)
preds = reg.predict(X_test)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { Neighbors } from '@kanaries/ml';

const reg = new Neighbors.RadiusNeighborsRegressor({
radius: 1.25,
weights: 'distance',
});
reg.fit(XTrain, yTrain);
const preds = reg.predict(XTest);
```

## Detailed API reference

### `new Neighbors.RadiusNeighborsRegressor(props?)`

| Parameter      | Type                                | Default             | Description                                                                      |
| -------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `radius`       | `number`                            | `1.0`               | Neighborhood radius for selecting contributing training points.                  |
| `weights`      | `'uniform' \| 'distance'`           | `'uniform'`         | Equal average (`'uniform'`) or inverse-distance weighted average (`'distance'`). |
| `metric` / `p` | `Distance.IDistanceType` / `number` | `'euclidean'` / `2` | Distance metric and Minkowski exponent.                                          |

### Methods & practical tips

- `fit(trainX, trainY)` / `predict(testX)` — check `Number.isNaN(pred)` when handling out-of-coverage queries in production UIs.
- Always scale features with [`StandardScaler`](/docs/apis/utils/preprocessing.md) so a single scalar `radius` treats every dimension evenly.
- **Related pages**: [KNeighborsRegressor](/docs/apis/neighbors/kneighborsRegressor.md), [RadiusNeighborsClassifier](/docs/apis/neighbors/radiusNeighborsClassifier.md), [NearestNeighbors](/docs/apis/neighbors/nearestNeighbors.md).

# Bernoulli RBM in JavaScript

## Algorithm overview

BernoulliRBM learns latent binary representations that can improve downstream supervised model quality.

This algorithm is especially useful when:

- You work with binary-valued or binarized feature inputs.
- Feature learning can improve separability for a later classifier.
- You need compact latent features in a JavaScript pipeline.

## JavaScript implementation

@kanaries/ml provides Bernoulli RBM in JavaScript for feature learning workflows where latent binary representations are useful before a downstream classifier or recommender. This is relevant for experimentation-heavy products and Node.js pipelines that want learned hidden features without leaving TypeScript.

Because RBMs are usually part of a broader preprocessing or exploration pipeline, keeping them in JS makes it easier to chain transformation, visualization, and downstream modeling in one place.

## Quick start

### BernoulliRBM: Python and JavaScript / TypeScript

The Python example uses scikit-learn; the TypeScript example uses @kanaries/ml in browser or Node.js runtimes.

#### Python (scikit-learn)

```python
from sklearn.neural_network import BernoulliRBM

X = [[1, 0, 1], [1, 1, 0], [0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1]]

rbm = BernoulliRBM(n_components=2, learning_rate=0.1, batch_size=2, n_iter=20, random_state=0)
hidden = rbm.fit_transform(X)
```

#### JavaScript / TypeScript (@kanaries/ml)

```ts
import { NeuralNetwork } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[1, 0, 1], [1, 1, 0], [0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1]];

const rbm = new NeuralNetwork.BernoulliRBM({ nComponents: 2, learningRate: 0.1, batchSize: 2, nIter: 20 });
const hidden = rbm.fitTransform(X);
```

### Quick JavaScript example

```ts
import { NeuralNetwork } from '@kanaries/ml';

const X = [[1, 0, 1], [1, 1, 0], [0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1]];

const rbm = new NeuralNetwork.BernoulliRBM({ nComponents: 2, learningRate: 0.1, batchSize: 2, nIter: 20 });
const hidden = rbm.fitTransform(X);
console.log(hidden);
```

## Detailed API reference

```ts
constructor(
    nComponents: number = 256,
    learningRate: number = 0.1,
    batchSize: number = 10,
    nIter: number = 10
)
```

A Restricted Boltzmann Machine with binary visible units and hidden units. The model is trained with contrastive divergence.

### Methods

- `fit(X: number[][]): void`
- `partialFit(X: number[][]): void`
- `transform(X: number[][]): number[][]`
- `fitTransform(X: number[][]): number[][]`
- `gibbs(V: number[][]): number[][]`

### Implementation workflow

1. Prepare binary feature matrix and configure hidden-unit size.
2. Fit RBM and generate transformed latent representations.
3. Train downstream models on latent features and compare lift.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Use Bernoulli RBM when your inputs are binary or can be meaningfully binarized.
- Treat it as a representation-learning step and compare downstream lift against raw features.
- For frontend demos or educational tools, keep datasets modest because iterative training can still be expensive.

# Lightweight Neural Models in JavaScript

## Module overview

The Neural Network module currently focuses on lightweight representation learning rather than full deep learning stacks. It is useful when you want to learn latent features inside a JavaScript pipeline and then feed those features into downstream models or visual workflows.

This module is a strong fit when:

- your data can benefit from compact learned representations
- you want a JS-native feature-learning step before a classifier or regressor
- you are building experimentation or educational workflows around latent features

## JavaScript implementation

`@kanaries/ml` provides lightweight neural feature-learning utilities in JavaScript and TypeScript so teams can keep representation learning close to the rest of the application stack. This is especially useful when transformed features need to flow directly into additional JS models, UI-driven exploration, or Node.js preprocessing stages.

If someone searches for "Bernoulli RBM in JavaScript" or "feature learning in TypeScript", this module is the right entry point.

## Quick navigation

- [Bernoulli RBM](/docs/apis/neural_network/bernoulliRBM.md): learn latent binary features from binary or binarized inputs

## Detailed module guide

### How to choose an algorithm

1. Start with [Bernoulli RBM](/docs/apis/neural_network/bernoulliRBM.md) when your inputs are binary or can be meaningfully binarized.
2. Use the learned features as an experimental preprocessing step before downstream classifiers or regressors.
3. Compare downstream lift against raw features before adopting the representation in production.

### JavaScript deployment notes

- Keep datasets moderate in size when running iterative representation learning in the browser.
- Use this module mainly for preprocessing, feature learning, and experimentation rather than as a complete neural stack.
- Pair learned features with simpler downstream estimators when you want the rest of the pipeline to remain easy to operate.
